abstract_original: Proteins can adopt intricate three-dimensional structures, including complex topologies such as knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and even more complex structures. These entangled architectures challenge traditional views of protein folding and stability, suggesting that nature may use topological complexity as a mechanism to fine-tune function, regulation, or mechanical resilience. Despite growing structural data, the evolutionary origins and functional consequences of these nontrivial topologies remain largely unexplored. This project aims to leverage existing databases to identify the evolutionary turning points at which topological changes first arose within protein families. By integrating sequence, structural, and phylogenetic data from resources such as UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold, AlphaKnot, and AlphaLasso, we will reconstruct annotated phylogenetic trees that map the emergence and diversification of entangled proteins across evolutionary time. We will analyze whether specific sequence motifs, disulfide patterns, or intrinsically disordered regions are associated with the onset of entanglement, and whether such proteins are enriched in pathogenic or stress-adapted organisms. Furthermore, we will assess how topological complexity correlates with functional hotspots, including catalytic or allosteric regions, to reveal possible adaptive advantages. This work will establish a framework to trace, predict, and design protein topologies with distinct structural and functional characteristics. The outcomes will not only deepen our understanding of how topology shapes evolution and biomolecular behavior but also provide an open, data-driven platform for studying entanglement as a functional and evolutionary principle in protein science.

title: Deciphering systemic biological networks through AI-driven multi-omic integration
title_norm: deciphering systemic biological networks through aidriven multiomic integration
abstract_text: The research domain of organismal physiology examines multi organ communication networks that coordinate systemic adaptation, yet previous studies predominantly examine the single organ level or rely on heterogeneous datasets that reduce biological accuracy. The molecular structure, directionality, and temporal regulation of inter organ signaling remain uncharacterized at the whole organism level, preventing the construction of interpretable multi organ network models. Addressing the primary objective to map inter organ molecular networks, this project will build a computational model simulating biological responses by integrating longitudinal data through principal component analysis, a reaction diffusion graph network, and physics informed neural networks. The project will integrate multi omic data from eighteen solid tissues of exercising rats in the public MoTrPAC dataset vertically across omic layers and horizontally across organs using graph Laplacian operators and neural networks. The resulting computational model will identify predictors of phenotypic adaptation and simulate multi organ communication to predict system level physiological regulation, direct future experiments, and reduce animal testing.
full_text: This project studies organismal physiology because the molecular structure and temporal regulation of multi organ communication networks remain uncharacterized. Previous studies of communication focus on single organ systems while existing multi organ models lack accuracy and interpretability. The proposed study maps molecular networks to simulate biological responses for predicting physiological regulation and reducing animal testing. The research strategy integrates longitudinal multi organ data using a mathematical framework to model temporal and spatial dynamics. Key analytical tools include principal component analysis alongside graph Laplacian operators and neural networks with physics informed loss. The team will validate computational predictions of genomic states through an iterative testing process using in vivo experiments. This project utilizes the publicly available MoTrPAC dataset containing comprehensive omic measurements from eighteen solid tissues of rats. Data integration occurs vertically across omic layers and horizontally across organs using graph Laplacian operators and neural networks. The team manages dataset heterogeneity by using matched subjects while mitigating sparse data volume via a hybrid model. First year milestones include initial data integration and grant submission while second year goals involve mapping complete networks. Constructing models from large scale datasets necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration between the lead biologist and machine learning specialists. The proposed research team features a lead biology investigator alongside required specialists in bioinformatics and computational data science. This collaborative group incorporates artificial intelligence professionals and may receive supplementary assistance from the dedicated institutional support staff.

abstract_original: Organ cross-talk refers to the bidirectional communication between different organs that enables the body to maintain physiological homeostasis, respond and adapt during dynamic states. Disturbances to these inter-organ communication networks may result in inappropriate physiological responses, thereby compromising systemic function. This proposal will leverage a unique publicly available large-scale, multi-organ, multi-omic dataset comprising 18 solid tissues from rats subjected to an endurance exercise training program. Our hypothesis is that organ-specific signaling hierarchies will determines the coordinated multiorgan responses that drive systemic adaptation. Following organ-specific multi-omic vertical integration, we will determine 1) the predictors of phenotypic adaptations, and 2) the cross talk between organs via horizontal integration. The computed networks will provide the foundation to generate a digital twin rat which will serve as a valuable tool to model organismal responses to physiological, environmental and pharmacological challenges. This comprehensive, temporally resolved analysis will offer unprecedented insights into how molecular interactions are coordinated across organs and levels of organization to determine whole-organism physiological function.

title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
title_norm: conserved disorder learning sequence conservation from functional constraints in intrinsically disordered regions
abstract_text: The fields of protein biophysics and bioinformatics investigate evolutionary conservation patterns in intrinsically disordered regions, which contain sequence features like short linear motifs and charge patterning that encode vital molecular functions. This project will define conserved intrinsically disordered regions by integrating human and viral proteomic data through AIUpred disorder prediction, explicit solvent all atom molecular dynamics simulations, sequence descriptors over moving windows, and machine learning. The study will integrate UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif, IDRome, MaveDB, and GISAID databases by filtering sequences for disorder thresholds and cross referencing them with deep mutational scanning and post translational modification data. This research will provide a unified map of conserved disordered regions, establishing essential baselines for functional annotation and creating reference points for future sequence alignments and comparative analyses.
full_text: This protein biophysics and bioinformatics project investigates how evolutionary sequence variations of intrinsically disordered regions encode functional specificity. Subsets of intrinsically disordered regions contain functional motifs but current annotations favor folded protein domains over these flexible segments. The team asks how sequence features generate conserved functions to establish reference points for analyzing the disordered proteome. The core strategy integrates evolutionary and structural data across human and viral proteomes to identify patterns of functional conservation. Key methods include structural predictions using the AIUpred algorithm and explicit solvent molecular dynamics simulations alongside machine learning models. The team validates all analytical results by measuring sequence conservation across diverse species using independent databases of orthologous proteins. Researchers utilize primary databases like UniProt and MaveDB alongside supplementary resources including OrthoDB and the Eukaryotic Linear Motif repository. The team synthesizes datasets by cross referencing filtered sequences with scanning data and predicted motifs to construct unified maps. Because current functional annotations favor structured domains the researchers mitigate missing information by utilizing alternative data repositories like MobiDB. The two year project timeline progresses from infrastructure setup and structural investigations to concluding database releases and manuscript submissions. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in bioinformatics and biophysical modeling across three independent laboratories. The project guarantees open access by hosting a public database of conserved regions on the CyVerse computational infrastructure. The team incorporates members from three distinct laboratories and provides robust training opportunities in computational and experimental analysis techniques.

abstract_original: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins play essential roles in regulation, signaling, and molecular recognition, yet their evolutionary conservation patterns remain poorly understood. While folded domains exhibit clear conservation of structure and function, IDRs evolve rapidly and appear sequence diverse, obscuring how they encode functional specificity. Bridging the sequence function relationship in IDRs and even their reliable functional annotation remains a major challenge. Emerging evidence, however, suggests that subsets of IDRs harbor conserved sequence features such as short linear motifs (SLiMs), charge patterning and aromatic clustering that give rise to transient structural elements and encode critical molecular functions. This project aims to systematically identify and characterize the most conserved IDRs across proteomes by integrating large-scale sequence alignments, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and experimental functional annotations from publicly available databases. By combining resources such as UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif (ELM), IDRome, and MaveDB, we will quantify the interplay between evolutionary, structural, and functional signatures of conservation in disordered regions. Our multidisciplinary Working Group unites computational and experimental biophysics to build a curated, open-access database of conserved IDRs. This synthesis effort will reveal how dynamic, flexible protein regions maintain specific and evolvable functions, an emergent property at the mesoscale interface between sequence evolution, molecular structure, and cellular regulation.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
title_norm: integrative multiomics synthesis to identify shared molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation
abstract_text: Mammalian hibernation is a distinct physiological state involving decreased metabolism, lowered body temperature, and fasting, making the investigation of its underlying gene expression mechanisms crucial for understanding metabolic adaptation across taxa. To identify conserved molecular processes controlling metabolic suppression, this project will map gene orthology and model longitudinal gene expression changes between active and hibernating states using custom bivariate Ornstein Uhlenbeck trait evolution models. The study will integrate Sequence Read Archive RNA sequencing datasets and reference genomes across multiple tissues by processing raw reads through a uniform mapping pipeline and cross referencing species data via orthology maps. Identifying these conserved differentially regulated genes will clarify mammalian metabolic evolution and establish a biological foundation for downstream research concerning human metabolic regulation, ischemia tolerance, and organ preservation.
full_text: This project investigates mammalian hibernation to determine if metabolic suppression relies on shared or lineage specific transcriptional mechanisms. Although transcript data exists for individual hibernating mammals the field lacks comparative analyses of expression across multiple species. The proposed study identifies conserved genes for metabolic suppression to clarify mammalian evolution and inform human organ preservation. The team integrates RNA sequencing data from multiple tissues to model changes of gene expression using phylogenetic frameworks. The analytical pipeline incorporates transcript quantification with featureCounts alongside phylogenetic analyses using custom bivariate models of trait evolution. The proposed study will validate the custom bivariate models of trait evolution through the use of simulation tests. The project uses public RNA sequencing data from the Sequence Read Archive alongside published genomes and sequence alignments. The team integrates distinct datasets through uniform processing pipelines and maps of gene orthology derived from genome alignments. The team will mitigate sparse sampling of tissues across species by developing phylogenetic tools to handle missing data. The two year timeline begins with transcript processing and concludes with data synthesis and preparation of academic manuscripts. Managing these diverse variables requires a cross disciplinary team with distinct expertise in molecular biology and computational phylogenetics. The team will distribute project findings through primary literature alongside open source software and datasets of hibernation studies. This diverse research group spans multiple career stages and provides technical mentoring for support personnel in the laboratory.

abstract_original: Hibernation is a complex physiological strategy that allows certain mammals to withstand prolonged periods of resource scarcity and low temperatures by dramatically suppressing metabolism, while maintaining organ integrity and preserving muscle and bone mass. Despite decades of study, the shared molecular and cellular regulatory mechanisms that drive and sustain hibernation remain largely unresolved. This project aims to unify existing omics-scale datasets, mostly transcriptomic, from numerous hibernating mammals to identify conserved pathways and molecular signatures underlying this extreme phenotype. Our project will leverage publicly available datasets and apply cutting-edge computational tools that are developed in the context of this project to analyze transcriptional variation underlying hibernation in a phylogenetic context.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
title_norm: revealing the ontology of allostery through communityscale synthesis
abstract_text: Protein biophysics and molecular evolution research investigates allosteric regulation in transporter proteins including the P type ATPase superfamily, utilizing existing databases and algorithms to catalog regulated proteins and predict binding sites. This project will identify amino acid sites controlling allosteric mechanisms and determine their evolutionary origins by statistically comparing transporter families using tools including AlphaFold, Direct Coupling Analysis, and Adaptive Steered Molecular Dynamics. The study will integrate data from UniProt, InterPro, the Protein Data Bank, and the Allosteric Database to build an augmented allosterome database combining sequence alignments, protein structures, and molecular dynamics trajectories. Identifying these allosteric control sites will enable the annotation of uncharacterized allosteric systems, the interpretation of disease associated mutations, and the experimental design of synthetic allosteric proteins.
full_text: Existing databases catalog regulated proteins and algorithms predict binding sites but lack curated negative examples of non regulated proteins. The proposed study compares transporter homologs to uncover allosteric mechanisms and enable the experimental design of synthetic allosteric proteins. The team will assemble a comparative database of transporter families and map evolutionary landscapes through statistical comparisons of properties. The methodology utilizes AlphaFold and PyTorch alongside established methods for direct coupling analysis and adaptive steered molecular dynamics. The team will benchmark results by testing the ability of models to categorize proteins and propose functional point mutations. The study draws data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Allosteric Database (ASD) alongside the UniProt repository. The team will build an augmented database by combining structural data and sequence alignments for fifty distinct protein families. The team will mitigate the known lack of negative examples by utilizing domain insertions as proxy markers for allosteric regulation. The two year timeline progresses from data curation and analysis to the final evaluation of models and manuscript preparation. This project requires multi lab collaboration to combine diverse expertise in machine learning and the computational modeling of molecular evolution. The team will publish their evolutionary findings and host the augmented database publicly on the CyVerse platform for community access. The research group features principal investigators and staff scientists specializing in machine learning and the biophysics of chemical materials.

abstract_original: Allostery is a fundamental property of proteins wherein perturbations at one site can influence another distant site. Understanding the sequence, structural, and dynamic determinants of allostery is critical to engineering new biosensors, designing allosteric modulators, and predicting the functional impact of mutations. For many proteins, allostery allows control of protein activity in response to external stimuli, such as ligand binding, protein or nucleic acid interactions, post-translational modifications, light, and redox state. There are proteins, though, that do not clearly exhibit such regulatory mechanisms, and are thus rarely included in publicly available allosteric databases. Consequently, it remains unclear what features distinguish regulated systems and regulatory sites from their non-regulated counterparts. To this end, we will focus our work on a specific class of proteins—namely transporter proteins—and assemble a database that is, on the one hand, very specific—restricted to all such proteins, and broad because it includes proteins for which there is a lack of evidence for allosteric regulation. This augmented allosteric database will provide a basis for identifying the degree of allostery in proteins. Through these databases, and associated computational interrogations, we will reveal the determinants of allostery in transporter proteins, a large and diverse family of membrane proteins comprised of allosteric and non-allosteric members.

title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis
title_norm: synevo discovering evolutionary principles of molecular organization through crossspecies data synthesis
abstract_text: Evolutionary systems biology studies the intermediate scale organization of gene regulation and metabolism in humans and mosquitoes, demanding the integration of population genetic variation with cross species multi omics data through biochemical models. Currently, no analytical framework connects population level genetic variation with isolated cross species multi omics data to explain how evolution structures regulatory and metabolic networks. This project will develop a machine learning framework using graph neural networks, variational autoencoders, and genome scale metabolic models to merge population genetics with multi omics data, determining the rules that govern cross species network adaptation. A standardized pipeline will integrate datasets from GTEx, TOPMed, Ag1000G, and VectorBase with databases like Reactome and BiGG through metadata harmonization and cross species feature alignment based on orthology frameworks and pathway scaffolds. This research will yield a novel framework that maps physiologically plausible network modules, providing fundamental knowledge directly applicable to evolutionary theory, human health, and vector biology.
full_text: Evolutionary systems biology lacks frameworks connecting population level genetic variation with intermediate scale organization for humans and mosquitoes. Systems biology models network dynamics using isolated datasets while integration with population genetics through biochemical models remains incomplete. The proposed study develops machine learning frameworks to determine network adaptation rules benefiting human health and vector biology. The study design utilizes hybrid machine learning models and cross species manifold alignment to identify conserved network modules. Key methods incorporate variational autoencoders and graph neural networks alongside genome scale metabolic models and orthology mapping tools. The team validates results through cross validation and benchmarks findings against flux balance analysis and curated pathway databases. The study utilizes population datasets from GTEx and All of Us alongside pathway databases including Reactome and BiGG. A standardized pipeline integrates these distinct datasets through metadata harmonization and cross species feature alignment using orthology frameworks. The team mitigates data sparsity for mosquito variants by prioritizing human datasets and developing adaptable transfer learning models. The two year timeline progresses from data harmonization and model training toward the final release of comprehensive toolkits. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to merge specialized expertise spanning machine learning and genome scale metabolic modeling. The project distributes version controlled workflows and interactive atlas data through open access repositories alongside comprehensive training materials. The team features principal investigators and staff scientists who provide mentorship for students and host specialized instructional workshops.

abstract_original: Living systems exhibit emergent organization that bridges molecular and evolutionary scales. Genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic dynamics interact across levels of complexity to produce coordinated cellular behavior, yet most datasets capture only one layer at a time. Despite vast genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic resources across species and environments, no synthesis framework connects these data to reveal how evolutionary forces shape the mesoscale—the intermediate level where genes, proteins, and metabolites assemble into adaptive networks. The SynEvo Working Group will develop a machine-learning–driven synthesis framework that unites population-genetic and multi-omics data to uncover conserved and divergent axes of molecular organization. Using well-characterized human and mosquito datasets, we will identify how genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic flux interact to produce conserved mesoscale modules reflecting evolutionary constraint and innovation. These contrasting systems serve as testbeds for uncovering evolutionary design principles of molecular coordination—how selection and constraint shape regulatory–metabolic organization across life. SynEvo integrates interpretable machine learning with genome-scale metabolic (GEM) and MiReN (Minimal Regulatory Network; MILP-based regulatory inference) approaches, producing an open SynEvo Atlas hosted within NCEMS infrastructure—a reusable resource for evolutionary systems biology. By revealing both species- specific adaptations and conserved mesoscale design principles, SynEvo will advance conceptual and computational frontiers, providing fundamental insight into how life organizes itself across molecular, physiological, and evolutionary dimensions, with applications to human health, malaria transmission, and environmental resilience.

title: A Unified Framework for Analyses of Proteome Turnover Dynamics
title_norm: a unified framework for analyses of proteome turnover dynamics
abstract_text: The proteostasis domain focuses on protein turnover rates across species and kingdoms of life, recognizing that degradation signals and protein stability mechanisms exhibit broad conservation throughout evolutionary history. This project will construct the Protein Stability Database to analyze protein turnover conservation by standardizing public data, refitting measurements using uniform kinetic models, and applying deep neural networks and protein language models to correlate biophysical traits with degradation rates. Dynamic labeling mass spectrometry data from the PRIDE repository will be integrated with structural and thermodynamic databases by reanalyzing raw intensity data using uniform kinetic models and controlled vocabularies for experimental metadata. This research will produce a standardized metadata resource connecting protein half lives to molecular features, enabling comprehensive cross kingdom comparisons of biophysical properties that govern protein turnover across species.
full_text: This proteostasis research investigates rates of protein turnover to understand how molecular mechanisms determine protein stability across different evolutionary contexts. Eukaryotic degradation signals exhibit broad conservation but unstructured existing datasets obscure how sequence properties and proteostasis networks determine protein lifetimes. This project builds a standardized database to analyze evolutionary conservation and identify biophysical properties governing cross kingdom protein turnover. The study design standardizes public data regarding turnover by refitting measurements with uniform models and applying machine learning to orthologs. Methods involve exponential decay modeling and Bayesian sampling combined with deep neural networks and protein language models including ESM2. Validation of model performance requires calculating reconstruction loss for proteins with fast turnover and measuring prediction accuracy against established databases. Primary sources feature mass spectrometry data from PRIDE alongside structural predictions from AlphaFold and repositories of genomic sequences including OrthoDB. Data integration involves reanalyzing raw intensities with uniform kinetic models and combining resulting rates with corresponding structural and omics variables. The team mitigates incompatible formats of data and physiological variations by correcting enrichment kinetics and applying unified models with metadata. The two year timeline spans initial development of the database during the first year and subsequent validation of models. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because harmonizing quantitative mass spectrometry data with computational modeling exceeds individual laboratory capacity. The project provides open access to the resulting database and analytical code through established repositories including CyVerse and GitHub. The research team includes principal investigators from proteomics and computational biology working alongside staff scientists to provide training opportunities.
authors: Sina Ghaemmaghami; Edward Lau; Christine Vogel

abstract_original: Proteins vary widely in how long they persist within cells, from minutes to years, and this variation plays a central role in regulating biological function and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Decades of research have revealed several mechanisms that influence protein half-lives across the kingdoms of life. However, the differential impact of these mechanisms on protein half-lives within and between species remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap can be addressed by comprehensive analyses of global proteome stability datasets enabled by recent advances in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. However, these datasets are currently fragmented across heterogeneous studies that are not easily amenable to meta-analysis. This Working Group will bring together complementary expertise in proteomics, computational biology, systems biochemistry, and evolution to systematically harmonize and integrate publicly available datasets on protein turnover across four representative species across two kingdoms of life - E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens. By reanalyzing existing data using consistent approaches and unifying metadata standards, we will generate a comprehensive, comparable, and publicly accessible resource, the Protein Stability Database (PSD). This database will enable us to identify the molecular and evolutionary principles that govern protein stability and assess how turnover patterns vary across different cell types and organisms. Beyond addressing these core questions, our Working Group aims to establish best practices and a shared vocabulary for measuring and reporting protein turnover, enabling seamless incorporation of future datasets and integration with other NCEMS data resources.

title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
abstract_text: The spatial omics field evaluates how subcellular molecular location influences cellular function, making the integration of spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics essential because bulk RNA and protein levels correlate poorly. Current analytical methods evaluate molecular abundances separately because the technical difficulty of aligning adjacent tissue sections restricts the ability to measure how subcellular organization determines cell behavior. This project will build a computational framework utilizing STalign diffeomorphic mapping, SEraster grid harmonization, and SubCell deep learning models with contrastive multimodal embedding algorithms to extract spatial relationships and predict cell fate decisions. The study will integrate human cancer datasets from the Spatch database by registering adjacent spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics sections into a common coordinate framework rasterized onto a shared pixel grid. This framework will shift spatial omics from abundance only observations to predictive models that link spatial molecular patterns directly to biophysical mechanisms and cellular phenotypes.
full_text: The field of spatial omics analyzes subcellular organization and lacks tools to integrate RNA and protein spatial locations. Subcellular location influences cellular function while difficult alignment of adjacent tissue sections limits comparisons of RNA and proteins. This computational framework tests whether integrated spatial relationships predict cell states better than abundance to uncover biophysical mechanisms. The strategy maps adjacent tissue sections onto a shared grid to train models for classification of cell states. Key tools include mapping algorithms like STalign and SEraster alongside deep learning models like SubCell for contrastive embedding. The team will benchmark results against models of abundance and validate the alignments using root mean square errors. The project utilizes the public Spatch database of human cancers and additional cohorts containing transcriptomic and proteomic data. The team will integrate distinct datasets by registering tissue sections into a common coordinate framework to generate patches. Adjacent tissue sections undergo non rigid distortions during imaging and the team will apply non linear alignment algorithms. The project spans two years and includes intermediate milestones for data harmonization before final release of a toolchain. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in machine learning and biophysics with scalable computing infrastructure. The team will release code and harmonized datasets under permissive licenses alongside a peer reviewed publication of findings. The collaborative team includes principal investigators specializing in artificial intelligence and staff scientists with expertise in cloud computing.

abstract_original: Cell states reflect not only molecular abundance but also where molecules reside. Public spatial omics (Spatch) now provide high-plex RNA (Xenium/CosMx) and protein (CODEX) maps, yet cross-modal synthesis at subcellular scales remain fragmented. We will develop an open, end-to-end synthesis framework that (i) registers adjacent-section spatial RNA-Protein images at subcellular resolution using diffeomorphic alignment (STalign), (ii) harmonizes RNA features into protein-scale rasters (SEraster) to create a one-to-one correspondence of patches to be compared (iii) quantify membrane/nuclear proximity, polarity, local density, and other features (iv) trains RNA-to-protein predictors and learn a unified biophysical fingerprint of cell state. Using the paired Xenium/CosMx-CODEX cancer atlas as a validation set and curated public cohorts as application sets, we will benchmark against abundance-only baselines. Framework performance will be assessed by overall registration quality, verified patch correspondence, and cross-modal predictive accuracy, with appropriate positive and negative controls to rule out leakage and spurious structure. We will test the hypotheses that RNA-protein spatial relationships yield predictive signals for cell state beyond abundance and that low- dimensional biophysical fingerprints precede and predict cell fate decisions. All code, trained models, and harmonized datasets generated from this work will be released under permissive licenses with containerized, reproducible workflows and scheduled public snapshots. This community-scale synthesis will convert dispersed spatial imaging datasets into predictive, interpretable models of cell state, while leveraging NCEMS (CyVerse compute, data harmonization, and project management) for scalable analysis and dissemination.

title: Decoding the Sequence-to-Mesoscale Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Phase Behavior, Interactome Architecture, and Cellular Function
title_norm: decoding the sequencetomesoscale grammar of biomolecular condensates a multiomic synthesis of phase behavior interactome architecture and cellular function
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation depend on specific protein sequence features to establish mesoscale material properties, making the unification of fragmented biophysical data essential for predictive modeling. Currently, no proteome scale framework links protein sequence features to emergent material states and multiphase architectures, leaving the mechanisms driving functional and disease related outcomes fundamentally uncharacterized. This project will develop the Condensate Mesoscale Atlas through a computational synthesis utilizing gradient boosted trees, graph neural networks, and network based algorithms to identify sequence and interaction rules predicting material states and disease disruptions. Data from resources including PhaSepDB, BioGRID, and the Human Protein Atlas will be programmatically extracted, standardized using UniProt identifiers, and assembled into a relational database linking structural metadata directly to protein sequences. This research will yield a predictive framework detailing how sequences determine specific condensate architectures, clarifying mechanisms behind pathological liquid to solid transitions while providing a generalizable data integration pipeline.
full_text: This research explores biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation because a unified framework for material states remains absent. Abundant data exists for protein composition but isolated databases prevent predictive models for mapping from sequence to material state. The study builds the Condensate Mesoscale Atlas to reveal how sequences and mutations dictate the architecture of condensate materials. The project executes a four phase computational synthesis to harmonize data and predict material states using techniques for machine learning. The analytical approach utilizes graph neural networks and gradient boosted trees with SHAP feature attribution alongside detection of network communities. The team validates the predictions from models against independent proteomic datasets and published measurements of fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. The project extracts data from repositories including PhaSepDB and BioGRID alongside structural archives and measurements of single molecules from literature. The researchers programmatically standardize the extracted information to a common identifier system before they assemble a comprehensive relational database. The team overcomes heterogeneity in data and naming discrepancies by standardizing identifiers and implementing manual curation for information from literature. The timeline spans twenty four months and includes overlapping phases for harmonization of data followed by model development and validation. This scope surpasses the capabilities of a single laboratory because integrating clinical genetics and predictive modeling demands broad expertise. The researchers share code via GitHub and release models through Zenodo alongside an interactive web tool for public exploration. The cross disciplinary team includes investigators and trainees from four institutions who receive comprehensive instruction regarding techniques for machine learning.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to organelle-scale structures with distinct material properties (liquid, gel, solid) that dictate cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects sequence-encoded molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale material states and their functional/pathological consequences across the proteome. This proposal assembles a Working Group to synthesize eight distinct public data ecosystems—(1) condensate composition databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), (2) IDR and phase-separation propensity predictors (PScore, catGRANULE, FuzDrop), (3) genome-scale interactome and co-complex data (BioGRID, STRING, hu.MAP), (4) subcellular localization atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell live-imaging library), (5) structural data from cryo-EM/ET of cellular condensates (EMDB), (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived material-property measurements curated from literature, (7) disease mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-forming proteins, and (8) evolutionary conservation data (UniProt, Pfam) across species. By integrating these previously siloed resources, we will build a computational framework—the Condensate Mesoscale Atlas (CoMA)—that links sequence features to predicted material properties, interactome connectivity, and functional/disease outcomes at proteome scale. Specific aims include: (1) constructing a harmonized, machine-readable dataset unifying sequence, structural, biophysical, and phenotypic condensate data for >2,000 human proteins; (2) applying interpretable machine learning and network-based approaches to identify sequence and interaction motifs (the 'molecular grammar') that predict emergent material states and multiphase organization (e.g., core-shell condensates); (3) testing whether disease-associated mutations preferentially disrupt predicted grammar features linked to material-state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer; and (4) validating framework predictions against independent public datasets not used in model training. This task exceeds single-lab capacity: it requires biophysicists who understand phase-separation thermodynamics, structural biologists interpreting cryo-EM data, computational biologists building predictive models, cell biologists validating localization/functional data, and clinicians/geneticists linking findings to disease—expertise no single laboratory possesses. NCEMS support is essential to provide computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous, differently formatted datasets, to convene the necessary interdisciplinary expertise, and to establish shared open-science standards for reproducible mesoscale data synthesis. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis pipelines will be released as FAIR, versioned resources via GitHub and Zenodo, accompanied by interactive visualization tools for the broader community. The Working Group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computational biology, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning interpretability, and collaborative open-science workflows—directly cultivating the data-savvy, cross-disciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. This synthesis effort promises to resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how simple sequence-encoded interactions give rise to complex, function-defining mesoscale organization, with direct implications for understanding proteinopathies and designing synthetic condensates.

title: From Sequence Grammar to Cellular Phenotype: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence
title_norm: from sequence grammar to cellular phenotype a multiscale data synthesis of biomolecular condensate emergence
abstract_text: Within the mesoscale biology domain, biomolecular condensates form through liquid liquid phase separation of intrinsically disordered regions and RNA to critically influence cellular processes via sequence derived material properties. Because large scale data remain fragmented, the field lacks a unified predictive framework to explain the multi scale relationship between molecular sequence grammar, condensate material properties, and cellular phenotypes. The primary objective is to construct a predictive framework for condensate formation; this project will retrospectively synthesize public data into a multi layer network graph and apply graph neural networks alongside deep generative models for comprehensive analysis. Diverse datasets including condensate protein databases, imaging atlases, interactomes, biophysical simulations, and disease variant records will be synthesized into a heterogeneous graph using unified protein level identifiers and standardized ontologies. This research will deliver a cross validated predictive framework for sequence to phenotype relationships, fundamentally supporting the downstream study of condensate linked diseases and multi scale biological systems.
full_text: Mesoscale biology investigates biomolecular condensates but lacks unified frameworks linking molecular sequences to material properties and downstream disease outcomes. Condensates form through multivalent interactions but fragmented data leave the relationship between sequence grammar and cellular phenotypes poorly understood. This project asks how sequence features determine condensate formation by building the first cross validated predictive framework for diseases. This retrospective data synthesis integrates public datasets into a network graph and uses systematic ablation to predict emergent properties. The analytical approach applies data harmonization alongside graph neural networks and deep generative models to evaluate sequences and variants. The team validates these models using cross database splits and benchmarking against experimental biophysical parameters and coarse grained simulations. Sources include condensate databases (PhaSepDB) and imaging atlases (OpenCell) alongside interactome records and clinical repositories (ClinVar and COSMIC). The team synthesizes these datasets by constructing a heterogeneous network graph using unified protein identifiers and standardized ontology terms. The researchers mitigate data fragmentation and annotation conflicts through automated quality checks and uniform recalculation of sequence derived biophysical descriptors. The two year project builds harmonization infrastructure before transitioning to model validation with regular synthesis sprints at six month intervals. The scope requires multi lab collaboration to integrate diverse expertise in polymer physics and clinical genetics beyond any single laboratory. The project shares findings through open access publications while distributing containerized code and databases via public repositories under FAIR principles. Four principal investigators jointly mentor postdoctoral researchers and graduate students to provide valuable training in machine learning and reproducible science.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level sequence features and interactions give rise to micron-scale structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular decision-making in stress response, signaling, and disease. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework linking intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence grammar to condensate composition, biophysical state, and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists not for lack of data—thousands of studies have generated condensate-component databases, high-content subcellular imaging atlases, proximity-labeling interactomes, cryo-electron tomograms, disease mutation catalogs, and AlphaFold-derived structural ensembles—but because these resources are scattered across incompatible formats, disciplines, and repositories, with no single lab possessing the expertise to harmonize and jointly analyze them. This working group proposes to close that gap through community-scale data synthesis.

We will integrate five previously siloed public data classes: (1) curated condensate-associated protein and sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro); (2) subcellular localization and dynamics imaging (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer); (3) proximity-labeling and interactome datasets defining in vivo condensate composition; (4) biophysical/simulation resources describing IDR sequence patterning (charge, aromaticity, stickers-and-spacers architecture) including coarse-grained simulation parameter sets (e.g., CALVADOS-derived); and (5) disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapping mutations onto IDRs linked to pathological condensate dysregulation. Using graph-based and deep generative models, we will construct a multi-layer network connecting molecular sequence features to condensate proteome composition, imaging-derived morphological/dynamic phenotypes, and organismal disease outcomes. A central analytical goal is to identify emergent “rules”—nonlinear, context-dependent combinations of sequence and interaction features—that predict when and where condensates form, what determines their material properties, and how perturbation (mutation, stress, drug treatment) shifts phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

This effort inherently requires cross-disciplinary integration beyond any single lab: polymer physicists and biophysicists to encode sequence-to-property relationships, cell biologists and imaging scientists to interpret phenotypic datasets, computational/AI scientists to build multi-modal integrative models, and clinical geneticists to connect molecular predictions to disease. NCEMS support is essential to convene this team, provide shared computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous ontologies (protein IDs, imaging metadata, mutation annotations), and establish reproducible, version-controlled pipelines. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, queryable resource (a “Condensate Emergence Atlas”) under FAIR principles, enabling community reuse and extension.

Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across institutions, receiving hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning for biophysical prediction, and open/reproducible science practices, while rotating through partner labs to gain cross-disciplinary fluency. By synthesizing existing but fragmented public data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology—how molecular sequence information encodes emergent cellular organization—while producing a durable, reusable resource and training pipeline for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

title: Decoding the Sequence-to-Mesoscale Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Omics Synthesis of Phase Separation Determinants and Cellular Consequences
title_norm: decoding the sequencetomesoscale grammar of biomolecular condensates a multiomics synthesis of phase separation determinants and cellular consequences
abstract_text: Mesoscale biology investigates biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation and their material properties, utilizing extensive molecular, structural, cellular, and clinical datasets to understand complex biological phenomena. Fragmented data domains separated across disciplines using incompatible ontologies currently prevent an integrated framework linking sequence encoded biophysics to emergent mesoscale behavior and cellular phenotypes. The primary objective will determine the sequence encoded biophysical grammar governing material properties by harmonizing databases and applying gradient boosted trees, random forests, and neural networks to predict property shifts and cell type vulnerabilities. Key resources including PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, UniProt, AlphaFold, ClinVar, and COSMIC will be integrated into a harmonized relational database anchored to UniProt accessions using automated ID mapping, conflict resolution pipelines, and standardized ontologies. This research will establish generalizable rules linking sequences to material properties and create reusable computational standards to provide a framework for prioritizing disease variants for experimental research.
full_text: Mesoscale biology studies condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation but lacks frameworks connecting sequence encoded biophysics to phenotypes. Public datasets span molecular and clinical scales but provide incomplete understanding because disciplines use incompatible ontologies and disparate standards. This project discovers the sequence encoded grammar governing material properties of condensates to establish generalizable rules and prioritize variants. The design harmonizes cross disciplinary databases to train machine learning models for predicting material properties and mapping disease mutations. Analytical tools include gradient boosted trees and sequence based neural networks alongside in silico mutagenesis inside containerized Python pipelines. Validation requires nested cross validation stratified by protein family alongside benchmarking against established predictors and held out experimental datasets. The study utilizes data from comprehensive public databases including UniProt and ClinVar alongside structural models from AlphaFold and ESMFold. These diverse datasets enter a harmonized relational database anchored to UniProt accessions using automated mapping pipelines and standardized ontologies. The study mitigates annotation artifacts and data leakage from homologous sequences through expert curation and stratified nested cross validation. This thirty month project executes data harmonization before advancing to predictive modeling and disease mapping alongside semi annual hackathons. The comprehensive scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating fragmented information demands simultaneous expertise across physics and clinical genomics. The team releases datasets and analytical code under permissive licenses while deploying an open web predictor for public access. The team comprises five specialized investigators alongside a dedicated data engineer and multiple trainees working in cross disciplinary pairs.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level features (disordered sequences, multivalent interactions, post-translational modifications) give rise to organelle-scale material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that in turn shape cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at each of these scales, the field lacks an integrated, predictive framework linking sequence-encoded biophysics to emergent mesoscale behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists not from lack of data but from its fragmentation across incompatible domains: biophysical LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), disorder and sequence-feature repositories (MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold/ESMFold structural predictions), high-content and super-resolution imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting), single-cell and bulk multi-omics (expression stoichiometry, PTM databases like PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) documenting condensate-associated disease mutations. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, cell imaging analytics, and clinical genomics needed to unify these resources.

This Working Group will address the central question: What sequence-encoded biophysical grammar governs the emergent material properties of condensates, and how do perturbations to this grammar propagate to cellular and organismal phenotypes? We will pursue three synthesis aims. (1) Construct a harmonized cross-database resource linking condensate-forming proteins to quantitative sequence/structural features (charge patterning, aromatic stickers, IDR length, predicted secondary structure) using standardized ontologies, resolving inconsistent annotations across LLPS databases. (2) Train interpretable machine learning models that predict mesoscale material properties (viscosity class, multiphase organization, dynamic exchange rates) from these molecular features, validated against quantitative imaging datasets (FRAP recovery curves, condensate size/number distributions from HPA and OpenCell), enabling discovery of emergent 'grammar rules' not evident from single-protein studies. (3) Map disease-associated mutations (ClinVar, COSMIC) within condensate-relevant sequence regions onto predicted mesoscale property shifts, and cross-reference with single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic data to identify cell-type-specific vulnerabilities where altered condensate stoichiometry may drive pathology (e.g., neurodegeneration, cancer).

This project intrinsically requires collaboration beyond any individual lab: biophysicists modeling polymer thermodynamics, structural bioinformaticians curating disorder predictions, cell biologists interpreting high-content imaging phenotypes, and clinical genomicists linking variants to disease—together with data scientists capable of harmonizing heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets into a single predictive framework. NCEMS support is essential to convene this diverse team, provide computational infrastructure for large-scale data harmonization, and establish shared analytical standards. All curated datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows will be released as an open-access resource (GitHub/Zenodo, FAIR-compliant), including a web-based condensate property predictor for community use. The Working Group will embed graduate students and postdocs directly in cross-disciplinary sub-teams, pairing computational trainees with wet-lab-trained condensate biologists, providing structured mentorship in reproducible multi-omic synthesis and building a cohort of researchers fluent in both molecular biophysics and data science—directly advancing NCEMS's mission to train a data-savvy mesoscale biology workforce.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation and related self-organization processes—exemplify mesoscale emergence: simple molecular interactions between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to complex, functionally consequential structures that cannot be predicted from single-molecule properties alone. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensate-forming proteins (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro), disorder and sequence features (MobiDB, DisProt), protein-protein and protein-RNA interactomes (BioGRID, STRING, RNAct), subcellular imaging (Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting, OpenCell), and emerging cryo-electron tomography maps of native cellular architecture (EMPIAR, CZ Imaging Institute datasets), no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features scale up to determine condensate material properties (viscosity, multiphasicity, exchange dynamics) and their downstream cellular consequences (transcriptional regulation, stress response, signaling compartmentalization). This gap persists because the requisite data are scattered across incompatible formats, curated by different scientific communities (biophysicists, structural biologists, cell biologists, and computational scientists), and require integration at a scale beyond any single laboratory's capacity.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team—including soft-matter biophysicists, structural/cryo-EM specialists, cell biologists studying condensate function, and machine-learning/data scientists—to build an integrated, open-access Mesoscale Condensate Atlas that harmonizes sequence-level features, empirically measured biophysical parameters (partition coefficients, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching rates, viscosity estimates), interactome connectivity, and high-resolution imaging/tomography data across human, yeast, and model organism datasets. Using this atlas, we will address three synthesis-driven questions: (1) What combinations of sequence grammar (charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, RNA-binding motifs) and interactome topology best predict condensate formation propensity and material state across proteomes? (2) Do condensates exhibit conserved scaling laws or percolation-like thresholds relating molecular valency/concentration to emergent material properties, and are these principles conserved across cell types and species? (3) Can integrated molecular-to-imaging data reveal generalizable ‘emergence signatures’—quantitative markers that predict when a condensate transitions from a passive assembly to one with regulatory or catalytic function at the cellular level?

We will develop novel network-based and generative AI models trained on this synthesized cross-scale dataset, producing publicly available, reproducible pipelines (via containerized workflows and FAIR-compliant repositories) that the community can extend to new proteins or organisms. This project requires NCEMS support because it demands sustained, coordinated data harmonization across incompatible legacy databases maintained by distinct research communities, computational infrastructure for large-scale multi-modal integration, and structured collaboration between biophysics and cell biology groups that rarely co-author work. The initiative will provide hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data science, biophysical modeling, and open-science practices, producing a new generation of scientists equipped to study emergence phenomena computationally. Ultimately, this work will establish generalizable principles governing how molecular-scale interactions generate mesoscale cellular architecture—a foundational advance for predictive cell biology.

Using this harmonized dataset, we will develop interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating sequence, structure, and interaction features) to predict emergent condensate properties from molecular composition, and test whether specific 'grammar motifs' generalize across unrelated protein families and species—a question unanswerable without large-scale cross-dataset synthesis.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where local biomolecular interactions give rise to system-level properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that dictate cellular function in transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets, no unified framework connects the molecular determinants of phase behavior (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalent 'sticker-spacer' motifs, post-translational modifications) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences. This gap persists because relevant data are scattered across incompatible resources: sequence/structure databases (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB), condensate-specific repositories (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), post-translational modification atlases (PhosphoSitePlus), protein abundance/localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb), and heterogeneous imaging/biophysical measurements (FRAP recovery curves, single-molecule tracking, cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, and machine learning required to harmonize these disparate data types into a predictive, mechanistic framework.

This Working Group will assemble condensate biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and machine learning experts to build an integrated, open-access resource—the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA)—that links molecular-scale features to mesoscale phase behavior and cellular outcomes. We will: (1) curate and cross-reference sequence-based determinants (disorder content, charge patterning, aromatic sticker density) with experimentally reported condensate material properties (liquid, gel, solid; FRAP-derived mobile fractions; concentration-dependent phase boundaries); (2) integrate interactome and stoichiometry data to model condensates as emergent network phenomena, testing whether percolation-like thresholds in interaction valency predict phase transition points; (3) incorporate PTM and cellular context data (abundance, localization, cell-type specificity) to explain condition-dependent condensate emergence versus dissolution; and (4) apply supervised and unsupervised machine learning to identify generalizable 'rules' distinguishing functional condensates from aberrant aggregates linked to disease (e.g., neurodegeneration-associated solidification).

A central scientific question we will address: Can mesoscale material properties of condensates be predicted from molecular-scale sequence and interaction features alone, or do emergent properties require irreducible knowledge of cellular context (concentration, crowding, PTM state)? Answering this tests fundamental assumptions about reductionism versus emergence in molecular systems biology.

This project is infeasible for any single lab given the scale of cross-database harmonization, the breadth of required expertise, and the need for standardized ontologies bridging biophysics and cell biology communities. NCEMS support will fund coordinated data-wrangling sprints, shared computational infrastructure, and workshops to establish community standards for condensate data annotation. All curated datasets, harmonization pipelines, and predictive models will be released under FAIR principles via a public repository and interactive web tool. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning—directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will yield a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale emergent properties from molecular data, with broad applicability beyond condensates to other emergent cellular phenomena.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation represent a critical biological phenomenon where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent domains, and RNA create assemblies with specific material properties. Understanding remains incomplete because disconnected databases with incompatible formats prevent the creation of a unified framework connecting molecular sequence grammar, interactome network context, material properties, and cellular phenotypes. This computational synthesis project will build a predictive model connecting sequence features and interactomes to material properties and phenotypes by applying data harmonization, feature engineering, graph neural networks, gradient boosted trees, and charge patterning metrics. Information from databases including PhaSepDB, MobiDB, BioGRID, and ClinVar will be integrated into a heterogeneous graph by mapping identifiers and establishing a controlled vocabulary to connect sequence nodes with confidence weighted interactions. This research will create a reusable harmonization framework and predictive model to establish design principles for mesoscale emergence and allow prediction of mutation effects on condensate material states.

Molecular interactions create specific material properties but understanding remains incomplete because current data reside across disconnected databases of varying standards. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—biophysicists studying condensate material properties, computational structural biologists, network biologists, cell imaging specialists, and clinical genomicists—to build the first cross-scale, harmonized data resource and predictive model connecting (1) sequence-encoded molecular features (IDR composition, stickers-and-spacers architecture, post-translational modification sites, RNA-binding motifs), (2) network-level context (interactome connectivity, co-condensation partners, stoichiometry), (3) empirically measured mesoscale material properties (FRAP-derived mobility, viscosity, multiphase demixing, aging/hardening propensity compiled from published biophysical studies), and (4) higher-order cellular and organismal outcomes (subcellular localization patterns, stress-responsive condensate remodeling, and disease-associated mutations affecting phase behavior). Model predictions will be rigorously validated against independent, held-out public datasets (orthogonal imaging studies, biophysical measurements not used in training) to ensure generalizability rather than dataset-specific overfitting. The working group will embed graduate students and postdocs in cross-lab data harmonization, biophysical modeling, and network-based machine learning, providing hands-on training in reproducible, large-scale synthesis science. By resolving inconsistencies across independently generated datasets and establishing shared standards for describing condensate material properties, this project will produce mechanistic insight into why and how mesoscale emergence arises from molecular interactions—addressing a fundamental, long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology that is intractable without cross-institutional, cross-disciplinary data synthesis at NCEMS scale.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid liquid phase separation possess critical mesoscale properties, but rich data concerning intrinsically disordered regions, protein interactions, and subcellular localization remain heavily fragmented across molecular, network, and phenotypic scales. Consequently, there is currently no integrated framework that connects molecular sequence features, network level organization, and cellular phenotypes to accurately predict condensate behavior. This project will synthesize diverse data to identify cross scale rules predicting condensate formation and disease related dysfunction by deriving integrated features and applying protein language models, graph neural networks, multi task learning, and coarse grained biophysical simulations. Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from weak multivalent interactions among biomolecules to produce compartments with system-level functions (e.g., stress granules, transcriptional hubs, nucleoli) that cannot be predicted from single-protein properties alone. Despite an explosion of public data describing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, subcellular localization, and disease-associated mutations, no integrated framework exists linking molecular sequence features to network-level organization to cellular phenotype. This gap persists because the relevant expertise—biophysics of disordered proteins, network science, cell imaging informatics, and clinical genetics—is distributed across disparate communities that rarely collaborate, and because no single lab possesses the computational infrastructure or cross-domain fluency to harmonize these heterogeneous data types at scale.

This Working Group will synthesize five major public resources: (1) sequence-based condensate databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS) and IDR predictors (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) proteome-wide interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct); (3) high-resolution subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, CellPainting); (4) structural and AlphaFold-derived conformational ensembles for disordered/multivalent proteins; and (5) disease-mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-associated proteins. Our central hypothesis is that emergent condensate behavior is governed by a decodable 'grammar' spanning three scales: (a) molecular grammar—sticker-spacer patterning, charge blockiness, and aromatic density within IDRs; (b) network grammar—topological features of interaction hubs (multivalency, promiscuity, community structure) that nucleate condensation; and (c) phenotypic grammar—how these features manifest as condensate size, dynamics, and localization observable in imaging data, and how their disruption by disease mutations produces pathological aggregation or loss-of-function.

The team will integrate machine learning (graph neural networks trained on PPI topology plus sequence embeddings), coarse-grained biophysical simulation benchmarking, and image-derived phenotypic quantification to build predictive models that generalize across protein families and cell types—an analysis impossible without cross-disciplinary data fusion at this scale. Deliverables include: a unified, versioned 'Condensate Emergence Atlas' linking sequence, network, and phenotype data with open APIs; predictive models identifying condensate-prone proteins and mutation-driven emergent dysfunction relevant to neurodegeneration and cancer; and a reproducible open-source pipeline (Snakemake/Nextflow, containerized) for community reuse. The Working Group will comprise biophysicists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomics researchers from institutions varying in size and geography, explicitly recruiting early-career co-PIs and including graduate students/postdocs in every workflow layer, with structured training in reproducible multi-omic synthesis, FAIR data practices, and interdisciplinary communication. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be deposited on public repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Synapse) under NCEMS open science guidelines, enabling the broader community to test, extend, and apply this cross-scale framework to other emergent mesoscale phenomena beyond condensates.

No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to harmonize these heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets—spanning atomic structure to cellular phenotype—into a unified predictive framework.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and data scientists to construct a curated, interoperable meta-database and companion machine-learning framework—CondensateAtlas—that integrates sequence features (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs), structural/ultrastructural data (condensate size, shape, multiphase organization from imaging archives), interactome-derived compositional networks, and quantitative material-property measurements curated via natural-language-processing-assisted literature mining and manual expert curation. Using this integrated resource, we will (1) test whether sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features quantitatively predict emergent viscoelastic properties across condensate types, (2) identify structural and compositional signatures that distinguish functional liquid-like condensates from pathological solid-like aggregates linked to neurodegenerative and oncogenic variants, and (3) develop generalizable biophysical/ML models capable of predicting mesoscale material behavior from primary sequence and cellular context, tested against held-out experimental datasets. Statistical and generative modeling approaches (Gaussian process regression, graph neural networks trained on interaction networks, physics-informed biophysical polymer models) will be co-developed by computational and wet-lab collaborators to ensure biological interpretability.

This project requires NCEMS support because it depends on cross-institutional data harmonization, standardized ontology development for condensate properties, and computational infrastructure beyond any single lab's capacity, while uniting communities (structural biology, soft-matter physics, cell biology, genomics) that rarely interact directly. The working group will include early-career researchers and trainees who will lead specific data curation and modeling modules, receiving hands-on training in FAIR data practices, reproducible workflow design (Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines), and multidisciplinary team science. All curated datasets, ontologies, trained models, and analysis code will be released as open-access community resources via Zenodo/GitHub, with a living database designed for continuous community contribution. By synthesizing molecular-to-mesoscale data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle—how simple molecular rules generate complex emergent condensate behavior—while generating a foundational, reusable resource for the mesoscale biology community.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membrane-less assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: they arise from collective, multivalent interactions among proteins and nucleic acids, yet exhibit properties (viscosity, selective permeability, catalytic enhancement, signaling thresholds) not predictable from any single component. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects molecular-level sequence/structural features to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across disconnected resources—intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predictors (MobiDB, IUPred), condensate component databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, CD-CODE), structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell), single-cell/spatial transcriptomics, and disease-variant catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC). Synthesizing these heterogeneous, multiscale datasets requires expertise spanning biophysics, structural biology, cell biology, computational modeling, evolutionary biology, and clinical genetics—expertise no single lab possesses, and integration efforts that exceed what any two-lab collaboration could reasonably undertake.

This Working Group will construct an open, queryable 'Condensatome' resource and analytical framework that integrates these disparate datasets to answer a fundamental question: What generalizable molecular features—sequence composition, IDR architecture, multivalent interaction motifs, post-translational modification sites, and structural flexibility—predict the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates (nucleation propensity, material state, compositional selectivity, functional output), and how do disease-associated mutations perturb these emergent properties to drive pathology?

Our approach proceeds in three synthesis phases. First, we will harmonize condensate component annotations, interaction networks, and structural/disorder predictions into a unified schema, applying network-based and machine-learning methods (graph neural networks, multivalency scoring) to identify molecular 'grammars' associated with distinct condensate material states and functions. Second, we will cross-reference these molecular grammars with imaging-derived phenotypic data (condensate size, number, dynamics from public live-cell datasets) and single-cell expression contexts to model how cellular environment (concentration, crowding, post-translational state) modulates emergent phase behavior across cell types. Third, we will overlay disease-variant data to test whether mutations disrupting predicted phase-separation grammar correlate with aberrant condensate formation implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and stress-granule pathologies, generating testable hypotheses for the broader community.

The Working Group will assemble investigators across career stages and institution types—biophysicists modeling phase behavior, structural biologists curating disorder/structure data, cell biologists with imaging expertise, computational scientists building integrative ML pipelines, and clinical geneticists connecting variants to disease—reflecting the transdisciplinary scope NCEMS uniquely enables. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis workflows will be released as open, versioned, reproducible pipelines (via GitHub/Zenodo) accompanied by tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on data harmonization and modeling subprojects, receiving structured training in FAIR data practices, cross-disciplinary communication, and reproducible computational biology, directly building the data-savvy workforce this call seeks to cultivate while resolving a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.
