abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (material state, composition, exchange dynamics) arise from combinatorial molecular interactions and cannot be predicted from any single molecule or interaction alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based predictors of disorder and multivalency, curated condensate composition databases, protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks, structural ensemble data, single-molecule dynamics measurements, and cellular phenotype datasets have been generated by disconnected communities using incompatible vocabularies and formats. No integrated framework currently links molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and its downstream cellular consequences. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public resources into a unified, predictive, and mechanistic framework for condensate emergence. We will integrate: (1) sequence-derived features of intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, and multivalent motifs from UniProt, MobiDB, and IDRome conformational ensemble data; (2) curated condensate composition and phase-behavior annotations from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, and CD-CODE; (3) protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction topology from BioGRID, STRING, and RNAct; (4) structural context from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and PDB; (5) subcellular localization and condensate imaging data from the Human Protein Atlas and Allen Cell Explorer; (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived exchange kinetics extracted from published literature and condensate databases; and (7) disease-associated variant data from ClinVar and COSMIC. Using this multi-modal resource, we will address three central questions: First, what combinations of sequence, network topology, and structural features best predict whether a protein participates in condensate formation, and do these features generalize across condensate types (stress granules, transcriptional condensates, nucleoli)? Second, does interactome topology (e.g., hub connectivity, clustering coefficients) correlate with emergent material properties such as liquid-to-solid transitions and exchange dynamics measured by FRAP? Third, can disease-associated mutations be systematically mapped onto this framework to identify variants that specifically perturb condensate emergence, and do such perturbations correlate with altered transcriptional noise or cellular phenotypes documented in single-cell RNA-seq datasets (ENCODE, Human Cell Atlas)? This synthesis requires computational infrastructure and cross-disciplinary expertise—spanning biophysical theory, network science, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics—that no single lab possesses, and it demands harmonization of heterogeneous, differently-curated public databases at a scale only achievable through coordinated collaboration. Deliverables include an open-access, version-controlled integrated database and machine-learning framework (CondensateAtlas), reproducible analysis pipelines, and a predictive model relating molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale phenotype. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in biophysical modeling, network analysis, and open, reproducible data science, directly building the data-savvy interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: their material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, component exchange dynamics) arise from collective interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications, yet these properties cannot be predicted from single-molecule features alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), condensate-specific proteomic and interactome maps (CD-CODE, BioGRID, IntAct), structural predictions (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-content imaging atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting), and functional perturbation screens (CRISPR-based condensate disruption studies, disease-mutation databases like ClinVar and COSMIC). No integrated framework currently connects molecular grammar to emergent material properties to downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell imaging, and machine learning—to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and predictive modeling framework addressing a fundamental question: What combinatorial rules of sequence composition, structural motifs, PTMs, and interaction networks give rise to specific emergent material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally determine cellular outcomes such as transcriptional bursting, stress granule dynamics, and signaling fidelity? 

The working group will first construct a harmonized meta-database linking condensate-resident proteins across sequence/structural feature sets, experimentally measured or imaging-inferred material properties (FRAP recovery rates, droplet fusion kinetics, aspect ratios extracted from public microscopy datasets), and interactome/expression context. Using this resource, we will train interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating AlphaFold-derived structural embeddings and disorder/PTM annotations) to predict emergent material properties from molecular features, explicitly testing whether scaling laws or phase diagrams generalize across protein families and cellular contexts. Second, we will cross-reference predicted material-property phenotypes with functional perturbation datasets (e.g., condensate-disrupting mutations linked to disease, optogenetic clustering screens) to test causal links between mesoscale material state and higher-order cellular function, addressing long-standing puzzles such as why chemically similar condensates (e.g., stress granules vs. P-bodies) exhibit distinct dynamics and functional consequences. 

This synthesis is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative imaging analysis, and cell biology, plus computational infrastructure to harmonize heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets. NCEMS support will enable dataset harmonization workshops, shared computational pipelines, and coordination across geographically distributed labs. All curated datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned community resource (FAIR-compliant), with tutorials and hackathon-style training events specifically designed to onboard graduate students and postdocs into data-intensive condensate biology, cultivating a new generation of researchers fluent in both wet-lab condensate biophysics and computational data synthesis.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic mesoscale emergent phenomenon, arising from multivalent, low-affinity interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct biophysical properties and cellular functions. Despite an explosion of data characterizing condensates across scales—from intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence features to interactome networks to live-cell imaging phenotypes—the field lacks an integrated framework connecting molecular grammar to cellular outcome. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize disparate, publicly available datasets spanning five layers of biological organization: (1) sequence/structural databases of phase-separating proteins (PhaSepDB, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CatGRANULE outputs); (2) proteome-wide interactome and post-translational modification data (BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus, STRING); (3) cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution imaging datasets depicting condensate ultrastructure (EMDB, CZI Imaging Data Resource); (4) single-molecule and FRAP kinetic measurements of condensate dynamics deposited in supplementary datasets across hundreds of published studies; and (5) single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic data linking condensate-associated protein expression to cellular phenotypes and disease states (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, CCLE). No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, biophysical expertise, and cell biology domain knowledge required to harmonize these heterogeneous, non-standardized datasets—many collected with different assay conditions, buffer compositions, and imaging modalities—into a unified predictive model. This is precisely the kind of large-scale, cross-disciplinary synthesis challenge NCEMS is positioned to catalyze. Our working group will bring together biophysicists specializing in polymer theory of LLPS, structural biologists with cryo-EM/ET expertise, computational biologists skilled in graph-based interactome analysis, and cell biologists studying condensate function in stress response, transcription, and neurodegeneration. We will develop a standardized ontology and data harmonization pipeline (leveraging FAIR principles) to align sequence features, biophysical parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity, surface tension), and phenotypic readouts into a unified multi-scale database. Using this integrated resource, we will apply machine learning and biophysical modeling to test three novel hypotheses: (i) whether condensate material properties (liquid vs. gel vs. solid) can be predicted from combinatorial sequence grammar and interactor stoichiometry; (ii) whether condensate emergence thresholds correlate with disease-associated mutations across cancer and neurodegeneration datasets; and (iii) whether evolutionary conservation patterns in IDRs predict condensate functional conservation across species. Deliverables include an open-access, versioned meta-database (deposited via Zenodo/GitHub with full analytical code), a generalizable predictive model of condensate emergence, and reproducible workflows adhering to community open-science standards. The project will directly train 4-6 graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, biophysical modeling, and open science practices through structured hackathons and co-mentorship across participating labs. By synthesizing molecular-scale sequence data with cellular-scale phenotypic outcomes, this working group will resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—how simple sequence and interaction rules generate the emergent complexity of condensate behavior—while establishing a template for future mesoscale synthesis research supported by NCEMS.

This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell biology, and machine learning—to integrate five classes of publicly available data: (1) curated LLPS driver/scaffold databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSepPro) and disorder annotations (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) structural and interaction data from the PDB, EMDB, and AlphaFold/ESMFold predicted structures, including cryo-ET tomograms of native condensates; (3) single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, HuBMAP, Tabula Sapiens) capturing condensate-associated protein expression across cell states; (4) high-throughput perturbation datasets (Perturb-seq, genome-wide CRISPR screens, ORFeome overexpression libraries) linking condensate-associated genes to cellular phenotypes; and (5) live-cell imaging repositories (e.g., OpenCell, LLPSDB) documenting condensate dynamics, material properties, and stress responses. No single dataset or lab possesses the breadth needed to bridge molecular sequence features to emergent mesoscale phase behavior and its physiological consequences—this synthesis requires simultaneous fluency in biophysical polymer theory, structural bioinformatics, single-cell genomics, and network-based phenotype mapping. Our central hypothesis is that a generalizable 'molecular grammar'—combinations of valency, disorder patterning, post-translational modification sites, and RNA-binding motifs—predicts not only condensate formation propensity but also material state transitions (liquid-to-gel-to-solid) that underlie both normal cellular function and disease-associated aggregation. We will develop multi-modal graph neural network models trained on integrated sequence-structure-interaction data, validated against independent perturbation and imaging datasets, to predict emergent condensate properties and their causal links to cellular outcomes such as stress granule dynamics, transcriptional condensate function, and neurodegeneration-associated aggregation. The working group will produce: (i) an open, harmonized multi-omic condensate database with standardized ontologies, (ii) predictive models and interactive tools for the community, and (iii) a mechanistic framework connecting molecular-scale grammar to mesoscale emergence and cellular phenotype. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be released under FAIR and open-science principles via community repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase). The project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, reproducible computational workflows, and collaborative team science, directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how simple molecular rules give rise to complex, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in living cells.

title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates: A Cross-Species, Multi-Omics Synthesis of Mesoscale Emergence and Its Cellular Consequences
title_norm: decoding the molecular grammar of biomolecular condensates a crossspecies multiomics synthesis of mesoscale emergence and its cellular consequences
abstract_text: The mesoscale emergence domain investigates biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation, where valuable datasets for phase behavior and clinical variants remain isolated by incompatible ontologies that prevent cross scale integration. Disconnected datasets leave a critical gap where no unified model connects the molecular sequence features of condensate forming proteins to mesoscale material properties and cellular scale phenotypic outcomes. The primary objective will determine quantitative rules connecting sequences to cellular phenotypes utilizing a four phase synthesis strategy that applies extract transform load pipelines, attention based models, and gradient boosted trees to map sequences to material states. The project will integrate databases including PhaSepDB, OpenCell, and ClinVar by building a unified relational and graph database schema that maps identifiers across sources and establishes a consensus material state ontology. A validated sequence to function model will predict pathological phase behavior from genetic data, explain evolutionary conservation patterns, and identify the mechanistic basis of disease associated mutations.
full_text: This project studies mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates and seeks unified models connecting molecular sequences to cellular phenotypes. Available datasets for phase behavior and clinical variants remain isolated and use incompatible ontologies that prevent cross scale integration. The study determines rules connecting sequences to condensate properties to enable prediction of pathological behavior from genetic data. The four phase strategy synthesizes data through harmonization and machine learning before validation of predictions against single cell datasets. The team applies extract transform load pipelines and gradient boosted trees alongside attention based models and sparse regression techniques. Results will undergo validation through nested cross validation and comparison against biophysical null models and held out perturbation datasets. The project extracts information from resources including PhaSepDB and OpenCell alongside the Human Cell Atlas and ClinVar databases. The researchers will integrate these sources by building a unified relational schema to map identifiers and establish consensus ontologies. The schema resolves incompatible units while stratified cross validation and independent test splits mitigate risks of overfitting and leakage. The two year timeline progresses from data harmonization to modeling of sequences before integration of variants and final validation. Processing large scale datasets requires cross disciplinary collaboration spanning biophysics and cell imaging alongside evolutionary genomics and structural biology. The project will publish open source code on GitHub and deposit harmonized data into repositories with persistent identifiers (DOIs). The team unites senior investigators with graduate students and visiting early career scholars from minority serving institutions for training.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation and related processes—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to functional subcellular compartments not predictable from any single molecule's properties. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive 'grammar' linking molecular-scale features (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalency, stoichiometry, post-translational modification patterns) to mesoscale material properties (droplet viscosity, multiphase architecture, client selectivity) and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes (stress granule dynamics, transcriptional bursting, cell fate transitions). This gap persists because the necessary data are scattered across incompatible resources curated by disconnected communities: biophysicists studying in vitro phase diagrams, cell biologists generating high-content imaging atlases, proteomicists cataloging condensate constituents, evolutionary biologists tracking IDR conservation, and clinical genomicists annotating disease-associated mutations. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these disparate data types into a coherent cross-scale model. This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, computational structural biologists, cell imaging specialists, evolutionary genomicists, and clinical variant scientists to synthesize existing public datasets—including PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and LLPSDB (condensate composition and phase behavior), OpenCell and the Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization imaging), BioGRID/IntAct (interactomes), Human Cell Atlas and single-cell perturbation atlases (transcriptomic consequences across cell states), OrthoDB/Ensembl (cross-species IDR conservation), and ClinVar/COSMIC/gnomAD (disease-linked mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Using this integrated dataset, we will: (1) train interpretable machine learning models that map sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features to empirically observed condensate material states and client recruitment specificity; (2) test whether evolutionary conservation patterns of IDR grammar predict functional robustness or tunability of condensate properties across orthologous proteins in diverse species; (3) determine whether disease-associated mutations in condensate scaffolds and clients cluster at predicted grammar 'hotspots' and whether this predicts pathological mesoscale-to-cellular phenotypic outcomes (e.g., aberrant stress granule persistence in neurodegeneration, altered chromatin condensate formation in cancer); and (4) build a generalizable cross-scale predictive framework linking molecular grammar to emergent cellular behavior, tested against independent public single-cell perturbation datasets. This synthesis is intractable for any individual lab given the scale of data harmonization, cross-domain expertise, and computational infrastructure required, and directly requires NCEMS support for data engineering, workshop convening, and shared analytical infrastructure. The Working Group will operate under FAIR and open-science principles, releasing all harmonized datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows via public repositories. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on each data-integration module, receiving structured training in multi-omics data science, biophysical modeling, and collaborative team science, while a rotating visiting-scholar program will recruit early-career researchers from primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions to broaden participation. The project's central deliverable—a public, cross-species 'condensate grammar atlas'—will provide the field's first quantitative bridge between molecular sequence, mesoscale organization, and cellular emergent behavior.

title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Mesoscale Emergence: A Cross-Database Synthesis Linking Biomolecular Condensate Sequence Features to Material States and Cellular Phenotypes
title_norm: decoding the molecular grammar of mesoscale emergence a crossdatabase synthesis linking biomolecular condensate sequence features to material states and cellular phenotypes
abstract_text: The research examines biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation and their emergent mesoscale material properties, which are extensively cataloged but currently omitted from predictive models of phase separating proteins. The field currently lacks a unified framework connecting primary amino acid sequence features to condensate physical material states across incompatible data repositories to explain cellular morphology and disease. The primary objective is to determine how amino acid sequence patterning dictates condensate physical states, and this project will apply protein language models, gradient boosted classifiers, and deep learning image segmentation to achieve this goal. Datasets including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, ClinVar, and the Human Protein Atlas will be integrated into a unified relational database utilizing automated entity resolution via UniProt crosswalks and a standardized material property ontology. This research will establish a mechanistic framework linking molecular sequences to mesoscale properties, providing essential insights into evolutionary constraints, organelle morphology, neurodegeneration, and cancer using exclusively existing data.
full_text: This research investigates biomolecular condensates formed by liquid phase separation and the missing framework linking sequences to material properties. Researchers have cataloged proteins for phase separation but data reside in incompatible repositories and predictive models ignore material states. The central question investigates how sequence patterns dictate material states to provide insights into evolutionary constraints and diseases using existing data. The overall study design synthesizes data from public repositories to train models of machine learning for predictions of material states in condensates. Key methods involve automated resolution of entities and language models for proteins alongside classifiers and algorithms for image segmentation. Model predictions require validation via nested loops of cross validation alongside structural data from cryo electron tomograms and imaging archives. The project utilizes public datasets from the Human Protein Atlas and UniProt alongside specialized repositories like ClinVar and COSMIC. Distinct datasets will form a unified relational database utilizing automated resolution of entities and a standardized ontology for material states of condensates. The team will mitigate leakage of data from homology through stratification and resolve heterogeneous metrics using a controlled material ontology. The project spans two years and sequences milestones from data harmonization to modeling and final analyses of diseases and evolution. This comprehensive scope requires collaboration across disciplines to unite biological expertise with computational infrastructure on a large scale across laboratories. The team will release code and data under licenses for open source software using public repositories to ensure full reproducibility. The team comprises investigators and trainees who will receive education across disciplines in biophysical modeling and workflows in open science.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation—represent a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon in which collective molecular interactions give rise to emergent material properties (liquid, gel, solid, multiphase architectures) that are not predictable from any single constituent protein or RNA. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, proteomic condensate composition datasets, cryo-electron tomography structural data, live-cell imaging archives, disease mutation catalogs, and functional genomics screens are housed in disconnected repositories, analyzed with incompatible metrics, and rarely cross-validated against one another. No individual laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, computational sequence analysis, cell imaging, evolutionary genomics, and clinical genetics needed to integrate these resources into a unified predictive framework. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize eight major public data classes—LLPSDB and PhaSepDB (experimentally curated phase-separating proteins and conditions), CD-CODE (condensate composition and localization), MobiDB/DisProt (intrinsically disordered region annotations), EMDB cryo-electron tomograms of native condensates, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular imaging, ClinVar/COSMIC disease variants mapped onto disordered regions, multi-species sequence conservation (OrthoDB, UCSC multiz alignments), and DepMap/BioGRID-ORCS functional perturbation screens—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Our central scientific question is: what molecular grammar (sequence patterning of stickers, spacers, charge blocks, and short linear motifs) determines the emergent mesoscale material state and multiphase organization of condensates, and how do these physical properties causally propagate to organelle-level morphology and cell-scale phenotypes, including their disruption in disease? We will apply stickers-and-spacers biophysical theory and modern sequence-to-function machine learning models, trained on the harmonized dataset, to predict material state and client selectivity directly from primary sequence, then validate predictions against orthogonal image-derived morphological signatures (condensate number, size, sphericity, coalescence dynamics) extracted computationally from public imaging archives. We will further test whether disease-associated mutations preferentially alter predicted material properties rather than simple phase separation propensity, and whether evolutionary conservation patterns track functionally important mesoscale properties rather than sequence identity alone. This effort demands NCEMS-scale infrastructure: standardized ontologies for condensate material properties, automated cross-database entity resolution (protein identifiers, cell lines, imaging conditions), and computational pipelines for large-scale image feature extraction—capabilities beyond any single lab or existing bilateral collaboration. The team will unite condensate biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational/AI researchers, evolutionary biologists, and clinical geneticists across institutions varying in size and geography. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across all analytical stages, receiving hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, biophysical modeling, and open-science workflows. All harmonized datasets, trained models, analysis code, and condensate material-property ontologies will be released under FAIR principles via public repositories, providing a durable community resource for predicting and interpreting mesoscale emergence in cell biology and disease.

abstract_text: In cell biology and biophysics, biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation represent an important phenomenon driven by intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent motifs, RNA binding domains, and post translational modifications. Fragmented data across disconnected databases currently prevents the development of a predictive model connecting protein molecular features to emergent condensate material properties and subsequent cellular or pathological effects. The primary objective is to predict condensate formation, material properties, and disease associated mutation impacts; this project will apply machine learning tools including ontology mapping, sequence based transformer models, graph neural networks, and logistic regression. This project will integrate LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PDB, AlphaFold DB, Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, BioGRID, STRING, ClinVar, COSMIC, and PhosphoSitePlus by developing a shared UniProt ontology and standardized feature representations. This research will identify generalized principles of self organization and disease mechanisms without new experimental measurements, providing a predictive framework to understand emergent mesoscale condensate behavior.
full_text: This cell biology and biophysics project investigates biomolecular condensates because no predictive models connect molecular features to emergent material properties. Intrinsically disordered regions and diverse motifs drive phase separation but understanding remains incomplete because relevant datasets are fragmented. The primary question tests whether integrating existing public datasets can predict condensate formation and material properties without new experiments. This computational project utilizes machine learning to analyze existing datasets across overlapping phases for harmonization and model development. The analytical approach deploys ontology mapping and enrichment statistics alongside transformer models based on sequences and graph neural networks. The team will validate results by excluding specific protein families and testing predictions against independent datasets (screens across the proteome). The team will extract information from phase separation databases (LLPSDB) alongside structural resources including AlphaFold DB and PDB. The team will integrate datasets by developing a shared ontology and creating standardized feature representations based on UniProt identifiers. The project will mitigate inconsistent nomenclature and varying experimental conditions by deploying the shared harmonization ontology to standardize data. The timeline of 24 months encompasses overlapping phases for model development and validation alongside multiple scheduled workshops for data synthesis. This project necessitates collaboration across disciplines because integrating diverse data types requires specialized expertise exceeding single laboratory capabilities. The team will release harmonized datasets and code on GitHub and Zenodo while providing a web interface for queries. The team embeds graduate trainees with principal investigators to facilitate training in the integration of multiple omics datasets.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications give rise to macroscopic material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that in turn drive cellular functions such as transcriptional control, stress response, and signal transduction. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across biophysics, structural biology, proteomics, and cell imaging, the field lacks a unified framework connecting molecular-scale determinants to emergent mesoscale behavior and downstream cellular/disease phenotypes. This proposal assembles a Working Group to synthesize disparate public datasets—including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and CD-CODE (condensate composition and in vitro phase behavior), AlphaFold DB and PDB (structural/disorder predictions), Human Protein Atlas and Human Cell Atlas (expression, subcellular localization, single-cell heterogeneity), BioGRID/STRING (interactomes), and ClinVar/COSMIC (disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—to build a predictive, cross-scale model of condensate emergence. Our central question: Can molecular-level features (sequence grammar, valency, PTM sites, structural disorder) combined with cellular context (expression stoichiometry, localization, network connectivity) predict which proteins form condensates, the material properties of those condensates, and their functional or pathological consequences when perturbed by disease mutations? This question cannot be addressed by any single lab, as it requires integrating fundamentally different data modalities—biophysical phase diagrams, structural predictions, single-cell transcriptomics/proteomics, network biology, and clinical genomics—each requiring distinct domain expertise (biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists). The Working Group will develop harmonized ontologies and standardized feature representations across these datasets, construct machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating interactome topology and sequence-based transformers for disorder/valency prediction) to predict condensate propensity and material state, and validate predictions against orthogonal public datasets (e.g., proteome-wide condensate screens, stress granule proteomics). A key innovation is testing whether emergent condensate properties can be predicted purely from public data integration without new wet-lab experiments, and whether disease mutations disrupt predicted phase behavior in ways that explain pathological phenotypes (e.g., ALS-associated FUS/TDP-43 mutations). The team will include biophysicists (LLPS theory), structural biologists (AlphaFold-based feature engineering), computational/systems biologists (network and ML integration), cell biologists (phenotypic validation using public imaging), and clinical genomics experts (mutation-disease linkage), spanning multiple career stages and institutions. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams, receiving training in multi-omics data integration, reproducible computational pipelines, and biophysical modeling. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with a FAIR-compliant condensate feature database, enabling the broader community to test hypotheses about mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. This work directly advances NCEMS's mission by using purely existing data to resolve a fundamental puzzle in emergent cellular organization, requiring collaboration far beyond individual lab capacity, and producing durable, reusable synthesis resources for the field.

full_text: This project explores mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates formed through separation of liquid phases to understand their material properties. Biomolecular condensates self organize via multivalent interactions into distinct structures but extensive multiscale data remain disconnected across specific systems. The proposed study investigates how molecular features govern properties of condensates to establish a predictive framework for emergent cellular phenomena. The two year project for synthesis of data harmonizes structural information and imaging features to construct a validated relational database. The analytical strategy applies gradient boosted trees and attention based models alongside automated segmentation of images and analysis of networks. Results undergo evaluation using stratified cross validation and sensitivity analyses against held out systems of condensates and imaging modalities. The team analyzes information from repositories of sequences (DisProt) and databases of structures such as AlphaFold DB and BioImage Archive. Integrating these diverse data requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide simultaneous expertise across fields of biophysics and computer vision. The investigators follow open science principles by sharing containerized workflows (Docker) and code via repositories and open access journals. The diverse team includes core investigators and graduate trainees receiving mentored instruction in reproducible computational biology and stewardship of data.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where collective molecular interactions produce organelle-like structures with properties (viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability) not predictable from any single protein's biochemistry. Despite thousands of published studies characterizing individual condensates, the field lacks a unified, cross-scale understanding of which sequence features, structural motifs, and interaction network topologies causally determine condensate material properties and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists because relevant data are fragmented across incompatible resources: intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence databases (e.g., DisProt, MobiDB), condensate proteome catalogs (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), protein-protein interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING), structural data from cryo-EM/cryo-ET and AlphaFold, quantitative live-cell imaging datasets (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, condensate size/number distributions from the Cell Image Library and BioImage Archive), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic datasets capturing phenotypic consequences of condensate dysregulation in disease contexts (ALS, cancer). Specific aims include: (1) Curate and harmonize condensate proteomic, sequence, and structural datasets into a standardized ontology capturing IDR composition, multivalency, post-translational modification sites, and predicted AlphaFold conformational ensembles; (2) Develop machine learning models trained on quantitative imaging-derived material property measurements (droplet fusion rates, FRAP recovery kinetics, aspect ratios) to identify sequence/network features predictive of condensate viscoelasticity and stability across previously siloed studies; (3) Integrate condensate composition data with protein interaction networks and single-cell omics to test whether network centrality and connectivity of condensate-resident proteins predict cellular sensitivity to condensate perturbation (e.g., in stress granule dynamics during disease); (4) Build a publicly accessible, version-controlled computational pipeline and interactive database (following FAIR principles) enabling the community to query molecular determinants of mesoscale emergence across cell types and organisms.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it demands reconciling incompatible data formats, resolving conflicting condensate classification schemes across independent labs, and computational infrastructure for cross-referencing structural, network, and imaging data at scale—tasks infeasible for any individual collaboration. The working group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computer science, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, FAIR data stewardship, and emergence-focused hypothesis generation. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open-source resource, establishing a reusable framework for mesoscale emergence research applicable beyond condensate biology to other multi-scale cellular phenomena.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related processes—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular processes such as transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, our understanding remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based predictors of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent motifs (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, PLAAC, catGRANULE outputs), curated condensate composition and localization databases (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), high-content imaging repositories capturing condensate morphology and dynamics (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Cell Explorer), interactome and PTM databases (BioGRID, STRING, PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) linking condensate-associated mutations to disease. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these heterogeneous, multi-scale datasets into a unified predictive framework. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists to synthesize these public resources and address a fundamental question: what molecular-level 'grammar'—sequence composition, valency, PTM patterning, and stoichiometry—determines the emergent mesoscale material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally propagate to higher-order cellular phenotypes and disease states?

Our approach will proceed in three integrated phases. First, we will construct a harmonized, ontology-linked meta-database that cross-references sequence/structural features of condensate-forming proteins with experimentally reported material properties (extracted via text-mining and manual curation from published biophysical assays) and cellular imaging phenotypes. Second, we will apply machine learning and biophysical polymer models to identify generalizable sequence-to-material-property relationships, testing whether emergent condensate behaviors (e.g., liquid-to-gel transitions, multiphase architecture) can be predicted purely from primary sequence and interactome context, independent of any single protein family. Third, we will link these mesoscale signatures to organismal and disease-relevant outcomes by integrating single-cell transcriptomic stress-response datasets (GEO, Human Cell Atlas) and disease variant databases, testing whether condensate-destabilizing mutations converge on shared material-property signatures across neurodegenerative and cancer-associated proteins.

This project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: it requires no new experiments, relies entirely on integration of existing public datasets across previously unlinked disciplines, and demands collaborative infrastructure beyond any individual lab's capacity, including standardized data harmonization pipelines, shared computational resources, and cross-domain expertise. All curated datasets, ontologies, and analysis code will be released as open-source, FAIR-compliant resources through NCEMS infrastructure, accompanied by a public database and interactive visualization tool for the condensate research community. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across sub-teams (data curation, ML modeling, biophysical validation, phenotype integration), receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and open data science practices, directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce central to NCEMS's mission while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how molecular-scale interactions generate emergent, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in cells.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid liquid phase separation regulate vital cellular processes through weak multivalent interactions, making the mesoscale emergence driven by intrinsically disordered regions, folded domains, and RNA fundamentally important. An integrated framework connecting primary sequence features to mesoscale material properties and disease phenotypes is lacking because existing biophysical and clinical data remain fragmented across disciplinary silos. To determine which sequence features predict condensate properties and how disease mutations perturb them, this project will derive quantitative rules linking primary sequences to cellular behaviors using gradient boosted trees, deep learning image segmentation, and mixed effects models. Sequence, condensate, imaging, and clinical variant databases, including UniProt, PhaSepDB, and ClinVar, will be integrated through a centralized data harmonization pipeline resolving identifier mismatches and linking image descriptors to biophysical predictors. Condensates regulate cellular processes through multivalent interactions but existing biophysical and imaging data remain fragmented across isolated academic disciplines. The project asks how sequence features predict condensate properties to provide a cross scale framework for designing targeted therapeutics. The investigators will freely share version controlled code and harmonized datasets through open access platforms including GitHub and Zenodo. Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (viscosity, selective permeability, reaction enhancement) arise from ensembles of weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, and RNA. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at multiple scales—proteomic composition (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS), sequence/disorder features (DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt), high-throughput in vitro phase diagrams, super-resolution and live-cell imaging (Cell Image Library, IDR/BioImage Archive), disease variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas)—these resources remain siloed within disciplinary boundaries (biophysics, structural biology, cell imaging, genetics, computational biology). No integrated framework currently links molecular-grammar features of condensate-forming proteins to their higher-order mesoscale material properties and ultimate cellular/phenotypic consequences, including disease-associated dysregulation.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and analytical framework: the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA). Our central scientific question is: What sequence-encoded and network-level features predict the emergent material and functional properties of condensates across scales, and how do disease-associated mutations perturb this sequence-to-phenotype mapping? We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Integrate sequence/disorder databases with biophysical phase-behavior datasets to derive quantitative 'condensate grammars'—stoichiometric and compositional rules linking IDR patterning, charge blockiness, and multivalency to phase diagram parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity); (2) Cross-reference these molecular grammars with public imaging datasets to test whether in vitro biophysical predictors explain observed in-cell condensate morphology, dynamics, and localization across cell types; (3) Map disease-associated variants (ALS, FTD, cancer) onto condensate-forming proteins to determine whether mutations systematically shift emergent mesoscale properties in ways that correlate with pathological cellular phenotypes from public multi-omic disease datasets.

This project is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics/phase-separation theory, machine learning on heterogeneous imaging/sequence data, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics, plus harmonization of incompatible data formats and scales across at least six major public repositories. NCEMS support will fund a coordinated data harmonization pipeline, shared computational infrastructure, and recurring cross-disciplinary working sessions to reconcile conflicting metrics of 'phase separation propensity' across source databases. All harmonized datasets, predictive models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with FAIR metadata standards, accompanied by interactive tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, co-developing cross-training modules in biophysics, imaging analytics, and genomics, and co-authoring resulting publications and open-source software—directly cultivating a new generation of data-savvy researchers equipped to study emergence phenomena at the mesoscale.

title: From Molecular Grammar to Mesoscale Material Properties: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence
title_norm: from molecular grammar to mesoscale material properties a multiomic synthesis of biomolecular condensate emergence
abstract_text: Within cell biology and biophysics, biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation possess distinct material properties and yield extensive sequence, structural, and imaging datasets critical for understanding cellular organization. Because these datasets remain in isolated and incompatible formats, researchers cannot systematically correlate molecular level sequence composition and valency to emergent mesoscale material behaviors across condensate types. To define rules governing condensate mesoscale properties and disease mutations, this project will execute a data synthesis pipeline extracting cross scale features using ontology harmonization schemas, graph neural networks, gradient boosted models, and Flory Huggins modeling. The project will integrate databases including DisProt, PhaSepDB, ClinVar, and JUMP Cell Painting via a standardized metadata schema, synthesizing diverse measurements into a unified relational cross scale property atlas. The resulting predictive cross scale biophysical framework will replace qualitative case by case observations, providing a fundamental basis for understanding and therapeutically targeting condensate related diseases.
full_text: This cell biology and biophysics project questions how molecular properties dictate material behaviors of condensates formed through phase separation. Incompatible formats of existing datasets currently prevent systematic correlations between molecular features and material behaviors of these condensates. The proposed study defines molecular rules of condensates to establish a predictive biophysical framework for targeting mutations related to disease. The non experimental design of this study uses a data synthesis pipeline to extract features and train machine learning models. The team will apply image segmentation and graph neural networks alongside gradient boosted models and SHAP value analysis. The team will validate results through generalization tests and benchmarking against null models based on physics including Flory-Huggins predictions. The proposed project utilizes biological datasets including DisProt and ClinVar alongside imaging repositories from the Allen Cell Institute. A controlled vocabulary will standardize identifiers of proteins and units of measurement to construct a relational cross scale property atlas. The team will mitigate inconsistencies in annotations and offsets in measurements by applying ontology schemas and conducting sensitivity analyses. The proposed two year project unfolds across four overlapping phases with milestone releases of data scheduled every six months. Integrating these diverse datasets strictly requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in polymer physics and machine learning. The researchers will publish open access preprints and deposit code on GitHub alongside datasets in FAIR compliant repositories. The cross disciplinary team includes faculty and trainees who will receive instruction in multiscale modeling and interdisciplinary communication.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: the collective behavior of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) gives rise to structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that are not predictable from any single molecular feature alone. Despite an explosion of publicly available data describing condensates at multiple scales—sequence-based IDR predictions (e.g., DisProt, MobiDB), condensate composition databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), in vitro phase diagrams, cryo-electron tomography of native condensate architecture, live-cell imaging with FRAP and single-molecule tracking (Allen Cell Institute, JUMP Cell Painting), proteome-wide interactome maps (BioGRID, STRING), and disease-associated mutation catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC)—these resources remain fragmented across incompatible formats, model organisms, and measurement scales. No unified framework currently links molecular-scale ‘grammar’ (sequence composition, valency, PTM state) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences (transcriptional output, stress granule dynamics, disease phenotypes).

This Working Group will synthesize these disparate public datasets into an integrated, multiscale resource and predictive framework for condensate emergence. Specifically, we will: (1) harmonize sequence/structural features (charge patterning, aromatic stickers, IDR length, PTM sites) across thousands of condensate-forming proteins; (2) integrate in vitro biophysical phase-diagram data with in-cell imaging-derived material property proxies (droplet size distributions, FRAP recovery rates, coalescence kinetics) to build a cross-scale property atlas; (3) apply machine learning and polymer physics-informed models to identify molecular determinants that predict emergent mesoscale behavior across condensate types (stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P-bodies); and (4) test whether disease-associated mutations systematically perturb predicted material properties, linking molecular lesions to mesoscale dysfunction and cellular phenotype.

This project is inherently a community-scale synthesis effort: no single lab possesses simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural biology, live-cell imaging analytics, proteomics, and machine learning required to integrate these heterogeneous datasets meaningfully. The Working Group will unite biophysicists specializing in phase separation theory, structural biologists working with cryo-ET/EM datasets, cell biologists with quantitative imaging expertise, computational biologists skilled in ML and network analysis, and data scientists focused on ontology harmonization—drawn from institutions varying in size, geography, and research intensity. NCEMS support is essential to provide the computational infrastructure, data harmonization pipelines, and cross-disciplinary coordination needed to reconcile disparate data modalities (sequence, structure, dynamics, phenotype) under shared ontologies and metadata standards.

All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analytical workflows will be released as an open, reproducible resource (via FAIR-compliant repositories and containerized pipelines), enabling the broader community to query condensate emergence principles across new protein systems. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across subteams, receiving hands-on training in data harmonization, multiscale modeling, and interdisciplinary science communication. By revealing generalizable rules connecting molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale material properties, this synthesis will resolve a long-standing puzzle in cell biology—how simple molecular interactions robustly generate complex, functional mesoscale architectures—and establish predictive tools for understanding condensate dysregulation in disease.

title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis from Sequence to Cellular Phenotype
title_norm: decoding the molecular grammar of biomolecular condensate emergence a multiscale data synthesis from sequence to cellular phenotype
abstract_text: Mesoscale cell biology investigates biomolecular condensates and liquid liquid phase separation, which requires computational integration across biological scales bridging in vitro sequence biophysics, cellular imaging, and systems biology network mapping. A fundamental gap persists regarding why specific proteins form condensates in certain cellular environments, as current studies lack computational models connecting molecular sequences to network interactions and cellular phenotypes. This research will determine whether emergent condensate properties are predictable by applying multi modal predictive modeling, graph neural networks, multi task learning, and interpretability algorithms to analyze molecular sequences, protein interaction networks, and biochemical states. Datasets including PhaSepDB, DisProt, BioGRID, and STRING will be integrated by mapping entries to UniProt accessions to structure sequence and biochemical data points as node features within a protein interaction network graph. This project will produce a quantitative multi scale model of condensate formation that will inform experimental design and improve the understanding of diseases such as neurodegeneration and cancer.
full_text: Mesoscale cell biology currently lacks models connecting molecular sequences to network interactions for predicting formation of biomolecular condensates. Current knowledge spans sequence biophysics and mapping of biological systems but lacks computational integration across distinct scales of biology. The proposed study asks if integrating public data predicts properties of condensates to improve multi scale models of neurodegeneration. The design of the study involves data harmonization and feature engineering followed by multi modal modeling and experimental validation. Key methods include graph neural networks and dimensionality reduction along with algorithms for interpretability like attention analysis and SHAP values. Validation utilizes stratified cross validation and benchmarking of single scale models against held out experimental data from plant proteomes. The proposed study will utilize datasets from public sources including MobiDB and DisProt along with OpenCell and PaxDb. Distinct datasets will map to UniProt accessions to structure sequence and biochemical data within a network of protein interactions. The team will mitigate identifier mismatches by building a pipeline for cross references using automated scripts and manual curation. The timeline spans two years to accomplish data harmonization and development of models prior to final validation and public dissemination. The expansive project scope requires collaboration across disciplines to combine simultaneous expertise in sequence biophysics and complex machine learning. The project will share preprints on bioRxiv and release containerized pipelines for analysis on GitHub to ensure open science. The team includes principal investigators and graduate students gaining experience across disciplines in data integration and multi modal modeling.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce organelle-like structures with distinct biochemical and mechanical properties. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across genomics, proteomics, structural biology, and live-cell imaging, the field lacks a unified, quantitative framework linking molecular sequence features to network-level interactions and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes. Individual labs have generated fragmented insights—biophysicists characterize intrinsically disordered region (IDR) grammar in vitro, cell biologists document condensate dynamics via imaging, and systems biologists map protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks—but no systematic integration exists to explain why some proteins condense in some cellular contexts and not others, or how emergent condensate properties (e.g., material state, composition, responsiveness) scale with underlying molecular features and network topology.

This Working Group proposes to synthesize five previously siloed classes of public data: (1) sequence-based IDR and low-complexity domain predictions (e.g., from MobiDB, PONDR-derived datasets); (2) curated condensate/LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro) cataloguing experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their in vitro conditions; (3) genome-scale PPI and co-expression networks (BioGRID, STRING, ProteomeHD); (4) quantitative single-cell imaging and localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas subcellular imaging, LLPSDB-linked microscopy) capturing condensate morphology, number, and dynamics; and (5) proteomic abundance and post-translational modification datasets (PhosphoSitePlus, PaxDb) that modulate condensation propensity in vivo. By harmonizing these disparate data types—spanning sequence, network, image, and abundance modalities—we will build predictive, mechanistic models of condensate emergence that no single dataset or disciplinary approach could achieve alone.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate emergence is governed by a combinatorial 'molecular grammar' operating simultaneously at three scales: intra-protein (IDR patterning, valency of interaction motifs), inter-protein (network connectivity, co-condensation partners), and cellular (local concentration, PTM state, compartment identity). We will use graph neural networks and multi-modal representation learning to integrate these layers, testing whether emergent condensate properties (size, number, material state, responsiveness to stress) can be predicted from lower-scale features, and identifying network motifs or sequence grammars that generalize across protein families and cell types. Validation will leverage held-out experimental datasets and cross-species comparisons (yeast, human, plant) to test universality of discovered rules.

This project requires collaboration among condensate biophysicists, network biologists, imaging data scientists, and machine learning experts—expertise no single lab possesses collectively—and NCEMS support for compute infrastructure, data harmonization workshops, and cross-database ontology alignment. The Working Group will include graduate students and postdocs in hands-on data integration, model-building, and reproducible workflow design, producing open-source pipelines, harmonized datasets, and a public condensate-emergence prediction resource. All code, integrated datasets, and models will be released under FAIR and open-science standards, providing a template for mesoscale emergence research broadly.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to new functional compartments with properties absent from their individual components. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets across biophysics, structural biology, proteomics, and cell imaging, no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features (sequence composition, disorder, post-translational modifications, multivalent interaction motifs) predict emergent mesoscale properties (condensate material state, size, dynamics, composition) and how these in turn shape cellular and organismal phenotypes. This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across incompatible repositories—biophysical LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), intrinsic disorder predictors (MobiDB, DisProt), structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome and proximity-labeling datasets (BioPlex, OpenCell, BioID studies), single-cell and super-resolution imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Cell Image Library), and disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC)—each curated by distinct research communities with disparate ontologies and quality standards. Synthesizing these resources into a coherent, queryable framework is beyond the scope of any single laboratory and requires sustained collaboration among biophysicists, structural biologists, cell biologists, computational scientists, and clinical genomicists.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team to build an integrated, open-access Mesoscale Condensate Atlas that links molecular sequence/structural features to emergent biophysical properties and downstream cellular outcomes. We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Harmonize existing LLPS, disorder, PTM, and interaction datasets into a standardized, machine-readable ontology, enabling systematic cross-referencing of condensate-forming proteins with their sequence-encoded valency, stickers-and-spacers architecture, and structural context. (2) Develop and validate machine learning and biophysical polymer models trained on this harmonized dataset to predict emergent condensate properties (formation propensity, viscosity, multiphase organization) directly from primary sequence and structural features, benchmarking against published in vitro and in-cell phase diagrams. (3) Connect predicted mesoscale properties to higher-order cellular phenotypes by integrating single-cell transcriptomic, proteomic, and imaging datasets, testing whether condensate material properties predicted from sequence correlate with transcriptional output, stress granule dynamics, or disease-associated mutation burden across public disease-variant repositories.

This effort satisfies NCEMS's synthesis mandate: it uses exclusively existing public data, requires integration across fundamentally distinct data modalities and expert communities, and promises insights—a predictive, generalizable grammar linking molecular sequence to emergent mesoscale behavior—unattainable by any single lab. The working group will include investigators from biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, and clinical genetics across multiple institutions and career stages, with explicit mechanisms for including early-career and underrepresented researchers. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analytical pipelines will be released as open, versioned, reproducible resources (via GitHub, Zenodo, and community platforms), accompanied by tutorials and hackathons that train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data synthesis, machine learning, and biophysical modeling—directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to build while addressing a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.

abstract_text: Within the domain of mesoscale emergence, biomolecular condensates perform vital cellular functions, and their formation and material properties are driven by isolated molecular characteristics like intrinsically disordered regions and RNA scaffolds. The primary objective is to determine if emergent condensate behaviors are predictable; this project will synthesize public datasets into a knowledge graph and train interpretable machine learning models including graph neural networks and matrix factorization. Resources including UniProt, Gene Ontology, BioGRID, and single cell atlases will be integrated into the knowledge graph by mapping data to stable identifiers and defining ontologies to represent typed molecular relationships. This work will output an analytical framework that shifts condensate biology to a predictive computational science, generating mechanistic hypotheses for disease associated phase transitions in mesoscale cellular systems.
full_text: Within mesoscale emergence this project studies biomolecular condensates to determine how molecular features and cellular contexts drive functional or persistent assembly. Current knowledge links isolated molecular characteristics to formation but these features cannot predict emergent behaviors across varying networks and contexts. The primary question asks whether integrated datasets can predict emergent behaviors to shift condensate biology toward a predictive computational science. This data synthesis study constructs a versioned knowledge graph from public data to train interpretable models without new experimental data. The core methods combine graph neural networks and matrix factorization with causal discovery analyses and Bayesian hierarchical models for interpretability. The models will be validated using held out benchmarks and cross dataset validation alongside the recovery of established biological mechanisms. The project will utilize curated condensate databases and spatial proteomics repositories alongside established resources like UniProt and the GWAS Catalog. These diverse datasets will be integrated into a versioned knowledge graph by mapping information to stable identifiers and controlled vocabularies. The team will mitigate data heterogeneity and missing negative classes by applying structured evidence scores and uncertainty aware machine learning. The thirty month timeline includes the initial development of a beta knowledge graph followed by refined models and community guidelines. This ambitious scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite domain expertise in cell biology with advanced machine learning capabilities. All harmonized metadata and orchestrated computational workflows will be released publicly under permissive licenses with stable version identifiers. The diverse team unites established researchers and graduate students across institutions to provide training in reproducible workflow development.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak, multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites can generate dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, compositions, and cellular functions. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some molecular assemblies form reversible, functional condensates, while others transition into aberrant, persistent, or disease-associated states? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from publicly available molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and perturbation phenotypes.

This working group will integrate existing public datasets spanning scales from sequence to cell state. Data sources will include curated condensate and phase-separation databases, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification repositories, protein-RNA interaction maps, affinity and proximity interaction datasets, spatial proteomics, public live-cell imaging datasets, CRISPR perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic atlases, and disease-variant resources. We will harmonize these datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph linking condensate-associated biomolecules to physicochemical features, interaction topology, cell-type context, subcellular localization, perturbation outcomes, and reported material or dynamical properties.

The central scientific question is: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts give rise to distinct mesoscale condensate phenotypes, including nucleation propensity, compositional selectivity, fusion dynamics, stress responsiveness, and pathological persistence? To answer this, the project will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models that distinguish condensate classes and identify higher-order feature combinations not apparent from individual datasets. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that cannot be inferred from single molecules alone, such as multicomponent interaction density, RNA-dependent buffering, post-translational modification logic, and context-specific rewiring during stress, differentiation, or disease.

This effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or infrastructure to synthesize the relevant public data types at community scale. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, network theorists, machine-learning researchers, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS workshops will enable consensus building around condensate ontologies, metadata standards, uncertainty scoring, benchmark datasets, and reproducible analytical workflows.

Expected outcomes include: an open condensate emergence knowledge graph; benchmark datasets for predicting mesoscale condensate behaviors; interpretable models identifying molecular and contextual rules of condensate formation and maturation; and community guidelines for integrating heterogeneous condensate data. The project will train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows through team-based data synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-disciplinary short courses on open science, graph analytics, and AI-assisted biological discovery. All code, harmonized metadata, model outputs, tutorials, and manuscripts will be released publicly under open licenses.

By synthesizing diverse public data rather than generating new experiments, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do molecular-scale features collectively produce emergent mesoscale organization that shapes cellular behavior? The resulting framework will advance predictive understanding of condensates and provide a reusable model for studying emergence across other subcellular systems.

title: Synthesis of Public Multi-Omic and Imaging Data to Predict Emergent Biomolecular Condensate States and Cellular Outcomes
title_norm: synthesis of public multiomic and imaging data to predict emergent biomolecular condensate states and cellular outcomes
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates form through multivalent interactions and intrinsically disordered regions, representing a critical mesoscale biology domain where disconnected imaging and omics data impede the development of complete predictive models. It remains unclear why identical scaffold proteins adopt different contextual states, leaving unresolved contradictions regarding specific protein behaviors and what differentiates adaptive condensate states from pathological conditions. This computational synthesis will identify rules linking molecular composition and cellular context to condensate behavior by applying multimodal representation learning, graph neural networks, and causal discovery algorithms to analyze public datasets. Databases including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, PhaSepDB, and ProteomeXchange will be standardized using a novel condensate state ontology and integrated into a comprehensive knowledge graph connecting molecules, phenotypes, and perturbations. This research will produce a comprehensive synthesis atlas and multimodal benchmark datasets to reconcile conflicting findings and distinguish adaptive from pathological condensates for future investigations.
full_text: This project investigates mesoscale biology of biomolecular condensates to understand differences between adaptive and pathological states across cellular contexts. Current knowledge of multivalent interactions lacks predictive models and produces contradictions because existing imaging and omics data remain disconnected. The research identifies rules connecting molecular composition to cellular phenotypes to produce a novel multimodal synthesis atlas for researchers. This purely computational study integrates public imaging and omics data into a knowledge graph to develop predictive models. The team applies multimodal representation learning and causal discovery algorithms alongside pipelines for image segmentation including CellProfiler and scikit-image. Results undergo validation via nested cross validation and tasks for negative control utilizing metrics (like balanced accuracy and calibration error). This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in biophysics and computational modeling for building integrative models. The team will release all code and outputs from models through version controlled repositories using permissive open source licenses. The cross disciplinary team provides graduate students and postdoctoral scholars with targeted training in biophysics and machine learning.
