abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, lipids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications generate dynamic compartments whose properties cannot be inferred from any single component. Yet a central puzzle remains unresolved: why do the same scaffold proteins form distinct condensate states across cell types, stresses, developmental programs, and disease contexts, and when do these states become adaptive versus pathological? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, cellular, and imaging datasets to identify generalizable rules linking molecular composition to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will integrate diverse resources including Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive datasets, Cell Painting profiles, ProteomeXchange and PRIDE proteomics, GEO and SRA transcriptomics, public phosphoproteomics and ubiquitinomics, RBP and RNA interactome datasets, PhaSepDB and DrLLPS condensate annotations, AlphaFold-derived structural features, DepMap perturbation screens, and public stress-response and neurodegeneration datasets. The project will address three questions: (1) Which combinations of molecular features predict condensate formation, morphology, dynamics, and localization across cellular contexts? (2) Which context variables, such as phosphorylation state, RNA abundance, expression stoichiometry, and stress history, explain apparent contradictions in published condensate behavior? (3) Which emergent condensate states are associated with beneficial stress adaptation, impaired proteostasis, altered signaling, or cell vulnerability? We will build an open condensate synthesis atlas that harmonizes heterogeneous public datasets into a FAIR knowledge graph connecting molecules, interactions, modifications, imaging phenotypes, perturbations, and cellular outcomes. Analytical innovations will include multimodal representation learning for combining images and omics, graph-based causal discovery to separate correlates from candidate drivers, biophysically informed machine learning features such as disorder, multivalency, charge patterning, and interaction valence, and community benchmark tasks for predicting condensate localization and phenotype transitions. NCEMS support is essential because the work requires coordination beyond any single laboratory: cell biologists and biophysicists to define condensate states, imaging scientists to standardize visual phenotypes, proteomic and transcriptomic experts to harmonize context-specific molecular measurements, computational scientists to develop scalable integrative models, and statisticians to establish uncertainty-aware cross-dataset inference. The Working Group will include researchers across institution types, career stages, and geographic regions, with dedicated roles for graduate students and postdoctoral scholars in data curation, reproducible workflow development, and collaborative model benchmarking. Trainees will participate in NCEMS-supported hackathons and short courses on open data integration, image analysis, graph machine learning, and team science. All code, harmonized metadata, analysis workflows, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly through version-controlled repositories and community-governed standards. The anticipated outcome is a predictive, reusable framework for understanding condensates as emergent mesoscale systems, transforming fragmented public data into testable principles for how molecular interactions scale into cellular organization and phenotype.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules, nucleoli, and disease associated protein assemblies, form through weak multivalent interactions and influence vital cellular processes across numerous physiological and pathological contexts. Fragmented public data prevents unified cross system analysis, leaving an open question regarding the generalizable rules that connect condensate molecular composition to emergent material states and cellular outcomes. This project will identify emergent molecular features driving adaptive, inert, or pathological outcomes by harmonizing heterogeneous datasets into interoperable knowledge graphs to train predictive models using feature engineering, graph neural networks, and Bayesian models. Proteomic, imaging, and genetic databases including PRIDE, BioGRID, and ClinVar will be integrated by mapping components to standardized identifiers to build a condensate centered knowledge graph featuring probabilistic membership assignments. The resulting framework will model condensates as integrated systems to predict cellular phenotypes, establishing essential metadata standards and reusable infrastructure to advance downstream research.
full_text: This project investigates biomolecular condensates (stress granules and nucleoli) to discover rules connecting composition to emergent states and cellular outcomes. Condensates form via weak interactions to influence cellular processes but existing public data remains fragmented across diverse disciplines. The primary objective identifies mesoscale features determining adaptive outcomes to model condensates as integrated systems and establish standards. This non experimental synthesis approach harmonizes existing public datasets into interoperable knowledge graphs to train predictive computational models. Key methods include feature engineering and random forests and graph neural networks alongside Bayesian models and causal discovery. The team validates results using nested cross validation against held out cell types and distinct temporal perturbation splits. A central innovation is to move beyond cataloging condensate components toward modeling condensates as mesoscale systems whose collective features explain higher-order outcomes such as stress survival, transcriptional bursting, genome stability, viral replication, and neurodegenerative toxicity. By synthesizing public data across scales, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular science, generate testable hypotheses for the broader community, and establish open analytical strategies for studying emergence in complex cellular assemblies.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are paradigmatic mesoscale structures: they emerge from weak, multivalent molecular interactions yet can reorganize signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and disease phenotypes. Despite thousands of studies, the field lacks a predictive synthesis explaining why the same protein can form a condensate in one cellular context but remain diffuse in another, or when condensate formation produces measurable cellular outcomes. This working group will integrate publicly available molecular, imaging, and functional genomic data to answer a central question: What combinations of molecular grammar, cellular state, and interaction context are sufficient to predict the emergence and phenotypic consequences of biomolecular condensates?

We will build an open, cross-scale Condensate Emergence Atlas by harmonizing existing datasets that are currently siloed across disciplines. Molecular features will be extracted from public protein sequence resources, AlphaFold structures, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification databases, RNA-binding datasets, protein-protein interaction maps, and condensate-specific repositories such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and curated literature-derived annotations. Mesoscale localization and morphology will be synthesized from public imaging resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, and published high-content microscopy datasets. Cellular state and outcome layers will incorporate public transcriptomics, proteomics, stress-response time courses, Perturb-seq and CRISPR screen datasets, DepMap dependencies, and disease-associated variant resources.

The project will develop reusable analytical strategies for emergence research. First, we will create controlled vocabularies and probabilistic labels for condensate presence, morphology, dynamics, and cellular context, explicitly representing uncertainty across datasets. Second, we will use interpretable machine learning and graph-based models to connect molecular features, interaction networks, RNA context, post-translational modifications, and cell-state variables to observed mesoscale condensate formation. Third, we will test whether inferred condensate states explain higher-level cellular outcomes, such as stress survival, transcriptional rewiring, growth defects, and disease variant impact, beyond predictions from single-molecule properties alone. The central deliverable will be a set of open models that distinguish generalizable principles from dataset-specific artifacts and generate prioritized, experimentally testable hypotheses for the broader community.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the combined expertise or infrastructure to integrate image analysis, protein biophysics, RNA biology, cell biology, network science, functional genomics, and open-science software engineering at this scale. The working group will include condensate biologists, computational biophysicists, bioimage analysts, data curators, machine-learning researchers, cell-state and genomics experts, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working sessions will be used to establish shared data standards, perform collaborative model benchmarking, train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible synthesis workflows, and engage community stakeholders who maintain relevant public resources.

All products will follow open science principles: curated metadata, harmonized feature tables, analysis notebooks, containerized workflows, model code, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released publicly with clear documentation and community contribution mechanisms. By transforming fragmented public observations into a predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental mystery in molecular and cellular sciences: how molecular-scale properties combine with cellular context to generate emergent mesoscale organization and cell-level consequences.

title: Predicting Emergent Membraneless Organelle States by Synthesizing Proteome-Scale Phase-Separation, Interaction, Imaging, and Perturbation Data
title_norm: predicting emergent membraneless organelle states by synthesizing proteomescale phaseseparation interaction imaging and perturbation data
abstract_text: Mesoscale cellular biology investigates the emergence of membraneless organelles and biomolecular condensates, but established molecular drivers like low complexity sequences and charge patterning frequently reflect measurement artifacts rather than general design principles. The field lacks a predictive systems level framework to differentiate context specific observations from fundamental rules determining functional versus aberrant disease linked condensate states. To determine how molecular features and cellular contexts dictate emergent condensate identity, this non experimental project will utilize graph neural networks, machine learning models, causal inference, and CellProfiler to extract phenotypes and evaluate functional outcomes. Information from repositories including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, UniProt, BioGRID, and Image Data Resource will be synthesized into a versioned knowledge graph that uses a shared condensate state ontology to link experimental conditions and phenotypes. This research will establish a cross scale predictive framework and create reusable community infrastructure to elucidate the mesoscale biological emergence and downstream cellular function of membraneless organelles.
full_text: Mesoscale cellular biology lacks a systems level framework to predict whether biomolecular condensates form functional or aberrant disease states. Current studies identify formation factors (like RNA valency) but yield context specific observations that cannot isolate general design principles. The proposed study asks how molecular features determine condensate identity to establish a cross scale framework using public data. This non experimental data synthesis project integrates diverse public datasets to build knowledge graphs and evaluate causal functional outcomes. The team will apply graph neural networks and Bayesian hierarchical models alongside image analysis tools (like CellProfiler and DeepCell). Results will undergo evaluation through nested cross validation and organism holdouts alongside strict comparisons against known negative control proteins. The project will utilize diverse databases (including UniProt and AlphaFold) alongside specialized repositories like PhaSepDB and the BioImage Archive. These datasets will map into an open knowledge graph utilizing a shared ontology to link molecular features and phenotypes. The team will mitigate incompatible identifiers and vocabulary differences by developing shared ontologies and standardizing evidence provenance across datasets. The two year project features three primary milestones to achieve ontology consensus and establish model comparisons during working group meetings. This synthesis requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the necessary expertise in machine learning and biophysics exceeds single laboratory capacities. The team will release all datasets and code under open source licenses in public repositories (such as Zenodo and GitHub). The cross institutional team spans multiple career stages while offering extensive training in reproducible data science and responsible artificial intelligence.

abstract_original:
Membraneless organelles such as stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, and transcriptional condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: dynamic assemblies arise from many weak molecular interactions yet produce higher-order cellular outcomes including RNA regulation, signaling, genome organization, and stress adaptation. Despite extensive studies of individual condensates, the field lacks a predictive, systems-level understanding of why some molecular mixtures form reversible functional assemblies whereas others yield aberrant, disease-linked states. This working group will synthesize existing public data to answer a central question: which combinations of molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and perturbations determine emergent condensate identity, material state, and downstream cellular function?

The project will integrate publicly available datasets spanning scales that are rarely analyzed together. These will include protein and RNA sequence features; curated phase-separation and condensate-partitioning databases; affinity-purification, proximity-labeling, and crosslinking mass spectrometry interaction maps; single-cell and bulk transcriptomic/proteomic perturbation datasets; microscopy image repositories reporting condensate number, size, localization, and dynamics; post-translational modification datasets; and disease-variant resources. We will harmonize these data into an open, versioned knowledge graph linking molecules, interaction motifs, cellular conditions, condensate phenotypes, and functional outcomes. The synthesis will explicitly address data heterogeneity by developing shared ontologies for condensate states, experimental conditions, and mesoscale phenotypes, enabling comparison across laboratories, organisms, cell types, and stress conditions.

Analytically, the group will combine biophysics, cell biology, network science, machine learning, and causal inference. We will build interpretable models that predict condensate membership and emergent material behavior from multivalent interaction architecture, intrinsically disordered region properties, RNA-binding features, modification states, and network topology. We will then test whether these mesoscale predictions explain higher-level outcomes such as translational repression, RNA stabilization, DNA damage response, or cytotoxic aggregation using only existing perturbation and imaging datasets. A major methodological product will be an open workflow for extracting quantitative condensate phenotypes from public microscopy images and connecting them to molecular datasets through reproducible pipelines. Rather than generating new experiments, the working group will produce benchmark datasets, uncertainty estimates, negative controls, and community standards for evaluating claims about biomolecular condensates.

This effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory currently spans the required expertise in condensate biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, image analysis, data curation, graph modeling, and open-science software engineering. The proposed team will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, national data infrastructure groups, and minority-serving institutions, with trainees embedded in cross-site analysis teams. NCEMS working-group meetings will enable iterative synthesis, ontology development, model comparison, and community consensus building that would not arise from a conventional bilateral collaboration.

The expected outcome is a predictive framework for condensate emergence that distinguishes general design principles from condensate-specific mechanisms. By integrating public data across molecular, mesoscale, and cellular levels, the project will clarify how weak interactions collectively generate organized subcellular states and how those states influence cell fate. All harmonized datasets, code, trained models, documentation, and tutorials will be released publicly under open licenses. Trainees will receive hands-on training in reproducible data science, collaborative software development, responsible AI, and team-based synthesis biology. The project will therefore advance a fundamental question in molecular and cellular sciences while creating reusable community resources for studying emergent mesoscale organization.

title: A Public-Data Synthesis Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence Linking Molecular Grammar, Mesoscale Material State, and Cellular Phenotype
title_norm: a publicdata synthesis atlas of biomolecular condensate emergence linking molecular grammar mesoscale material state and cellular phenotype
abstract_text: The research domain of mesoscale molecular emergence focuses on biomolecular condensates such as stress granules and disease linked aggregates, which are critical for understanding phase separating proteins and intrinsically disordered regions. It is currently not understood how specific cellular contexts dictate condensate formation and physical states, or why proteins with similar disordered regions exhibit varying behaviors. This secondary data analysis project will determine how molecular properties and cellular context control condensate emergence by extracting multimodal features and training graph neural networks, gradient boosted trees, and foundation model embeddings. This project will harmonize multi omics, imaging, and structural data from databases including AlphaFold, Human Protein Atlas, and OpenCell into a unified knowledge graph linking molecular components, cell states, and phenotypes. This framework will elucidate how interaction networks dictate material states, enabling researchers to differentiate between functional biological structures and pathological aggregates as context dependent emergent systems.
full_text: The domain of mesoscale molecular emergence lacks understanding of how cellular contexts dictate the physical states of biomolecular condensates. Abundant datasets exist but fail to explain how mutations alter mesoscale structures without changing the canonical functions of proteins. The proposed study determines how interaction networks control the emergence of condensates to differentiate functional structures and pathological aggregates. This project involves the secondary analysis of data to extract multimodal features and train predictive models for biological cases. The analytical strategy utilizes statistical modeling and graph neural networks alongside the extraction of microscopy features via computer vision. The team validates results using nested cross validation and external testing on databases alongside extensive analyses of feature attribution. The proposed study gathers information about the structures of proteins from public databases that include AlphaFold and ClinVar. The team harmonizes imaging data and structural information into a versioned knowledge graph through the use of controlled vocabularies. The researchers mitigate the presence of ambiguous morphological labels by assigning evidence codes and uncertainty scores to the data. The project timeline includes the generation of predictive models at month eighteen and a final atlas at month thirty. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in the extraction of features from images and multimodal modeling. The team shares derived data in public repositories alongside the release of code and executable notebooks on GitHub. The research team includes molecular biophysicists and network scientists alongside postdoctoral trainees who conduct analyses across multiple disciplines.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, metabolites, and membranes produce dynamic compartments whose collective properties cannot be inferred from any single component. Despite thousands of public datasets on protein localization, phase separation, RNA binding, perturbation phenotypes, and disease variation, a central question remains unresolved: what molecular and cellular contexts determine when condensates form, what material states they adopt, and whether they buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build and test an integrative, predictive framework for condensate emergence across human cells and model organisms.

The project will assemble a community-scale team spanning molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure. The group will integrate existing public resources including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold and protein language model embeddings, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, public stress-response transcriptomics, CRISPR perturbation screens from DepMap and BioGRID ORCS, and ClinVar/gnomAD disease variant annotations. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize these heterogeneous datasets into a FAIR, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular state, mesoscale morphology, dynamics, and phenotypic outcomes.

The core scientific innovation is to treat condensates not merely as lists of phase-separating proteins, but as emergent systems whose properties depend on multivalent molecular grammar, expression stoichiometry, post-translational modification potential, RNA context, interaction network topology, and cellular stress history. We will develop transparent AI and statistical models to predict three linked outcomes: condensate membership, emergent material or morphological class, and downstream cellular consequence after perturbation. By comparing predictions across stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P bodies, nuclear speckles, and disease-associated aggregates, we will test whether shared rules govern distinct condensate systems or whether each represents a context-specific emergent regime. A special focus will be placed on long-standing puzzles, including why proteins with similar intrinsically disordered regions produce different condensate behaviors, why some condensates are protective while others become pathological, and how disease mutations shift mesoscale organization without necessarily altering canonical molecular function.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis beyond the scope of any single laboratory: cross-dataset ontology alignment, image-derived feature extraction, multimodal model development, biological interpretation across condensate classes, and community governance for reusable data products. Working-group meetings will produce shared standards for condensate metadata, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and open tutorials. Trainees from diverse institutions will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams and trained in data integration, responsible AI, reproducible workflow design, and collaborative synthesis science.

All outputs will be released openly, including curated datasets, code, model cards, workflow containers, documentation, and interactive visualization tools. The expected outcome is a generalizable synthesis framework for predicting how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behavior and cellular phenotypes, providing a foundational resource for emergence-focused molecular and cellular biology.

title: A Public-Data Synthesis Atlas of Emergent Biomolecular Condensate States and Their Coupling to Cellular Phenotypes
title_norm: a publicdata synthesis atlas of emergent biomolecular condensate states and their coupling to cellular phenotypes
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates form through multivalent molecular interactions, and investigating their transitions between functional and dysfunctional states is critical to understand their varied cellular outcomes across diverse biological systems. This project will build a predictive atlas using public data by harmonizing datasets and applying graph neural networks, multimodal representation learning, and image extraction tools to determine how combined factors influence specific condensate states and cellular phenotypes. Data from resources including the Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting, and DisProt will be integrated by harmonizing metadata with standardized ontologies to construct a knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, images, perturbations, and phenotypes. The resulting predictive atlas will shift focus from cataloging components to identifying universal rules of emergent mesoscale states, enabling computational prediction of condensate behavior across different systems.
full_text: This project investigates biomolecular condensates to identify the molecular and environmental factors driving their transitions into dysfunctional aggregates. These condensates form through multivalent molecular interactions but fragmented studies obscure the general rules governing their cellular outcomes. The proposed study asks how diverse factors dictate condensate states to uncover universal rules enabling broad computational predictions. The study design harmonizes existing public datasets into a unified framework for computational modeling of conserved condensate states. The analytical approach employs multimodal representation learning alongside graph neural networks (GNNs) and image extraction tools like CellProfiler. The predictive models require validation through benchmarking against held out datasets that span diverse organisms and cell types. The project utilizes diverse public databases including the Human Protein Atlas alongside specialized repositories such as OMIM and BioGRID. The team will harmonize metadata using standardized ontologies to construct a knowledge graph linking molecules and cellular phenotypes. The researchers will mitigate confirmation bias through curation of negative examples and bypass redistribution restrictions using accession links. The timeline spans 36 months and includes intermediate milestones for a prototype knowledge graph and robust predictive models. The expansive project scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration to unite essential expertise in machine learning and cell biology. The team will release derived data and code under permissive licenses via public repositories including GitHub and Zenodo. The diverse group includes investigators from minority serving institutions alongside postdoctoral fellows gaining expertise in reproducible computational workflows.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions, yet their organizing principles remain difficult to generalize across cell types, stresses, and organisms. A central unresolved question is: which combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and environmental perturbations cause condensates to transition from adaptive, dynamic assemblies to dysfunctional states that alter gene expression, signaling, or viability? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build a predictive, open atlas linking condensate composition, material properties, spatial organization, and cellular outcomes. The project will integrate existing datasets from proteomics of stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated aggregates; fluorescence imaging and image-derived phenotypes from resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting, and Image Data Resource; public perturbation data including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, LINCS, DepMap, and stress-response transcriptomics; and curated databases of intrinsically disordered regions, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding proteins, phase-separation assays, protein interaction networks, and disease variants. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize heterogeneous datasets into a common representation of condensate-associated mesoscale states. We will develop graph- and representation-learning approaches that combine molecular features, interaction topology, localization patterns, perturbation responses, and phenotypic readouts to identify recurrent ‘condensate state modules.’ These modules will be tested computationally for conservation across organisms, sensitivity to stress, enrichment for disease variants, and association with emergent cellular phenotypes such as translational repression, transcriptional bursting, DNA damage response, senescence, or toxicity. A key innovation is to move beyond cataloging condensate components toward identifying emergent state rules: for example, whether specific combinations of low-complexity sequence composition, RNA abundance, phosphorylation potential, network centrality, and local concentration predict reversible assembly versus persistent pathological aggregation. The project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, RNA biology, network science, machine learning, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data resources, and computational biology groups, with structured roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in FAIR data curation, reproducible workflow design, cloud-based analysis, image feature extraction, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly accessible condensate-state knowledge graph, reusable analysis pipelines, benchmark datasets for predicting condensate behavior, community-developed metadata standards for condensate-related public data, and a synthesis manuscript defining cross-system principles of condensate emergence. By transforming dispersed public datasets into a unified framework, this project will address a fundamental mystery in molecular and cellular biosciences: how collective mesoscale assemblies acquire properties not predictable from individual molecules alone, and how those emergent properties propagate upward to shape cellular physiology and disease.

title: Data-Synthesis Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence Across Cell Types, Perturbations, and Disease States
title_norm: datasynthesis atlas of biomolecular condensate emergence across cell types perturbations and disease states
abstract_text: Within mesoscale cellular biology, biomolecular condensates form through multivalent molecular interactions to regulate essential cellular processes, making the understanding of their formation and function vital for the field. This project will synthesize public data to identify general rules of emergent condensate behaviors using sequential metadata harmonization, graph based data integration, and diverse machine learning methods including weakly supervised computer vision, graph neural networks, and contrastive representation learning. Standardized metadata from repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, ENCODE, and AlphaFold will be mapped into a heterogeneous knowledge graph linking molecules, condensates, cellular contexts, biological perturbations, images, and phenotypes. This research will produce a predictive framework linking physical condensate properties to specific cellular phenotypes, thereby transitioning the field from isolated descriptive catalogs toward generalized rules of disease vulnerabilities.
full_text: This project examines mesoscale cellular biology to determine how molecular features and cellular contexts form functional condensates and disease associated assemblies. Condensates regulate cellular processes through multivalent interactions but fragmented data from isolated cases obscure the general principles of their emergence. The goal is to synthesize public datasets into a predictive framework that connects physical properties of condensates with cellular phenotypes. This computational synthesis of public data combines metadata harmonization and machine learning to construct a predictive atlas of molecular features. The analytical methods incorporate weakly supervised computer vision and graph neural networks alongside contrastive representation learning and Bayesian hierarchical models. Results will be validated using nested cross validation and the testing of external datasets alongside ablation analyses and permutation controls. The researchers will utilize datasets from the Human Protein Atlas and BioImage Archive alongside protein databases like AlphaFold and UniProt. The project will integrate data by mapping standardized metadata into a heterogeneous knowledge graph that connects molecules with cellular phenotypes. Known data limitations include batch effects and incomplete labels that require mitigation through controlled vocabularies and strict grading of evidence. The two year timeline delivers a prototype atlas at month nine and concludes with a public release at month 24. The synthesis of diverse data from omics and imaging demands cross disciplinary collaboration across biology and computer science beyond one laboratory. The team will release all harmonized datasets and code publicly under permissive licenses while adhering to established FAIR principles. The cross disciplinary team unites cell biologists and machine learning researchers from diverse institutions to provide substantial mentoring opportunities for trainees.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are a defining mesoscale phenomenon: dynamic assemblies arise from many weak molecular interactions, yet display emergent properties such as selective partitioning, viscoelasticity, spatial organization, and regulatory influence on transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and signaling. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and cellular contexts determine when condensates form adaptive regulatory hubs versus pathological or dysfunctional assemblies? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and perturbational data to build an open, cross-scale atlas linking condensate composition and physicochemical features to cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease states.

The project will integrate existing datasets from public repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, Cell Painting and fluorescence microscopy datasets, PRIDE and MassIVE proteomics studies, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic and chromatin datasets, DepMap and CRISPR perturbation screens, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold structural models, and published condensate interactomes. We will harmonize heterogeneous data describing protein localization, intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA-binding capacity, expression stoichiometry, interaction networks, and perturbation phenotypes. Using graph-based data integration, weakly supervised computer vision, representation learning, and interpretable machine learning, we will identify combinations of molecular features and environmental conditions that predict emergent condensate behaviors such as stress-induced assembly, nucleolar or nuclear body reorganization, granule persistence, and links to phenotypes including growth, differentiation, viral response, neurodegeneration, and cancer vulnerability.

The core scientific goal is to move beyond single-condensate case studies toward general principles of mesoscale emergence. We will test three synthesis questions: (1) Are there conserved molecular “design rules” that distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent disease-associated assemblies? (2) How do changes in expression, modification state, and interaction-network topology combine nonlinearly to produce condensate formation or dissolution? (3) Can condensate-level properties explain cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from individual protein abundance or interaction data alone? The resulting models will generate community-testable hypotheses, such as specific combinations of low-complexity domains, RNA availability, phosphorylation sites, and network position that confer context-dependent condensate behavior.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, standardize, and analyze the breadth of imaging, proteomic, structural, genomic, and perturbation data needed to infer general principles of condensate emergence. The working group will assemble cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, data curators, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, and trainees from research-intensive, primarily undergraduate, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS working group meetings will enable consensus development on metadata standards, benchmark tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable modeling strategies.

All products will follow open science principles: harmonized datasets, code, model weights, workflows, documentation, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories with reproducible containers and community governance. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary analysis sprints, receive training in FAIR data stewardship, image analysis, network science, and responsible AI, and co-lead open tutorials for the broader community. By synthesizing existing public data at community scale, this project will provide a predictive framework for how molecular features give rise to emergent mesoscale condensate states and how those states shape cellular function.

title: Predicting Emergent Biomolecular Condensate States from Public Multi-Omics, Imaging, and Perturbation Data
title_norm: predicting emergent biomolecular condensate states from public multiomics imaging and perturbation data
abstract_text: The domain of mesoscale emergence investigates membraneless biomolecular condensates, which are crucial structures that regulate cellular processes through multivalent weak interactions, intrinsically disordered regions, nucleic acid scaffolds, and post translational modifications. Despite extensive multi omics and imaging datasets, these resources remain disconnected, preventing systematic prediction of why certain condensates form adaptive assemblies while others transition into pathological states. This project will determine which combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts predict emergent condensate states by extracting microscopy phenotypes via computer vision and training interpretable multimodal graph neural networks. The research will integrate diverse databases, including UniProt, BioGRID, and the Human Protein Atlas, into a unified knowledge graph connecting molecular components, sequence features, and imaging phenotypes via mapped community ontologies. This framework will computationally predict emergent cellular organization, enabling the interpretation of disease variants and the generation of specific perturbation hypotheses based on context dependent assembly rules.
full_text: This project explores mesoscale emergence of membraneless condensates (stress granules) to understand why adaptive assemblies transition into pathological states. Multivalent weak interactions drive these condensates but extensive molecular data lack integration to connect specific features with mesoscale phenotypes. The study determines which molecular combinations predict emergent condensate states and subsequently enables computational interpretation of variants associated with disease. The study design features secondary analysis of public data to construct a knowledge graph and train multimodal computational models. The team applies graph neural networks and foundation models for microscopy through containerized environments and dedicated workflow managers. The researchers validate results through nested cross validation and benchmark performance against negative controls of non condensate proteins. The project utilizes diverse genomic and imaging data from public databases including UniProt and the Human Protein Atlas. A unified knowledge graph integrates these datasets to connect molecular components and cellular outcomes with phenotypes from imaging. The team mitigates incompatible data repositories and batch effects through specific sensitivity analyses and harmonization of imaging channels. The project spans 24 months and delivers an initial knowledge graph before culminating in a final integrated resource. Harmonizing these diverse data types requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite specialized expertise in molecular biophysics and machine learning. The researchers will release code and data under permissive licenses through public platforms like GitHub to ensure reproducibility. The diverse team spans multiple career stages and offers mentored leadership roles through virtual sprints and trainee exchanges.

abstract_original:
Membraneless biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and DNA damage foci exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, chromatin, metabolites, and post-translational modifications produce collective material states that regulate cellular physiology. Despite intense study, a central puzzle remains unresolved: why do some condensates form adaptive, reversible mesoscale assemblies whereas others transition into pathological or dysfunctional states? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to develop a predictive, publicly available framework linking molecular features to emergent condensate behaviors and downstream cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease contexts.

This Working Group will integrate existing public data spanning complementary modalities: protein and RNA sequence features; intrinsically disordered region annotations; post-translational modification databases; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction resources; proximity labeling datasets; CRISPR and RNAi perturbation screens; single-cell and bulk transcriptomics; proteomics; live-cell and fixed-cell imaging repositories; and curated disease mutation databases. Rather than generating new experimental data, the project will harmonize and reanalyze these resources to ask: which combinations of molecular grammar, interaction network topology, expression context, and environmental perturbation are sufficient to predict condensate assembly, dissolution, localization, material maturation, and cellular consequences?

The analytical strategy will combine expertise from molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, image analysis, machine learning, network science, and open-source software engineering. We will first create an interoperable condensate knowledge graph connecting molecular components, sequence features, interaction evidence, perturbations, imaging-derived phenotypes, and cellular outcomes using transparent provenance standards. Second, we will develop reusable computer vision workflows to extract mesoscale condensate phenotypes from public microscopy data, including size distributions, number, spatial organization, coalescence signatures, and temporal reversibility where time-lapse data exist. Third, we will train interpretable multimodal AI models to identify predictive rules for condensate emergence and state transitions, explicitly testing whether conserved mesoscale behaviors can be inferred from molecular features across different biological contexts. Finally, we will perform cross-dataset validation using held-out perturbation and disease datasets to identify general principles and context-specific exceptions.

NCEMS support is essential because this synthesis exceeds the scope of a single laboratory: it requires coordinated data curation across many repositories, shared standards for condensate phenotypes, integration of heterogeneous molecular and imaging data, and sustained collaboration among experimentalists, computational scientists, statisticians, and trainees. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource communities, with explicit roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in data stewardship, reproducible workflow development, and collaborative team science.

All outputs will follow open science principles. We will release curated datasets, ontologies, analysis notebooks, trained models, image-analysis pipelines, and benchmark tasks through public repositories with documented metadata and community governance. The project will also produce training modules on multimodal biological data synthesis, interpretable AI, and reproducible mesoscale cell biology. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent predictive resource, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular properties generate emergent condensate states and how those states influence cellular adaptation, dysfunction, and disease.

Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and DNA repair foci exemplify emergence in cell biology: collective mesoscale assemblies arise from multivalent molecular interactions and generate new spatial, kinetic, and regulatory properties not predictable from individual components alone. Despite intense study, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when specific proteins and RNAs will form condensates, how condensate material properties vary across cellular contexts, and which emergent assemblies causally influence cell state. This Working Group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: what combinations of molecular features, interaction network architecture, expression stoichiometry, and cellular context predict the emergence and functional consequences of mesoscale condensates in human cells?

The project will integrate existing public resources that are individually powerful but rarely analyzed together: subcellular localization images from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, and Cell Painting datasets; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction maps from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, ENCODE, POSTAR, and published AP-MS, BioID, and CLIP-seq studies; sequence-derived features including intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, charge patterning, prion-like domains, and multivalent motifs; transcriptomic and proteomic abundance data from GTEx, DepMap, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, and single-cell atlases; and public perturbation datasets including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, stress-response time courses, and drug response studies. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will create harmonized, FAIR data products linking molecular composition, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, interaction networks, and cellular outcomes.

Our analytical strategy will combine computer vision, network science, statistical physics-inspired descriptors, and interpretable machine learning. First, we will use reproducible image-analysis pipelines to extract condensate-related phenotypes from public microscopy data, including puncta number, size distributions, co-localization, spatial organization, and context-dependent relocalization. Second, we will build multilayer interaction and feature networks capturing sequence grammar, binding multiplicity, RNA association, abundance, and compartmental localization. Third, we will train and benchmark models that predict condensate membership, condition-specific assembly, and emergent mesoscale phenotypes from molecular and network features. Finally, we will connect predicted condensate states to cellular outcomes such as stress survival, transcriptional reprogramming, proliferation, and disease-associated vulnerability using public perturbational and phenotypic datasets.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it is beyond the scope of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in condensate biology, cell imaging, RNA biology, proteomics, biophysics, machine learning, network theory, and open-science software engineering. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data repositories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in reproducible workflows, metadata harmonization, image analysis, machine learning, and collaborative team science.

Expected outputs include an open atlas of predicted and observed human condensate-forming systems, validated computational workflows, benchmark datasets for community model development, and testable hypotheses about how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale organization and higher-order cell behavior. By transforming fragmented public data into an integrated predictive framework, this project will address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how dynamic molecular interactions generate emergent cellular organization.

abstract_text: The research domain of molecular and cellular biology focuses on how weak multivalent interactions form biomolecular condensates that exhibit emergent mesoscale properties essential for organizing cellular processes. A critical gap is the inability to predict condensate participation, mesoscale structures, and phenotypic effects, because it remains unclear why similar molecules assemble differently across cellular contexts. To determine how intrinsic molecular features and cellular contexts combine to dictate condensate participation, this project will synthesize data into a knowledge graph to build nested predictive models using protein language models, graph neural networks, and multimodal representation learning. This research will integrate databases including AlphaFold, UniProt, BioGRID, and Human Protein Atlas into a versioned knowledge graph using standardized ontology terms, persistent identifiers, and evidence codes to link molecular entities, interactions, and phenotypes. This project will output a predictive framework that clarifies the contributions of intrinsic traits versus cellular contexts, yielding novel tools to identify condensate regulators and interpret variants associated with disease.
full_text: This molecular and cellular biology project addresses the inability to predict mesoscale properties and phenotypic effects of biomolecular condensates. Weak multivalent interactions form cellular condensates but fragmented data obscures why similar molecules exhibit distinct assembly behaviors across contexts. The project investigates how molecular and cellular features dictate condensate participation to provide a predictive framework for disease variants. The study design synthesizes diverse public datasets into a knowledge graph to build nested predictive models of condensate formation. The analytical approach applies protein language models and graph neural networks alongside causal inference and physical feature engineering. The researchers will validate results using cross validation and temporal data splits alongside negative controls and feature ablation. The project relies on public databases including AlphaFold and UniProt alongside repositories like ENCODE and the BioImage Archive. The team will integrate these diverse resources into a versioned knowledge graph using persistent identifiers and standardized ontology terms. The researchers will mitigate data leakage and inherent biases by employing temporal data splits and publishing model cards. The two year timeline includes quarterly virtual meetings and in person synthesis workshops alongside trainee led analysis sprints. This cross disciplinary collaboration is required because integrating soft matter physics and machine learning exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. The team will share all code and trained models publicly under open licenses using public repositories (including GitHub). The group includes biologists and machine learning researchers across multiple career stages who provide instruction in open science.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: weak, multivalent molecular interactions produce mesoscale assemblies with properties not predictable from individual components alone, including selective partitioning, altered reaction kinetics, and coordinated cellular responses. Despite rapid growth in condensate research, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when a protein or RNA will participate in condensates, what mesoscale state will emerge, and how that state influences cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: which molecular features and cellular contexts jointly determine emergent condensate behavior and downstream cell-state outcomes? We will integrate complementary public resources spanning molecular sequence, structure, localization, interaction, and phenotype. Data sources will include condensate and phase-separation databases, AlphaFold and Protein Data Bank structural models, UniProt and RNAcentral annotations, BioGRID and STRING interaction networks, OpenCell and Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive datasets of stress granules and nuclear bodies, PRIDE proteomics, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic data, LINCS perturbational signatures, and genome-scale CRISPR or RNAi screens from DepMap and related repositories. The project will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will harmonize heterogeneous public datasets into an open, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features to mesoscale assemblies and phenotypic consequences. The working group will develop transparent analytical strategies combining computer vision, protein language models, graph machine learning, causal inference, and physical feature engineering. Image-based models will quantify condensate morphology, number, size distributions, coarsening, and spatial relationships across published microscopy datasets. Sequence and structure models will extract multivalency, disorder, charge patterning, interaction motifs, RNA-binding potential, and post-translational modification sites. Network and perturbation analyses will test whether emergent condensate states mediate cellular outcomes such as stress resistance, transcriptional repression, cell-cycle arrest, viral infection response, or cancer dependency. Rather than producing a black-box predictor alone, the group will compare mechanistic hypotheses: whether condensate emergence is best explained by intrinsic molecular grammar, cellular concentration and stoichiometry, interaction-network topology, post-translational regulation, or combinations of these factors. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or coordination capacity to integrate high-content imaging, proteomics, structural bioinformatics, RNA biology, soft-matter physics, machine learning, and causal modeling at community scale. The proposed team would include molecular and cell biologists studying condensates, computational biologists, biophysicists, statisticians, imaging scientists, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working-group meetings will enable consensus on metadata standards, benchmarking tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable model evaluation. All code, workflows, harmonized metadata, trained models, and derived feature tables will be released under open licenses through reproducible containers and public repositories. Trainees will lead cross-institutional analysis modules, participate in data-integration hackathons, and receive training in open, team-based synthesis science. The expected outcomes are a reusable public atlas of condensate-associated molecular and cellular features, validated predictive models for emergent mesoscale organization, and testable hypotheses explaining how condensates convert molecular interactions into higher-order cellular phenotypes. By transforming fragmented public data into a coherent synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental puzzle in cell biology and provide a community resource for predicting emergent organization across the molecular-to-cellular scale.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: thousands of weak molecular interactions can collectively produce spatially organized, dynamic compartments that alter signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, and stress responses without membrane boundaries. Yet a central unresolved question remains: when do molecular features such as intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA binding, and interaction-network topology combine to generate a condensate state with predictable cellular consequences? This working group will synthesize public molecular, imaging, proteomic, and functional genomics data to derive generalizable rules linking molecular composition to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes.

We will integrate existing datasets from Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, ENCODE, DepMap, BioGRID, STRING, UniProt, AlphaFold, DisProt, PhosphoSitePlus, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and publicly available single-cell transcriptomic and perturbation screens. The project will focus on human nuclear and cytoplasmic condensates involved in transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, DNA damage response, and stress adaptation. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will build a harmonized, open synthesis resource that connects protein sequence features, structural disorder, interaction valency, RNA association, post-translational modification, subcellular localization dynamics, cell-type context, and genetic dependency phenotypes.

The core scientific objective is to test whether condensate formation and functional impact can be predicted from multiscale public data better than from any individual data modality. We will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models to identify combinations of molecular features that distinguish constitutive condensate scaffolds, context-dependent clients, and disease-sensitive regulatory nodes. We will then ask how these mesoscale states map onto higher-order outcomes, including transcriptional programs, proliferation dependencies, stress resistance, and mutation-associated disease phenotypes. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that are not obvious from single-protein annotations, such as cooperative recruitment thresholds, modification-sensitive phase switching, and cell-type-specific condensate rewiring.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, computational imaging, graph theory, machine learning, RNA biology, structural bioinformatics, and open-science software engineering. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource teams, with intentional participation by early-career scientists, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows. NCEMS convening infrastructure will enable sustained cross-disciplinary synthesis, community standards for condensate data annotation, and collaborative benchmarking of computational models.

Deliverables will include an open Condensate Emergence Atlas; reproducible workflows for data harmonization, image-derived localization feature extraction, and multimodal modeling; benchmark datasets for predicting condensate membership and context-dependent function; and community-authored guidelines for integrating condensate-related public data. Trainees will participate in hackathons, model-building sprints, and team-science workshops focused on reproducible analysis, FAIR data practices, and responsible AI. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent mesoscale synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how do distributed molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular organization and function?

abstract_text: The biomolecular condensation of membraneless organelles, including stress granules and disease associated assemblies involving FUS, dictates cellular organization, yielding indispensable component catalogs, dynamic quantifications, intrinsically disordered region mappings, and phase separation measurements. To determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from molecular grammar and cellular state, this project will synthesize public data using ontology driven harmonization, multimodal representation learning, graph neural embeddings, and probabilistic graphical models. Repositories including PhaSepDB, DisProt, Cell Painting, and the Human Protein Atlas will be integrated to construct a comprehensive knowledge graph connecting molecules, condensates, cell states, material properties, and phenotypes through evidence weighted edges. The resulting predictive framework will reveal how identical molecular features yield adaptive compartments or pathological aggregates, fundamentally distinguishing general mesoscale principles from organelle specific mechanisms.
full_text: This project investigates biomolecular condensation of membraneless organelles (including stress granules) to determine how cellular context drives pathological outcomes. Current knowledge covers the molecular composition of condensates but fragmented information across public repositories obscures universal biological principles. The primary question asks if emergent behaviors are predictable from molecular grammar to distinguish general principles from organelle specific mechanisms. The study integrates structural and imaging features into a knowledge graph to train predictive models on predefined partitions. Key computational methods include probabilistic graphical models and multimodal representation learning alongside graph neural embeddings for robust analysis. The team will benchmark results using calibrated probabilities and negative controls across distinct partitions for training and validation. The researchers will utilize public databases (including the Human Protein Atlas) and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database for analysis. These resources will be integrated into a knowledge graph connecting molecules and cell states via evidence weighted edges. The team will mitigate missing data by using probabilistic graphical models to propagate uncertainty into the final conclusions. This three year project progresses from defining standards to extracting features and developing predictive models during phase three. The integration of diverse datasets requires cross disciplinary collaboration among experts in biology and machine learning for success. The researchers will share code and data using open source licenses to ensure compliance with FAIR (Findable Accessible Interoperable Reusable) principles. The collaborative team includes diverse domain experts and trainees who will receive instruction in reproducible coding and statistics.

abstract_original:
Membraneless organelles formed by biomolecular condensation exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites produce dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, biochemical activities, and cellular consequences. Yet a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and environmental contexts determine whether a condensate becomes adaptive, inert, or pathological? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, biophysical, and phenotypic datasets to derive generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes. The project will focus on stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies involving proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1, MED1, NPM1, G3BP1, and DDX family helicases.

The effort will integrate existing data from public repositories including BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting datasets, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, ENCODE, DepMap, and disease variant resources such as ClinVar and gnomAD. We will harmonize heterogeneous data types spanning protein sequence features, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding properties, interaction networks, in vitro phase-separation measurements, live-cell condensate imaging, FRAP-derived dynamics, perturbational transcriptomics, proteomics, genetic dependency profiles, and disease-associated mutations. No new experimental data will be generated.

The primary scientific objective is to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from combinations of molecular grammar, network context, and cellular state. Specifically, we will ask: (1) Which sequence, structural, and interaction features best distinguish condensates with liquid-like, gel-like, or solid-like behaviors? (2) How do post-translational modifications and RNA abundance shift mesoscale material states? (3) Which condensate properties are associated with downstream cellular phenotypes such as stress resilience, altered transcription, impaired translation, cytotoxicity, or disease vulnerability? (4) Are there conserved cross-organelle principles that explain why some condensates buffer cellular noise whereas others amplify pathological transitions?

Methodologically, the group will develop an open, reproducible computational framework combining ontology-driven data harmonization, probabilistic graphical models, multimodal representation learning, interpretable machine learning, and network-based causal discovery. A key deliverable will be a community-curated condensate knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, condensate types, material properties, perturbations, cell states, and phenotypes. We will benchmark predictive models across independent datasets and prioritize interpretable rules rather than black-box correlations, enabling the field to evaluate proposed principles of condensate emergence.

This project requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise and data integration exceed the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, computational biologists, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, database curators, and trainees from diverse institution types and geographic regions. NCEMS will provide the collaborative infrastructure needed to establish shared standards, resolve conflicting annotations, train early-career scientists in synthesis science, and produce community resources. All workflows, harmonized metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, models, and derived datasets will be released openly under FAIR principles. By transforming fragmented public data into testable rules of mesoscale organization, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how collective molecular interactions generate emergent compartments that shape cell fate.

title: A Cross-Scale Public Data Synthesis to Predict Emergent Cellular Functions of Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: a crossscale public data synthesis to predict emergent cellular functions of biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates form through weak multivalent interactions to influence cellular processes, making mesoscale emergence across transcriptional condensates, stress granules, and DNA damage associated repair foci a critical research domain. A predictive methodology remains absent, leaving it unclear whether specific forming assemblies drive functional cellular changes or merely represent incidental passive molecular grouping. To identify the molecular characteristics and conditions dictating functional condensate behavior, this data synthesis project will harmonize variables and apply predictive machine learning, graph neural networks, and network based causal inference. This effort will integrate databases including UniProt, BioGRID, ENCODE, and DepMap by constructing a knowledge graph linking proteins, RNAs, and cellular states through documented physical interactions, colocalization, and perturbation responses. By identifying molecular combinations dictating functional behavior, these predictive models will facilitate rational interventions in condensate biology and establish a synthesis framework applicable to other mesoscale cellular structures.
full_text: Research on the mesoscale emergence of transcriptional condensates lacks predictive methodology to distinguish functional consequences from passive grouping. Biomolecular condensates form through weak multivalent interactions but fragmented metadata obscures which biological assemblies drive functional cellular changes. This project identifies conditions that dictate cellular behavior to shift condensate research from descriptive categorization to predictive modeling. This data synthesis project harmonizes existing variables into a central graph structure to develop predictive machine learning models. The team will deploy regularized regression and graph neural networks alongside causal graphical modeling and gradient boosting algorithms. The team will validate all predictive models through external repository comparisons and negative controls utilizing nonfunctional molecular assemblies. The study integrates datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus and the Human Cell Atlas alongside multiple CLIP-seq resources. The team will construct a knowledge graph to link biological nodes through edges that represent documented molecular relationships. The researchers will mitigate inconsistent biological nomenclature and incompatible dataset annotations through community curation to establish standardized ontologies. The project involves progression through four data workstreams to produce six deliverables alongside quarterly meetings and annual workshops. This broad scope necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration because the integration of biophysics and computational modeling exceeds single laboratory expertise. The team will share synthesized data and model outputs via platforms like GitHub under permissive licenses to ensure reproducibility. This diverse team includes data scientists and biostatisticians alongside graduate students who will lead computational subprojects for training.
