abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and chromatin can generate dynamic compartments with system-level effects on transcription, signaling, stress adaptation, and disease phenotypes. Yet the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when condensate formation produces functional cellular outcomes rather than passive molecular co-localization. This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, genomic, and phenotypic data to answer a fundamental question: what combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and environmental state make condensates causally associated with emergent cellular behavior? We will integrate existing datasets spanning curated condensate atlases, proteome-wide phase-separation measurements, intrinsically disordered region annotations, protein-RNA and protein-protein interaction networks, post-translational modification databases, ENCODE and 4D Nucleome chromatin datasets, public live-cell and fixed-cell microscopy repositories, Perturb-seq and CRISPR-screen datasets, single-cell transcriptomic atlases, and stress-response phenotyping resources. The project will focus initially on three well-studied but mechanistically unresolved condensate classes: transcriptional condensates, stress granules, and DNA-damage-associated repair foci. These systems provide rich public data and represent distinct emergent outcomes across information processing, cellular adaptation, and genome maintenance. The working group will develop an open analytical framework that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. First, we will harmonize heterogeneous public datasets into a community-accessible knowledge graph connecting condensate components, biophysical features, interaction partners, cell types, perturbations, imaging phenotypes, and downstream molecular responses. Second, we will use interpretable machine learning and network-based causal inference to identify feature combinations that distinguish functional condensate-associated states from nonfunctional co-assemblies. Third, we will test whether shared design principles emerge across condensate classes, including thresholds in multivalency, RNA dependence, post-translational modification state, chromatin context, and stress history. The expected product is not new experimental data, but a reusable synthesis platform, benchmark datasets, predictive models, and testable hypotheses that can guide future experimental studies. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise needed to integrate biophysics, cell biology, microscopy, genomics, computational biology, machine learning, and open-science infrastructure at this scale. The working group will include condensate biologists, quantitative microscopists, RNA and chromatin experts, systems biologists, data scientists, biostatisticians, and trainees from research-intensive universities, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS convening resources will enable iterative community curation, shared standards for condensate-relevant metadata, cross-training workshops, and sustained collaboration across disciplines. All code, workflows, harmonized metadata, knowledge graph schemas, model outputs, and tutorials will be released through open repositories under permissive licenses, with reproducible computational environments and community documentation. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will lead subprojects in data integration, model interpretation, and open workflow development, receiving training in team science, FAIR data practices, and AI-assisted synthesis. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a cross-scale predictive framework, this project will advance a central goal of NCEMS: explaining how emergent mesoscale organization gives rise to higher-order cellular function.

title: A Public-Data Atlas for Predicting Emergent Biomolecular Condensate States from Molecular Features, Cellular Context, and Perturbation Responses
title_norm: a publicdata atlas for predicting emergent biomolecular condensate states from molecular features cellular context and perturbation responses
abstract_text: The molecular and cellular biology domain focuses on biomolecular condensates and their mesoscale emergence from interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, but understanding remains incomplete because observational data are currently fragmented. The gap is the absence of a predictive synthesis framework, leaving researchers unable to determine when molecular components and cellular contexts generate specific condensate behaviors across incompatible imaging formats. The primary research objective is to identify which molecular features and cellular contexts predict condensate formation, and this project will computationally synthesize existing public data using metadata harmonization, computer vision algorithms, and causal inference models. The project will integrate key databases like PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, Human Protein Atlas, and BioImage Archive by mapping controlled terms to standard ontologies and constructing a multiscale knowledge graph with experimentally supported relationships. This research will produce a predictive framework to determine condensate consequences, which will transition condensate biology from descriptive cataloging toward predicting how molecular interactions create cellular functions.
full_text: Within molecular biology the mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates lacks a predictive framework connecting components to cellular consequences. Current catalogs of condensate behaviors remain incomplete because observational data are fragmented across incompatible databases and conceptual vocabularies. This project asks how molecular features predict condensate formation to advance biology from descriptive catalogs to predictive frameworks. The study design involves the computational synthesis of existing data through metadata harmonization and a multiscale knowledge graph. The analytical approach utilizes computer vision algorithms alongside causal inference models and graph neural networks to process data. The project validates the computational models using blocked cross validation alongside negative controls and expert annotated validation labels. The study integrates public databases such as PhaSepDB alongside structural resources like the Human Protein Atlas and ENCODE. The project integrates these distinct datasets by mapping controlled terms to standard ontologies within a multiscale knowledge graph. The team mitigates the limitation of incompatible image formats by harmonizing features and flagging datasets with insufficient resolution. The three year timeline includes milestones for constructing knowledge graphs and developing predictive models to produce emergence maps. This ambitious scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in molecular biophysics with machine learning and proteomics. The project shares all data and code through public repositories using reproducible containers and permissive open source licenses. The team features software engineers and postdoctoral fellows who receive specialized training through reproducible workflow workshops and hackathons.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: dynamic assemblies arise from weak multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet produce new cellular properties such as spatial biochemical compartmentalization, stress adaptation, and disease-associated aggregation. Despite extensive public data on phase-separating proteins, RNA localization, proteomes, transcriptomes, live-cell imaging, and genetic perturbations, the field lacks a synthesis framework that predicts when molecular components collectively generate condensate behavior in specific cellular contexts. This working group will integrate existing public datasets to address a central question: which combinations of molecular features and cellular states are sufficient to predict the emergent formation, dissolution, material properties, and functional consequences of biomolecular condensates?

The project will synthesize publicly available data from phase-separation and condensate databases, Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images, OpenCell protein localization measurements, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic profiles, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, RNA-binding protein and RNA interactome datasets, intrinsically disordered region and low-complexity sequence annotations, post-translational modification resources, DepMap/CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq datasets, and published stress-granule, nucleolar, P-body, transcriptional condensate, and disease-aggregate studies. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize metadata, develop interoperable ontologies for condensate identity and material state, and construct a multiscale knowledge graph linking molecular composition, sequence grammar, RNA abundance, post-translational regulation, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, perturbation responses, and cellular outcomes.

We will develop open analytical strategies combining computer vision, network science, representation learning, causal inference, and biophysical modeling. Image foundation models will extract condensate features such as number, size distribution, morphology, coarsening behavior, and localization from public microscopy. Graph neural networks and interpretable statistical models will then test whether emergent condensate states can be predicted from molecular interaction potential, expression stoichiometry, RNA context, and perturbation history. Comparative analyses across cell types, stresses, developmental states, and disease models will identify generalizable principles and context-specific exceptions. A key deliverable will be a public “condensate emergence map” that predicts transitions among dispersed, liquid-like, gel-like, and aggregate-like states and links these transitions to downstream phenotypes including transcriptional regulation, translation repression, proteostasis, and cell viability.

This effort requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, bioimage analysis, machine learning, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data repositories, and computational biology centers, with trainees embedded in cross-institutional analysis teams. Graduate students and postdocs will receive hands-on training through hackathons, reproducible workflow workshops, FAIR data curation sprints, and mentored team-authored publications.

All harmonized metadata, code, workflows, trained models, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released openly under community-approved licenses using reproducible containers and version-controlled repositories. By transforming fragmented public observations into a predictive synthesis of condensate emergence, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale cellular organization and higher-order cellular phenotypes.

title: Predicting Emergent Cellular Outcomes from Biomolecular Condensate Composition, Material State, and Network Context
title_norm: predicting emergent cellular outcomes from biomolecular condensate composition material state and network context
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates are important mesoscale cellular structures lacking membranes that form through multivalent molecular interactions, yet structural information regarding the numerous participating proteins and RNAs remains decentralized and lacks standardized terminology. The primary objective is to determine whether cellular outcomes will be accurately predicted by combining condensate composition, material state, and network data using causal modeling, graph neural networks, and containerized bioimage analysis workflows. This project will integrate diverse biological databases including PhaSepDB, UniProt, AlphaFold, and BioGRID into a knowledge graph connecting biological entities with edges that define evidence type, confidence levels, and cellular context. This framework will transition condensate research from basic component cataloging to a mechanistic model by standardizing terminology and establishing whether mesoscale properties possess independent predictive value for cellular function.

The study evaluates whether combined properties of condensates predict cellular outcomes accurately and advance research toward mechanistic models. The team applies graph neural networks and directed acyclic graphs alongside reproducible workflows for the analysis of images. abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions and reorganize cellular biochemistry without membrane boundaries. Although thousands of proteins and RNAs have been implicated in condensates, a central puzzle remains unresolved: when do condensates act as adaptive organizers that buffer cellular stress, and when do they become amplifiers of dysfunction leading to altered signaling, growth, or disease phenotypes? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, transcriptomic, and phenotypic datasets to identify generalizable principles linking condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes.

The project will use only existing public data, integrating resources such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, UniProt, AlphaFold structures, post-translational modification repositories, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, ProteomeXchange stress-response proteomics, Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, LINCS perturbational transcriptomics, DepMap fitness screens, and published high-content imaging screens. We will construct an open, versioned knowledge graph connecting condensate-associated proteins and RNAs to sequence features, predicted disorder, interaction valency, post-translational modifications, localization, microscopy-derived condensate morphology, stress conditions, pathway activity, and cellular phenotypes. Using interpretable machine learning, network modeling, and causal-inference strategies, we will test whether specific combinations of molecular features and network positions predict emergent condensate behaviors such as nucleation, fusion, hardening, reversibility, recruitment selectivity, and downstream effects on transcription, translation, signaling, and cell viability.

The central scientific question is whether mesoscale condensate properties can be predicted from integrated molecular features and, in turn, whether those properties explain cellular-scale outcomes better than the properties of individual molecules alone. This directly addresses emergence across scales: local molecular interactions give rise to condensate material states, which then reshape information flow, biochemical reaction organization, and cellular decisions. The project will also resolve a long-standing inconsistency in the field by harmonizing heterogeneous condensate annotations, imaging measurements, and experimental contexts into a shared ontology that distinguishes evidence for phase separation, clustering, aggregation, and functional compartmentalization.

NCEMS support is essential because the work exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. The Working Group will bring together condensate biophysicists, cell biologists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, bioimage analysts, data scientists, network theorists, ontology developers, and trainees from research-intensive universities, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS will enable structured team science, dataset harmonization, cloud-based analysis, benchmark development, and community governance for open resources.

All outputs will follow open science principles: curated datasets, ontologies, code, workflows, trained models, documentation, and interactive visualization tools will be released publicly with reproducible computational environments. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary synthesis sprints, receive training in FAIR data practices, bioimage analysis, graph machine learning, and responsible AI, and co-lead benchmark challenges. The expected outcome is a community resource and predictive framework that transforms condensate biology from a catalog of components into a mechanistic, data-driven understanding of how mesoscale assemblies generate emergent cellular functions.

title: Predicting Emergent Mesoscale Biomolecular Condensate States from Public Proteome, Interaction, Perturbation, and Imaging Data
title_norm: predicting emergent mesoscale biomolecular condensate states from public proteome interaction perturbation and imaging data
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates govern critical spatial organization within human cells, but intrinsic protein sequences and modular domains cannot predict these emergent mesoscale material states without accounting for complex cellular contextual factors. The field currently lacks an understanding of how combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts precisely determine condensate assembly, maturation, pathological transitions, and subsequent cellular outcomes. This project will synthesize public datasets into a predictive framework by creating a curated atlas and applying computer vision, graph learning, causal inference, and machine learning to link molecular properties to emergent condensate states. The study will integrate databases including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, and AlphaFold by developing a shared data model that links molecules, images, and phenotypes using controlled vocabularies. This predictive framework will transition condensate biology from descriptive studies to predictive modeling, defining how interacting molecules generate mesoscale properties and why specific condensates behave pathologically.
full_text: This domain studies biomolecular condensates to determine how features of molecules and cellular contexts drive specific pathological transitions. Current studies identify features of proteins but these traits cannot predict the formation of condensates without modeling cellular contexts. The objective synthesizes public datasets to predict how properties of molecules cause adaptive and pathological behaviors of condensates. The overall design harmonizes public databases into a curated atlas to evaluate hypotheses using workflows for computational analysis. The analytical strategy applies tools for computer vision (CellProfiler) alongside models for causal inference and algorithms for machine learning. Validation occurs through curation by humans and independent evaluation on reserved datasets alongside analysis of samples for negative controls. The proposed study utilizes databases like the Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell alongside repositories such as the BioImage Archive. The project integrates these resources by establishing a structural model for data using controlled vocabularies and reproducible identifiers. The team mitigates inherent limitations with incompatible metadata by establishing community standards and triangulating diverse types of data. The timeline delivers a pilot atlas in year one alongside models in year two and tutorials in year three. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the necessary integration of diverse expertise exceeds capacities of solitary laboratories. The team shares all models and workflows under permissive licenses using accessible platforms (GitHub) following established community guidelines. The diverse team spans multiple career stages and scientific disciplines while providing extensive training opportunities through interactive hackathons.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, and signaling clusters exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: multivalent molecular components collectively generate mesoscale material states, spatial organization, and cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from any single molecule alone. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts determine whether condensates assemble, dissolve, mature, or become pathological, and how do these emergent mesoscale states influence cell-level outcomes? We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, perturbational, and phenotypic datasets into a predictive, open framework for condensate emergence across human cells. The project will integrate existing resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, BioGRID/IntAct protein interaction networks, LLPSDB/DrLLPS/PhaSepDB condensate annotations, DepMap and genome-scale CRISPR perturbation data, AlphaFold structural predictions, post-translational modification databases, and public transcriptomic and stress-response datasets. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize these heterogeneous resources to create a community-curated atlas linking sequence composition, disorder, multivalency, interaction topology, expression stoichiometry, localization dynamics, perturbation sensitivity, and cellular phenotypes. The scientific goal is to identify generalizable rules by which molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behaviors and higher-order cellular consequences. We will develop interoperable analytical workflows that combine computer vision for condensate morphology and dynamics, graph learning on interaction and co-localization networks, biophysical feature extraction from sequence and structure, and causal inference from genetic and pharmacological perturbation datasets. These methods will be used to test three linked hypotheses: first, that condensate-forming systems occupy distinct regions of a multiscale feature space defined by disorder, valency, interaction network architecture, and regulated modifications; second, that emergent condensate material states can be inferred from public static and live-cell imaging signatures when integrated with molecular context; and third, that specific condensate state transitions predict downstream phenotypes such as stress tolerance, transcriptional reprogramming, cell-cycle arrest, or loss of viability. This effort requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in cell biology, soft-matter biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, database curation, and open-source software engineering, as well as coordinated community standards for condensate data representation. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data repositories, with balanced participation across career stages. Trainees will participate in hackathons, reproducible workflow development, cross-disciplinary journal clubs, and team-authored data papers, gaining practical training in synthesis biology, FAIR data practices, and responsible AI. Deliverables will include an open condensate synthesis atlas, reproducible analysis pipelines, benchmark datasets for machine learning, community metadata standards, and testable predictions for future experimental studies. By transforming fragmented public data into a unified framework, this project will advance a mechanistic understanding of how molecular interactions generate emergent mesoscale organization and how that organization shapes cellular behavior.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: weak, multivalent molecular interactions generate mesoscale compartments with material properties and regulatory functions that cannot be inferred from single molecules alone. Yet the field lacks generalizable, data-driven rules connecting protein sequence features, interaction networks, subcellular organization, environmental context, and cellular consequences. We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, and perturbation datasets to answer a central question: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts give rise to emergent condensate organization, and when do these mesoscale assemblies produce measurable cellular phenotypes? This project will use only existing public data, integrating resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, BioPlex and STRING interaction maps, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold structural predictions, post-translational modification databases, stress-response transcriptomic atlases, and DepMap/GenomeCRISPR perturbation screens. The working group will build an open, harmonized condensate-centric knowledge graph linking protein sequence grammar, intrinsically disordered regions, predicted interaction interfaces, multivalent binding motifs, localization patterns, condensate annotations, stress conditions, interaction partners, evolutionary conservation, and phenotypic effects of perturbation. We will then develop interpretable machine learning and network-based synthesis methods to identify mesoscale organizing principles that explain why some proteins form dynamic cellular bodies, why some condensates are robust or stress-sensitive, and which condensate components are most likely to control higher-order cellular outcomes such as viability, transcriptional state, signaling adaptation, or proteostasis. The project is intentionally beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires expertise in cell biology, phase separation biophysics, protein disorder and structural bioinformatics, microscopy image analysis, graph machine learning, causal inference, database engineering, and open-science workflow development. NCEMS support is essential to convene a geographically and institutionally diverse team, including researchers from R1 universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and data-science groups, to establish shared standards for integrating heterogeneous condensate-related data. Trainees will receive hands-on training through hackathon-style synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow development, image-derived feature extraction, graph analytics, and collaborative manuscript preparation. Expected outcomes include: an open FAIR database of condensate-associated molecular and cellular features; reusable pipelines for harmonizing public imaging, proteomic, and perturbation data; predictive models for condensate propensity and functional impact; and a community-authored framework defining testable principles of condensate emergence. By synthesizing existing data across molecular, mesoscale, and cellular scales, this working group will address a long-standing puzzle in cell biology: how dynamic molecular collectives become functional cellular structures. The resulting resource will enable the broader community to prioritize mechanisms, reinterpret existing experiments, and design future studies of emergent mesoscale organization without generating new experimental data during the funded synthesis effort.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from weak multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet their cellular consequences remain difficult to predict: under what conditions do condensates buffer perturbations, amplify stress signals, sequester regulatory factors, or drive pathological transitions? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and phenotypic data to identify generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to cellular stress responses and fate decisions. The central hypothesis is that condensate function is not encoded by individual components alone, but emerges from network-level features such as interaction valency, compositional diversity, RNA coupling, post-translational modification state, and subcellular context. Testing this hypothesis requires integration across data types and expertise beyond any single laboratory.

We will build an open, harmonized condensate-to-phenotype atlas by integrating existing datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, PRIDE, GEO, SRA, LINCS, DepMap, Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, BioGRID, IntAct, POSTAR, ENCODE, and curated phase-separation resources such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS. The atlas will link condensate-associated proteins and RNAs to sequence features, predicted disorder, interaction networks, post-translational modifications, localization dynamics, microscopy-derived mesoscale properties, perturbation responses, and cellular phenotypes under stress conditions including heat shock, oxidative stress, nutrient limitation, viral infection, and DNA damage. No new experimental data will be generated.

The working group will address three questions. First, which molecular features best predict emergent condensate behaviors such as fusion, dissolution, hardening, spatial relocalization, and selective recruitment? Second, when do condensates act as robust buffers versus switch-like amplifiers of stress-response pathways? Third, can conserved mesoscale organizational principles explain why similar molecular components produce divergent outcomes across cell types, organisms, and perturbations? To answer these questions, we will combine computer vision, protein biophysics, RNA biology, network science, causal inference, and interpretable machine learning. Analytical products will include standardized image-derived condensate descriptors, a cross-dataset knowledge graph, benchmark prediction tasks, and multiscale models that relate molecular interaction features to cellular outcomes.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated community-scale curation, common data standards, shared computational infrastructure, and iterative synthesis among specialists who rarely work together: cell biologists studying stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and DNA repair foci; biophysicists modeling phase transitions; data scientists developing multimodal foundation models; statisticians focused on causal inference; and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. The working group will hold synthesis sprints, open code reviews, trainee-led benchmarking challenges, and cross-training modules in reproducible workflows, microscopy metadata standards, and responsible AI for molecular and cellular biology.

All outputs will follow open science principles. Curated datasets, metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, model code, benchmark results, and visualization tools will be released through public repositories with persistent identifiers and community documentation. The project will provide a reusable framework for synthesizing heterogeneous data on mesoscale cellular organization, while producing testable principles for how emergent condensate properties shape higher-order cellular behavior. By transforming fragmented public data into predictive, interpretable models, this working group will help resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences: how dynamic molecular assemblies acquire system-level functions that cannot be inferred from their individual components alone.

title: Predicting Emergent RNP Condensate Assembly and Cell-State Consequences from Public Multi-Omic and Imaging Data

abstract_text: Within molecular and cellular biology, individual studies identify components of membraneless ribonucleoprotein condensates including stress granules and nucleoli, but findings remain inconsistent across experiments and extensive public data remains unintegrated. This project will determine which molecular, biophysical, network, and cellular features predict condensate assembly by synthesizing public datasets, extracting quantitative image features using computer vision algorithms, and applying interpretable graph machine learning and causal discovery techniques. The strategy will integrate resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting resources, and BioGRID by mapping metadata to established ontologies and structuring molecular components and phenotypes as typed graph nodes and edges. This research will provide harmonized metadata, reproducible pipelines, and predictive models to test whether generalized rules govern condensate formation and link molecular interactions to cellular structures.
full_text: This study in cellular biology explores the emergence of ribonucleoprotein condensates to predict their formation and downstream phenotypic impacts. Individual studies have identified various components and biophysical determinants but findings remain inconsistent and extensive public data remains unintegrated. The primary objective determines the features that predict the assembly of condensates and tests rules governing formation across cellular contexts. The proposed study synthesizes existing public datasets to extract image features and integrate them using computational models without experimental generation. Key tools include computer vision algorithms for image segmentation alongside interpretable graph machine learning and physics informed models. The analytical approach validates model performance using baseline statistical benchmarks and stratified cross validation to ensure external generalization. The project utilizes public databases including the Human Protein Atlas and the Image Data Resource alongside established interaction datasets. The synthesis plan maps metadata to established ontologies and structures the extracted features as typed nodes within graph models. The team mitigates limitations like heterogeneous annotations and batch effects by establishing confidence tiers and implementing quality control flags. The proposed timeline delivers a pilot atlas in year one and final integrated models upon completion of the project. Integrating heterogeneous public data at a community scale necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration spanning quantitative imaging and machine learning expertise. The project shares all findings and code through public repositories (such as GitHub) using accessible open source data formats. The diverse team encompasses principal investigators and graduate students from multiple research institutions to provide multidisciplinary training opportunities.

abstract_original: Membraneless ribonucleoprotein condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, and nuclear speckles are archetypal mesoscale systems: they emerge from many weak molecular interactions yet shape translation, RNA fate, signaling, and cell survival. Despite extensive public data, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework explaining when specific RNAs and proteins form condensates, how condensate composition varies across cellular contexts, and which mesoscale properties causally associate with downstream cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize existing public datasets to answer a central question: what molecular, biophysical, and network features predict the emergent assembly, composition, dynamics, and cellular consequences of human RNP condensates? The project will integrate only publicly available data, including fluorescence imaging datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer, and published live-cell stress-granule studies; proteomic and interactome data from BioGRID, IntAct, AP-MS, proximity-labeling, and condensate-enrichment studies; RNA localization and RNA-protein interaction data from ENCODE, POSTAR, CLIP-seq, APEX-seq, and subcellular fractionation studies; perturbation and phenotype data from DepMap, genome-scale CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, and drug-response repositories; and sequence-derived features such as intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, prion-like domains, charge patterning, RNA-binding motifs, post-translational modification sites, and predicted structures. The synthesis will produce a cross-scale atlas linking molecular features to mesoscale condensate behaviors and cellular outcomes. We will develop harmonized ontologies for condensate identity, experimental perturbation, stress condition, cell type, and measured mesoscale phenotype, then use computer vision to extract comparable features from public images, including condensate number, size distribution, shape, colocalization, dissolution kinetics, and spatial relationship to organelles. These features will be integrated with molecular interaction networks and perturbation phenotypes using interpretable graph machine learning, causal discovery, and physics-informed models of multivalent assembly. The goal is not simply to classify condensate components, but to identify generalizable rules explaining how emergent mesoscale properties arise from molecular composition and how these properties influence higher-order cell states such as translational arrest, antiviral response, proteostasis failure, and stress adaptation. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can assemble the needed expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, quantitative imaging, biophysics, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure, nor can it coordinate the community standards required to make heterogeneous public data interoperable. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, data science centers, and experimental condensate laboratories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will participate in reproducible workflow development, image-analysis hackathons, model benchmarking, and community annotation jamborees. All outputs will be open: curated datasets, metadata standards, analysis notebooks, trained models, uncertainty estimates, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories. The expected outcome is a reusable predictive framework for mesoscale emergence in RNP condensates, providing testable hypotheses for the broader community and a model for synthesis-driven discovery in molecular and cellular biology.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and chromatin can collectively generate dynamic compartments with properties not predictable from any single component. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some predicted phase-separating molecules form functional condensates in cells, while others do not, and when do condensates become pathological or phenotypically consequential? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular and cellular datasets to develop a generalizable, data-driven framework linking molecular features to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular outcomes. The project will integrate existing resources including human and model-organism proteomes, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification databases, RNA-binding and protein interaction maps, public proximity-labeling datasets, single-cell and bulk transcriptomic atlases, high-content microscopy repositories, CRISPR perturbation screens, disease variant catalogs, and curated condensate databases such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, and RNA granule resources. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize heterogeneous datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph describing condensate-associated molecules, their biophysical features, interaction contexts, cellular locations, perturbation responses, and phenotype associations. We will address three linked questions: (1) What combinations of molecular features and cellular context best predict condensate membership and mesoscale compartment identity? (2) Which emergent properties, such as compositional buffering, stress responsiveness, spatial co-localization, and dynamic exchange, can be inferred by integrating public imaging, proteomic, and perturbation data? (3) Which condensate states are associated with higher-order cellular outcomes, including stress tolerance, altered gene regulation, neurodegeneration-related toxicity, and cancer cell fitness? Analytically, the group will combine graph machine learning, interpretable multimodal models, causal inference from perturbation screens, and image-derived phenotype embeddings. A major methodological deliverable will be an open benchmark for condensate prediction and emergent-property inference, including negative controls, uncertainty estimates, and reproducible workflows. This synthesis requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise spans biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, microscopy, proteomics, machine learning, knowledge engineering, and open-science infrastructure, and because the data integration challenge exceeds the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will deliberately include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data repositories, and international open-data communities, with participation from graduate students and postdoctoral fellows as core analysts. Trainees will receive hands-on training through hackathons, reproducibility clinics, FAIR data curation sprints, and team-based manuscript and software development. All outputs, including harmonized metadata, analysis notebooks, trained models, benchmark datasets, and visualization tools, will be released publicly under permissive licenses with community governance. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent synthesis framework, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular interactions produce emergent mesoscale organization and how that organization shapes cellular phenotype.

abstract_text: Cellular biology research investigates the formation of biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles via liquid liquid phase separation, which constitutes a critical process that fundamentally regulates diverse cellular functions. Highly siloed data currently prevents a unified understanding of how biophysical rules and stoichiometric thresholds govern condensate assembly to drive macro scale global cellular outcomes. This project will construct a multi scale biological knowledge graph and apply multi modal graph neural networks with geometric deep learning to identify concentration and stoichiometric thresholds for condensate assembly and predict subcellular phenotypes from molecular perturbations. Public datasets from PRIDE, GEO, PhaSepDB, the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, the Image Data Resource, and UniProt will be integrated by harmonizing metadata and mapping biological entities into the unified knowledge graph. This framework will establish rules for condensate assembly, explain in vivo and in vitro concentration discrepancies, and create a predictive model linking amino acid sequences to organelle level phenotypes.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—represent a paradigm-shifting example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. These dynamic assemblies bridge the critical gap between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, orchestrating essential cellular functions ranging from gene regulation to stress response. However, despite an exponential increase in individual laboratory studies, the universal biophysical rules and stoichiometric conditions that dictate the unexpected emergence of these mesoscale structures remain a long-standing mystery. Furthermore, predicting how localized condensate dynamics influence global, higher-order cellular outcomes remains beyond current capabilities. This gap in knowledge persists largely because existing experimental data—ranging from atomic-resolution structural biophysics to whole-cell spatial transcriptomics and high-content imaging—are highly siloed across disparate public repositories.

To address this, we propose the establishment of the "Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group" (MCS-WG), a transdisciplinary collaborative initiative designed to synthesize existing multimodal public datasets to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. By integrating fragmented data from PRIDE (mass spectrometry proteomics), GEO (transcriptomics), PhaSepDB (phase separation curation), AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (structural conformations), and the Image Data Resource (high-content cellular microscopy), our team will construct a massive, multi-scale biological knowledge graph. Crucially, this project will rely entirely on publicly available data, generating no new experimental data, thereby directly answering the NCEMS call for community-scale synthesis.

Our working group will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically geometric deep learning and multi-modal graph neural networks, to identify hidden patterns that drive mesoscale phase separation. Our research objectives are threefold: (1) Answer novel questions regarding the evolutionary conservation of disordered protein regions and their emergent phase-separation behaviors across distinct cellular stress states; (2) Solve the long-standing puzzle of how varied macromolecular concentrations dynamically trigger mesoscale assembly and disassembly; and (3) Develop an innovative, open-source AI analytical framework that predicts subcellular phenotypic outcomes based on molecular-level perturbations.

The complexity of this synthesis requires the unique support and resources of NCEMS, as it extends far beyond the computational or domain expertise of any single laboratory. The MCS-WG will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, data ontologists, and machine learning experts from varied geographic locations and institutional tiers. In strong alignment with NCEMS goals, our initiative places a heavy emphasis on workforce development. We will actively recruit and cross-train early-career researchers (graduate students and postdocs) from historically underrepresented backgrounds, equipping them with a dual skill set in molecular biology and advanced data science. Furthermore, committing strictly to open science principles, all curated datasets, harmonized ontologies, AI model architectures, and analysis pipelines will be released publicly via open-access community portals, ensuring reproducibility and providing a lasting resource for the molecular and cellular biosciences community. Through this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will unravel how mesoscale emergence dictates cellular fate.

abstract_text: Within molecular and cellular biology, biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation mediate critical multi scale biological phenomena across nucleoli, stress granules, and processing bodies. A unified framework is currently absent because public datasets remain isolated across biological scales, yielding a fragmented understanding of how nanoscale molecular interactions drive mesoscale condensate properties. To map intrinsically disordered proteins and post translational modifications to cellular outcomes, this project will synthesize existing data utilizing natural language processing, multimodal graph neural networks, self supervised representation learning, and transformer based attention mechanisms. The project will integrate resources including UniProt, DisProt, LLPSDB, and spatial transcriptomic atlases into a cloud based repository, structuring this information as a knowledge graph defining individual protein interaction probabilities. This work will deliver a unified predictive framework for liquid liquid phase separation, which could identify novel therapeutic targets for complex diseases involving abnormal phase transitions.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a paradigm-shifting example of emergent mesoscale organization. These membraneless compartments organize biochemical reactions dynamically, yet bridging the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and their mesoscale architectural properties remains a critical challenge. While abundant public data exist detailing the sequence characteristics of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and the cellular phenotypes of their dysregulation, a unified framework mapping this cross-scale emergence is absent. Currently, critical datasets—such as sequence features (UniProt, DisProt), structural predictions (AlphaFold), in vitro phase behaviors (LLPSDB, PhaSePro), mesoscale cellular imaging (Image Data Resource), and high-throughput phenotypic screens (DepMap)—remain highly siloed. No individual research laboratory possesses the combined expertise in molecular biophysics, spatial transcriptomics, artificial intelligence, and cellular biology necessary to bridge these data islands. To address this compelling scientific puzzle, we propose the 'Mesoscale Condensate Computome (MCC)' Working Group. This highly collaborative, transdisciplinary team will synthesize entirely publicly available datasets to decipher the rules governing emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. We will employ advanced AI and data science methodologies, specifically developing multimodal graph neural networks, to seamlessly integrate cross-scale data. The project is structured around three core synthesis objectives: (1) Map the molecular grammar of IDPs and associated post-translational modifications to mesoscale emergent properties such as condensate viscosity, critical concentration thresholds, and multiphase spatial architecture; (2) Link these emergent mesoscale features directly to cellular-level outcomes, specifically focusing on stress granule dynamics and neurodegenerative protein aggregation pathways; and (3) Develop open-source predictive algorithms capable of inferring higher-order cellular phenotypes strictly from primary molecular sequences and available interactome topologies. This initiative goes far beyond the capabilities of an individual lab, necessitating the centralized support of NCEMS to unite diverse experts across geographic locations, institutional research levels, and career stages. The MCC Working Group will recruit diverse computational and biological scientists, intentionally embedding postdoctoral researchers and graduate students into the core data science workflows. This will provide unprecedented training opportunities, actively cultivating a data-savvy, next-generation workforce fluent in cross-disciplinary AI and biological synthesis. Furthermore, our initiative commits rigorously to community-created open science policies. We will release all harmonized multi-scalar datasets, machine learning models, and reproducible analysis pipelines via public GitHub repositories and a dedicated web portal, ensuring long-term utility for the molecular biosciences community. By decoding how simple molecular inputs trigger complex, non-linear mesoscale emergence, this synthesis project will answer long-standing mysteries regarding biological phase transitions, ultimately pioneering innovative analytical strategies for understanding cellular organization in health and disease.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where transient, multivalent interactions among thousands of biomolecules spontaneously give rise to highly organized, functional, membrane-less organelles. These mesoscale structures dictate critical subcellular outcomes, ranging from stress adaptation to gene regulation. However, the precise rules governing how molecular-level features—such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA secondary structures, and post-translational modifications (PTMs)—dynamically scale to produce emergent mesoscale physical properties remain a long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. Despite the exponential growth of publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, structural, and spatial imaging datasets, these rich resources remain deeply siloed across disparate repositories. Addressing this complex emergent phenomenon requires a community-scale data synthesis approach that far exceeds the computational and disciplinary capabilities of any individual research laboratory.

We propose the establishment of the Condensate Emergence Synthesis (CES) Working Group to decode the multiscale grammar of condensate formation. This transdisciplinary team will unite domain experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, cell biology, and multi-omics. Adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate, we will generate no new experimental data. Instead, we will synthesize massive public datasets, including molecular interaction networks (BioGRID), structural and disorder profiles (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), high-throughput proteomics (PRIDE), and mesoscale spatial imaging (Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Atlas). 

Our primary scientific objective is to develop an innovative, multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework to uncover the hidden principles of mesoscale emergence. We will address a novel question: How do heterogeneous molecular inputs synergistically trigger the spatiotemporal emergence of specific condensates, such as stress granules, under shifting environmental pressures? By harmonizing these disparate, multi-scale data streams into a unified, dynamic knowledge graph, our AI-driven analytical strategy will predict how distinct molecular perturbations cascade upward to alter mesoscale properties—such as condensate size, viscosity, and composition—and ultimately influence cellular phenotypes.

Executing this transdisciplinary integration fundamentally relies on the unique infrastructure, computational resources, and collaborative ecosystem provided by NCEMS. By bringing together diverse scientific perspectives across career stages and institutional levels, we will translate fragmented biological data into a cohesive understanding of subcellular emergence. 

Crucially, the CES Working Group will adhere strictly to community-created open science policies. All integrated databases, AI models, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be distributed through open-source repositories following FAIR principles. Furthermore, this initiative will provide unparalleled training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through intensive, cross-disciplinary co-mentorship in advanced data science and systems biology, we will empower the future data-savvy workforce required to solve the next generation of biological mysteries.

A unified, predictive understanding of how molecular grammar and transient cellular states (such as stress or energy depletion) cooperatively govern the emergence, material properties, and dissolution of these mesoscale structures represents a major, long-standing puzzle. This project proposes a comprehensive, community-scale data synthesis initiative to decode the emergent rules of biomolecular condensates. Crucially, no new experimental data will be generated. Instead, our Working Group will synthesize a massive array of existing public data, including curated LLPS databases (PhaSePro, LLPSDB), AlphaFold3 structural and conformational predictions, single-cell RNA-sequencing from cellular stress models, spatio-temporal proteomics (Human Protein Atlas), and high-content microscopy imaging (e.g., public Cell Painting datasets). By integrating these multi-scale resources, we will address compelling scientific questions regarding the spatio-temporal dynamics of mesoscale assembly. To achieve this, we will develop and deploy innovative AI-driven analytical strategies, specifically utilizing multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning. abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules and nucleoli, represent a quintessential example of emergent properties at the mesoscale. Arising from the dynamic, multivalent interactions of proteins and RNA, these membraneless organelles bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular functions. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress adaptation, and disease pathogenesis, the fundamental rules dictating how physical interactions at the atomic and molecular levels scale up to govern mesoscale condensation and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remain a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Current biological research often captures these phenomena in isolated silos—producing disparate datasets on molecular structure, pairwise protein-protein interactions, or cellular imaging—leaving a critical knowledge gap in bridging these temporal and spatial dimensions.

To address this fundamental question of emergence, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of publicly available biological data to decode the mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates. We will systematically integrate structural and sequence data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt, PDB), high-throughput interaction and proximity labeling networks (BioGRID, IntAct, PRIDE), transcriptomic profiles under distinct cellular stress states (GEO, SRA), and high-resolution spatial imaging data (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Crucially, this project will rely entirely on existing public data and will not generate any new experimental outputs.

Leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science, specifically multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and contrastive representation learning, we will develop an innovative analytical strategy to fuse these disparate, multi-scale data types. Our primary objective is to construct 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet,' a predictive foundation model that mathematically maps how molecular grammars (such as intrinsically disordered regions, amino acid spacing, and interaction valencies) dictate emergent mesoscale properties (including droplet formation, material state transitions, and biochemical partitioning) and their subsequent cellular outcomes like gene regulation and stress survival.

This ambitious synthesis project fundamentally exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. It necessitates the specialized resources, computational infrastructure, and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS. We have assembled a transdisciplinary team encompassing structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and data ontologists. This diverse partnership deliberately bridges multiple geographic locations, career stages, and institutional types to ensure a breadth of scientific perspectives.

Committed to gold-standard open science principles, all curated multimodal datasets, AI architectures, and reproducible analytical workflows will be openly shared via GitHub and Zenodo, strictly adhering to FAIR data practices. Furthermore, this working group will serve as a premier training incubator for the future data-savvy workforce. Through dedicated hackathons and cross-disciplinary mentorship, graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be cross-trained at the cutting edge of artificial intelligence and mesoscale biology. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve a critical mystery in molecular biology, providing a transformative, open-access computational framework to predict condensate-driven emergent behaviors across the cellular landscape.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence: An AI-Driven Synthesis of Multi-Omic and Structural Data to Uncover the Rules of Biomolecular Condensate Formation
title_norm: decoding mesoscale emergence an aidriven synthesis of multiomic and structural data to uncover the rules of biomolecular condensate formation
abstract_text: Molecular and cellular biology focuses on the emergence of biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation, generating essential public data spanning intrinsically disordered regions, post translational modifications, and protein protein interactions. Identifying the generalizable rules governing condensate physical properties and formation from microscale molecular features remains unachievable because these critical datasets are currently unintegrated and siloed across independent repositories. To determine the sequence grammar and thermodynamic principles underlying condensate emergence, this purely computational data synthesis project will apply Graph Neural Networks, protein language models, standardized ontologies, and coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations to public multi omic data. The project will integrate PDB, DisProt, IDEAL, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, BioGRID, STRING, PRIDE, and GEO into heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks by assigning biomolecules as nodes with sequence embeddings and interactions as thermodynamically weighted edges. Ultimately, this research will introduce an artificial intelligence framework for multi scale data integration, providing predictive modeling of condensate behaviors based on fundamental sequence grammar and microscale molecular signatures.
full_text: The discipline of molecular and cellular biology lacks generalizable rules connecting microscale features to condensates from phase separation. Public databases hold extensive data on protein sequences and intrinsically disordered regions but these repositories remain fundamentally siloed. The proposed study investigates principles of emergence for condensates by introducing an artificial intelligence framework for synthesis of biological data. The proposed study employs a purely computational strategy over three phases to aggregate data and predict emergence of condensates. The analytical approach utilizes graph neural networks and protein language models like ESM-2 alongside coarse grained simulations of molecules. The team will validate results through a temporal hold out strategy supplemented by coarse grained simulations of molecular dynamics. The team will extract information from repositories for structural and interaction data including the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and DisProt. The team will mitigate inherent variations in data formats and resolution scales by developing a standardized ontological framework. The project milestones progress sequentially through aggregation of data and modeling with artificial intelligence to prediction of emergence at the mesoscale. Processing this immense volume of data necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration across domains like polymer physics and artificial intelligence. The team will ensure rigorous reproducibility and open access by sharing code on GitHub and data on Zenodo. The team spans multiple career stages and provides training opportunities through mentorship programs and cross disciplinary workshops for data synthesis.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, dynamic membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergence at the mesoscale. Arising from the multivalent interactions of proteins and nucleic acids, these mesoscale structures bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and complex cellular organelles, orchestrating critical subcellular processes ranging from stress response to gene expression. Despite the recent explosion of experimental data regarding LLPS, a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology remains: What are the fundamental, generalizable rules that govern the unexpected emergence of biomolecular condensates from constituent molecular features across dynamic cellular environments?

To address this gap, we propose the establishment of a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize massive, heterogeneous, publicly available datasets to uncover the multi-scale rules of mesoscale emergence. Our project strictly utilizes existing public data, bypassing new experimental data generation, to conduct a community-scale synthesis that integrates structural databases (PDB), intrinsically disordered protein repositories (DisProt, IDEAL), specialized LLPS databases (PhaSePro, LLPSDB), global protein-protein interactomes (BioGRID), and condition-specific spatial multi-omics (PRIDE, GEO).

Through the application of advanced artificial intelligence and data science techniques, specifically Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, our Working Group will construct a unified theoretical and computational framework. This framework will map the thermodynamic and kinetic emergence of condensates from microscale molecular properties—such as sequence grammar, post-translational modifications, and RNA-binding capacity—up to mesoscale structural properties and eventual cellular phenotypic outcomes. By integrating data across spatial, temporal, and energy scales (e.g., cellular homeostasis versus acute stress states), we aim to predict emergent mesoscale behaviors under diverse physiological contexts.

This synthesis initiative fundamentally requires the collaborative ecosystem and cyberinfrastructure of NCEMS. The sheer volume and dimensionality of the data, combined with the required integration of polymer physics, computational structural biology, multi-omics, and AI, place this effort far beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory or traditional collaboration. Our team brings together a diverse assembly of molecular biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists from across geographic locations and career stages, encompassing both R1 universities and Minority Serving Institutions (MSIs) to ensure varied scientific perspectives and tap diverse new talent.

In strict adherence to Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be made openly accessible via an interactive, open-source platform. Furthermore, this Working Group is deeply committed to training the future data-savvy workforce. We will host cross-disciplinary data synthesis workshops and provide dedicated mentorship programs for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, equipping them with the unique skills needed to navigate both molecular biology and advanced computational AI. Ultimately, this project will decode the principles of mesoscale emergence, providing a transformative, open-access resource that accelerates discovery across the molecular and cellular biosciences.

title: Synthesizing the Mesoscale: AI-Driven Integration of Multi-Omic and Structural Data to Decode the Emergence of Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: synthesizing the mesoscale aidriven integration of multiomic and structural data to decode the emergence of biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: This research examines the formation and material properties of biomolecular condensates driven by liquid liquid phase separation, a phenomenon requiring the integration of siloed molecular, structural, and cellular data. To determine how molecular features and stoichiometry dictate condensate architecture, this project will synthesize existing public datasets and apply physics informed graph neural networks constrained by polymer physics to predict material states and phase transitions. Automated computational pipelines will integrate DisProt, Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold DB, and BioGRID into a multi relational knowledge graph where nodes represent biomolecules and edges denote physical interactions and transition probabilities. This computational framework will model pathogenic fluid to solid transitions and map physical properties to cellular phenotypes, advancing targeted therapeutics for cancer and neurodegenerative diseases.
full_text: This project explores the formation of biomolecular condensates to discover how molecular sequences and cellular stoichiometry dictate mesoscale properties. Existing public datasets capture nanoscale structures of proteins and cellular phenotypes but remain unintegrated to explain collective multivalent interactions. The proposed study models transitions from fluid to solid phases to advance the understanding of neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. The research strategy relies upon the secondary synthesis of existing public data via machine learning to model mesoscale properties. The team applies physics informed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with thermodynamic constraints to classify nodes and predict edges. Domain experts validate the computational predictions by comparing generated results against historical literature and held out orthogonal datasets. The proposed study utilizes the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold DB alongside cellular repositories including the Allen Cell Explorer. Automated computational pipelines integrate these distinct datasets into a unified knowledge graph connecting structural domains and cellular phenotypes. The team addresses variable formats and inconsistent standards of metadata by engineering automated pipelines for the comprehensive harmonization of data. The timeline features sequential phases for the harmonization of data and development of models driven by biannual synthesis sprints. The integration of structural biophysics and machine learning requires a broad cross disciplinary collaboration exceeding the capacities of individual laboratories. The team distributes integrated datasets and containerized computational workflows via public repositories and publishes findings in open access articles. abstract_original: The transition of individual biomolecules into mesoscale assemblies—particularly membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represents a quintessential example of emergence in cellular biology. These biomolecular condensates exhibit unique material properties that govern critical cellular functions, from gene regulation to stress adaptation. Despite an explosion of single-discipline studies, predicting how mesoscale material properties (e.g., viscoelasticity, fluid-to-solid transitions) and subsequent cellular phenotypes emerge from localized molecular interactions remains a persistent enigma. Unlocking this puzzle requires transcending the capabilities of any single research laboratory through the large-scale integration of existing but highly siloed data. This Working Group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergence of biomolecular condensates at the mesoscale by integrating publicly available molecular, structural, and cellular imaging data. We will systematically synthesize intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequence data (DisProt), atomistic structural ensembles (AlphaFold DB, PDB), proteomics and protein-protein interaction networks (BioGRID, PRIDE), and high-resolution spatial imaging data (EMPIAR, Allen Cell Explorer, PhaSePro). By exclusively leveraging these vast open-access repositories with zero de novo experimental data generation, we will employ advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and multimodal data science to construct the first comprehensive 'Mesoscale Condensate Knowledge Graph.' Our project addresses three compelling scientific objectives: (1) Answer the long-standing puzzle of how the interplay between molecular grammar (sequence/structure) and cellular stoichiometry dictates the emergent mesoscale architecture of condensates; (2) Develop innovative, physics-informed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to predict condensate material states and aberrant transitions (which are frequently linked to neurodegeneration and cancer) under varying environmental cellular stresses; and (3) Map these mesoscale properties to their higher-order phenotypic outcomes. Because this effort requires bridging Angstrom-level biophysics with micron-level cell biology via sophisticated AI, it necessitates the transdisciplinary environment, collaboration, and infrastructural support unique to NCEMS. Our Working Group deliberately spans a diverse spectrum of expertise—incorporating computational biophysicists, molecular biologists, structural database engineers, and AI/machine learning scientists—across varied geographic locations, institution types, and career stages. Crucially, this project will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be co-mentored by cross-disciplinary experts, gaining hands-on experience in multimodal AI, biological data harmonization, and cloud computing. Committed to gold-standard Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, and reproducible analytical workflows will be distributed under permissive licenses through GitHub and a dedicated, community-accessible web portal. By synthesizing existing data to reveal the hidden rules of mesoscale emergence, this project will not only answer fundamental biological questions but also establish a transformative methodological blueprint for community-scale synthesis in the molecular and cellular sciences.

The project will achieve its primary objective by synthesizing datasets to determine condensate formation rules and cellular stress effects using a computational approach with graph neural networks and three dimensional convolutional long short term memory networks. The project will integrate data from DisProt, UniProt, AlphaFold DB, PhaSePro, CD CODE, BioGRID, PRIDE, and the Image Data Resource into standardized matrices using a unified graph ontology and latent space alignment. The output will establish the deterministic rules of cellular organization, enabling the prediction of emergent cellular behaviors from primary sequence data to fundamentally inform synthetic condensate design.

abstract_original:
The emergence of mesoscale biological structures—those bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and functional organelles—represents a fundamental frontier in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Biomolecular condensates, dynamic membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation, are paradigm examples of mesoscale emergence. While they critically regulate cellular outcomes such as stress response and gene expression, the principles dictating how 1D molecular sequences and local physical interactions collectively scale into complex, emergent 3D mesoscale behaviors remain a long-standing puzzle. The global research community has generated massive, yet deeply siloed, datasets spanning protein sequences, interactomics, biophysical measurements, and subcellular imaging. Addressing the complexity of mesoscale phase separation far exceeds the capacity of any single research group, necessitating a transdisciplinary, community-scale data synthesis approach.

We propose the establishment of the 'Condensate Emergence Synthesis and Analytics' (CESA) Working Group to decode the multiscale rules of mesoscale condensate emergence. Strictly leveraging existing, publicly available data without generating new experimental datasets, this project will integrate sequence and structural databases (e.g., DisProt, AlphaFold DB), biophysical phase separation repositories (e.g., PhaSePro, CD-CODE), massive-scale stress-response proteomics (PRIDE, BioGRID), and high-resolution microscopy datasets from the Image Data Resource (IDR). 

To synthesize these highly heterogeneous modalities, our diverse team will develop innovative artificial intelligence and data science analytical strategies. Specifically, we will utilize multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and spatio-temporal deep learning to build predictive models. These models will map the continuum from molecular-level features (e.g., intrinsic disorder, valency) to mesoscale emergent properties (e.g., condensate viscosity, complex assembly/disassembly kinetics) and ultimately to cellular phenotypic outcomes, such as cellular resilience to environmental stress. 

This initiative heavily relies on the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. The CESA Working Group will convene a diverse assembly of experts, including molecular biophysicists, cell biologists, computational biologists, and AI/ML engineers. Our team is strategically assembled to reflect a broad spectrum of career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels (including primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions), ensuring diverse scientific perspectives.

A cornerstone of our proposal is the rigorous training of the next-generation, data-savvy scientific workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees embedded within the Working Group will undergo intensive cross-training at the intersection of molecular cell biology and advanced computational data synthesis, gaining essential, highly translatable skills in AI-driven biology.

Adhering strictly to Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, analytical workflows, and educational materials will be made publicly accessible via FAIR-compliant repositories (e.g., Zenodo, GitHub) and disseminated through an interactive, community-facing web portal. By synthesizing disparate public data to map the continuous trajectory from molecular biophysics to emergent mesoscale architecture, the CESA Working Group will solve critical mysteries of cellular emergence, provide the community with transformative open-source analytical tools, and establish a new paradigm for transdisciplinary discovery in the biosciences.
