abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. These dynamic, membrane-less compartments bridge individual molecular interactions—specifically between intrinsically disordered proteins and RNAs—with organelle-level organization and cellular-scale outcomes. During environmental stress, condensates such as stress granules rapidly emerge to protect cellular viability. However, a fundamental long-standing puzzle remains: what are the universal, emergent rules governing how molecular-scale perturbations collectively propagate to alter mesoscale condensate properties and subsequent global cellular responses? Currently, the molecular and cellular sciences are rich with fragmented data concerning condensate formation. Massive, publicly available repositories house transcriptomic and proteomic profiles of stress responses (GEO, PRIDE), high-resolution microscopy of cellular compartments (Image Data Resource), and structural predictions of intrinsically disordered regions (AlphaFoldDB, DisProt). Yet, deciphering the emergent properties of these mesoscale structures is beyond the capability of any single research laboratory. It requires the community-scale synthesis of these disparate datasets using advanced artificial intelligence and transdisciplinary expertise. To address this compelling scientific question, our proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize diverse, publicly available multi-omics, structural, and high-content imaging datasets to uncover the rules of mesoscale emergence in stress condensates. We will develop a novel, AI-driven computational framework that integrates molecular sequence and structural disorder data with cellular-level phenotypic imaging. By employing multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and computer vision algorithms, we will map multi-scale relationships, identifying the precise biophysical thresholds where atomic and molecular interactions collectively trigger mesoscale phase transitions. Our project is defined by three primary objectives. First, we will construct a comprehensive, open-access multi-scale knowledge graph unifying public molecular, interaction, and cellular imaging data related to cellular stress states. Second, we will leverage machine learning to extract hidden physicochemical rules governing how emergent mesoscale networks dynamically reconfigure in response to distinct stressors. Third, we will develop predictive models linking mesoscale condensate behavior to macro-cellular fate. This synthesis necessitates the unique collaborative environment and computational resources provided by NCEMS. Our team brings together a diverse array of experts—spanning biophysics, structural biology, machine learning, and cellular imaging—from multiple geographic regions, career stages, and institutional research levels. Crucially, this initiative relies entirely on existing public data, requiring no new experimental generation. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, AI models, and analytical workflows will be publicly distributed following FAIR guidelines, ensuring complete reproducibility. Furthermore, this working group will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be integrated into the core leadership of the analytical subgroups, receiving cross-disciplinary mentorship in AI-driven data synthesis, biophysics, and reproducible team science. Ultimately, this collaborative effort will resolve critical mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence, catalyzing a paradigm shift in how we understand subcellular organization through the lens of big data.

abstract_original: The emergence of biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—represents a profound paradigm shift in our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization. Bridging the critical spatial gap between individual biomolecules and functional membrane-bound organelles, these condensates regulate vital cellular processes, notably stress responses, RNA metabolism, and gene expression. Despite the recent explosion of isolated experimental datasets, a unified understanding of how nanometer-scale interactions of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and nucleic acids collectively drive the emergence of micrometer-scale mesoscopic phenotypes remains a major, unresolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Currently, vast amounts of heterogeneous, publicly available data exist in isolated silos: sequence-level IDP annotations (DisProt), large-scale proteomic profiles of isolated condensates (PRIDE), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold DB), and mesoscale live-cell imaging datasets mapping spatial dynamics (BioImage Archive). No single research laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, diverse domain knowledge, or cross-disciplinary expertise required to harmonize these multi-modal, multi-scale datasets. Addressing this fundamental gap necessitates a community-scale data synthesis approach, aligning perfectly with the core mission of NCEMS. We propose a transdisciplinary Working Group to integrate disparate multi-omic, structural, biophysical, and spatial imaging datasets to decode the fundamental physicochemical rules governing condensate emergence. By leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies, specifically multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, we will synthesize over 50,000 publicly available records spanning from the molecular to the cellular scale. Our collaborative synthesis project will address three compelling scientific questions: (1) What are the universal sequence and structural grammar rules that dictate multi-component, mesoscale condensate assembly? (2) How do emergent mesoscale biophysical properties, such as viscoelasticity and surface tension, arise predictably from the dynamic interactome of IDPs? and (3) How do these emergent mesoscale network properties dictate global cellular phenotypes, particularly cellular survival and adaptation during environmental stress? Crucially, this project will rely exclusively on the rigorous synthesis of existing public data, generating no new experimental data, but rather pioneering an innovative, AI-driven analytical framework for mesoscale biology. To achieve this, our Working Group convenes a diverse, multi-institutional collaborative team encompassing molecular biophysicists, structural biologists, AI/ML data scientists, and cell physiologists. This team spans early-career and established investigators from R1 institutions, Primarily Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs), and historically underrepresented institutions, ensuring a wide array of scientific perspectives and geographic diversity. Deeply committed to open science principles, our team will ensure all integrated datasets, trained AI models, and analytical workflows are disseminated through public repositories (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) using reproducible, containerized pipelines. Furthermore, this initiative is highly dedicated to training the future data-savvy workforce. We will actively fund and integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers into the collaborative research efforts. Through specialized 'synthesis hackathons,' structured peer-mentorship networks, and intensive cross-training at the intersection of AI and molecular biophysics, we will equip early-career researchers with the transdisciplinary computational skills required to lead the next generation of emergence-focused biological synthesis research.

title: Synthesizing the Mesoscale: An AI-Driven Integration of Multi-Omic and Biophysical Data to Decode the Emergent Properties of Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: synthesizing the mesoscale an aidriven integration of multiomic and biophysical data to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: The research domain of mesoscale cellular biology focuses on biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation, which are critical because they compartmentalize reactions and mediate cellular stress. However, existing reductionist models fail to capture the non linear interactions among intrinsically disordered regions and post translational modifications that determine condensate biophysical properties and cellular phenotypes. The primary objective is to determine how sequence features control condensate material properties, and this computational synthesis project will apply automated ingestion pipelines, protein Large Language Models, and multimodal Graph Neural Networks to predict cellular phenotypes. The project will integrate DisProt, PhosphoSitePlus, CD-CODE, PhaSePro, DepMap, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, and GEO into a relational database, converting sequences into language model embeddings that serve as graph neural network input nodes. This predictive modeling framework will transition the field from descriptive observation to establishing fundamental biophysical rules that inform the manipulation of condensates in cancer and neurodegeneration.
full_text: This project investigates mesoscale emergence in biology to determine how molecular sequences dictate the biophysical properties of condensates. Biological condensates compartmentalize reactions and mediate stress but isolated datasets and reductionist models obscure their highly complex interactions. The team asks whether artificial intelligence can predict phenotypes from protein sequences to establish rules for disease manipulation. This computational data synthesis project harmonizes public databases to link modeled biophysical features with cellular phenotypes through machine learning. The team applies automated pipelines and a relational database alongside large language models and multimodal graph neural networks. The team validates all predicted condensate states by correlating model outputs against established transcriptomic signatures and cellular survival metrics. abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. Formed via liquid-liquid phase separation, these membraneless organelles bridge the nanometer scale of individual biomolecules and the micrometer scale of cellular architecture. Despite their critical roles in regulating gene expression, stress responses, and metabolic compartmentalization, a fundamental puzzle remains: how do sequence-level molecular features, such as intrinsically disordered regions and transient post-translational modifications (PTMs), synergistically encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates (e.g., viscosity, multiphase organization, and dissolution dynamics) that ultimately govern cellular phenotypes? Addressing this complex multiscale challenge is beyond the capacity of any single laboratory and requires a community-scale synthesis of siloed, publicly available datasets. This Working Group proposes an ambitious, computationally driven data synthesis project to decode the rules of mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates. By adhering strictly to the use of existing public data, we will not generate new experimental results but will instead perform a massive integration of molecular, biophysical, and cellular databases. We will synthesize structural and sequence data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), PTM annotations (PhosphoSitePlus), biophysical phase-separation registries (CD-CODE, PhaSePro), and cellular phenotypic and transcriptomic data (DepMap, GEO). To achieve this, our diverse, transdisciplinary team of biophysicists, computational biologists, machine learning experts, and cell biologists will develop an innovative, AI-driven analytical strategy. We will construct a multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN) and leverage protein large language models (LLMs) to map how energy-dependent PTMs alter molecular motion and information transfer, triggering the spatial emergence of condensates. By modeling these mesoscale properties, our AI framework will predict higher-order subcellular and cellular outcomes across diverse stress conditions. This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to investigate emergent properties at the mesoscale, linking spatial and temporal dynamics from molecules to organelles. The proposed synthesis fundamentally requires the unique support and collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. The requisite integration of physical chemistry, structural biology, and multi-omic systems biology demands a sustained, cross-disciplinary Working Group environment that bridges geographic locations and institutional tiers. Our team deliberately incorporates researchers from varying career stages, ensuring a diverse array of scientific perspectives and expertise. Furthermore, this Working Group is deeply committed to open science and workforce development. All integrated datasets, AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented, version-controlled, and made freely available to the public following FAIR and open science principles. Crucially, the project will serve as a premier training ground for the next-generation data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees integrated into our team will receive unparalleled, cross-disciplinary mentorship in advanced data science, AI methodologies, and multiscale biological modeling. By illuminating the mesoscale rules of condensate emergence, this synthesis will solve long-standing molecular puzzles, pioneer novel analytical paradigms, and significantly advance our predictive understanding of cellular organization.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where individual macromolecules collectively phase-separate to form dynamic, functionally distinct membraneless organelles. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress response, and disease—such as neurodegeneration and cancer—the fundamental rules governing how multi-scale biological properties cooperate to drive condensate emergence remain a long-standing puzzle. Specifically, the field lacks a holistic understanding of how changes in atomic-level structure, energetic states, and cellular information flows dictate the spatial and temporal emergence of these mesoscale assemblies. Currently, data capturing molecular properties and condensate behavior are highly fragmented across independent biophysical, structural, interactomic, transcriptomic, and imaging databases. This Working Group proposes to synthesize these vast, publicly available datasets to uncover the universal, predictable principles of mesoscale emergence. By integrating structural predictions (AlphaFold DB, PDB), biophysical phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB), interactomes (BioGRID, STRING), expression atlases (GEO, SRA), and high-content cellular imaging (Image Data Resource), we will construct a unified, multi-modal knowledge graph of condensate dynamics. Critically, in strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, this project will generate no new experimental data; rather, it relies entirely on the community-scale synthesis and integration of existing datasets using advanced data science. Our primary objectives are threefold. First, we aim to answer the novel question of how condition-specific cellular profiles (e.g., thermal shock, oxidative stress, or metabolic shifts) predict the emergent mesoscale material properties and compositional dynamics of condensates. Second, we will develop a novel analytical AI framework—an open-source 'Condensate Emergence Predictor' (CEP)—utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) capable of forecasting the spatial and temporal formation of these structures based solely on multi-omic and structural inputs. Third, we will explore how these emergent mesoscale properties are conserved or rewired across evolutionary time in diverse eukaryotic lineages. This massive data synthesis fundamentally requires NCEMS support and resources, as it far exceeds the computational and domain-specific capabilities of any single laboratory. Achieving our goals demands the cross-disciplinary convergence of experts in AI, bioinformatics, structural biophysics, and cell biology. Our Working Group deliberately convenes a geographically and institutionally diverse team—spanning R1 universities and primarily undergraduate institutions—to foster rich, collaborative partnerships. Furthermore, we are deeply committed to training the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. The Working Group will provide rigorous cross-training opportunities for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, who will co-lead the data harmonization and AI development phases under joint multidisciplinary mentorship. Adhering to the highest standards of open, reproducible science, all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines will be publicly disseminated via community repositories and a user-friendly interactive web portal. Ultimately, this synthesis project will illuminate how mesoscale architectural emergence bridges the gap between individual biomolecules and complex cellular outcomes.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergent phenomena at the mesoscale. These membraneless organelles dynamically assemble from interacting networks of proteins and nucleic acids, fundamentally bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and complex subcellular organization. While recent years have seen an explosion of publicly available data on LLPS—ranging from intrinsic disorder profiles and high-throughput proteomics to live-cell imaging and mutational databases—these datasets remain heavily siloed across disparate platforms. Consequently, a long-standing puzzle remains: How do the sequence-level 'grammars' of thousands of distinct molecules interact collectively to drive the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates, and how do perturbations in these systems cascade into cellular dysfunction? 

To address this compelling question, we propose the 'Condensate Emergence Synthesis Network' (CESN), a multidisciplinary Working Group designed to synthesize massive, heterogeneous public datasets using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and data science. Our transdisciplinary team unites experts in computational biophysics, structural biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and cell biology. By integrating protein structure and disorder databases (e.g., AlphaFold DB, DisProt), phase separation repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale interactomes (BioGRID), and clinical genomic datasets (ClinVar, TCGA), we will develop a unified, open-source computational framework. 

Our project will employ Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and multimodal deep learning to construct a predictive multi-scale model of condensate emergence. We aim to (1) define the molecular and thermodynamic rules governing the co-partitioning of multi-component mesoscale assemblies, (2) predict the emergent biophysical states of these condensates under varying cellular stress conditions, and (3) map how disease-associated mutations disrupt mesoscale homeostasis to drive pathological cellular phenotypes, such as neurodegeneration and oncogenesis. 

This community-scale synthesis project uniquely aligns with the NCEMS mission. It generates no new experimental data but rather extracts unprecedented value from existing repositories, a task computationally and intellectually beyond the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will leverage NCEMS resources to facilitate intensive, cross-disciplinary collaboration among researchers from diverse geographic, career-stage, and institutional backgrounds. 

Furthermore, this initiative places a strong emphasis on workforce development and open science. We will integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers as core drivers of the project, providing them with essential cross-training at the critical intersection of AI, big data management, and mesoscale biology. All integrated databases, machine learning pipelines, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented and released through open-access portals following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will not only solve fundamental mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence but also establish innovative analytical strategies and cultivate a data-savvy workforce poised to lead the next generation of molecular and cellular sciences.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence: Synthesizing Multimodal Data to Predict Biomolecular Condensate Dynamics and Cellular Stress Responses via AI-Driven Multiscale Modeling
title_norm: decoding mesoscale emergence synthesizing multimodal data to predict biomolecular condensate dynamics and cellular stress responses via aidriven multiscale modeling
abstract_text: Within mesoscale biology, membraneless organelle formation through liquid liquid phase separation is an essential process driven by intrinsically disordered regions and multivalent interactions producing abundant multi omic and imaging data. Because existing datasets remain isolated in discipline specific formats, current approaches cannot predict condensate behavior or understand how molecular sequences and microenvironments combine to cause irreversible pathological aggregation. To determine the rules governing biomolecular condensate formation and cellular stress resilience, this project will synthesize multiscale data using semantic web technologies and apply geometric deep learning and multiscale graph neural networks to predict phase transitions. The analytical strategy will integrate databases including the Protein Data Bank, DisProt, PRIDE, and BioGRID by developing a standardized ontology and automated metadata extraction to link molecular features directly to cellular imaging metrics. This framework will transition the field from descriptive observation to quantitative prediction, providing a mechanistic explanation for the formation of pathological aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases.
full_text: Mesoscale biology explores liquid liquid phase separation to determine how sequence features and microenvironments drive the formation of irreversible aggregates. Multivalent interactions drive phase separation but isolated multi omic datasets prevent the prediction of aggregates from molecular sequences. This project defines rules for the formation of condensates to enable the quantitative prediction of cellular stress resilience. The team synthesizes public datasets across biological scales and applies artificial intelligence models to predict phase separation thresholds. The methodology relies on semantic web technologies and geometric deep learning and multiscale graph neural networks within Docker containers. A cross disciplinary review validates predictions as physicists assess thermodynamic feasibility and cell biologists verify cellular stress responses. Data sources include DisProt and public metabolomics records alongside the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Image Data Resource. Automated extraction of metadata and semantic web technologies integrate these datasets to link molecular features with imaging metrics. The team resolves the fragmented format of existing databases by developing pipelines for data harmonization to create unified datasets. The proposed study utilizes quarterly hybrid meetings across three phases of data harmonization and artificial intelligence modeling and synthesis. The integration of multiscale data exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory and requires a cross disciplinary collaboration. The team will publish findings in open access journals and share data and code through Zenodo and GitHub. Early career and established researchers from six institutions offer training opportunities for graduate students to lead machine learning hackathons.

abstract_original: The formation of membraneless organelles, such as stress granules and nucleoli, via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represents a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. While massive amounts of experimental data exist detailing the intrinsic disorder of individual proteins, in vitro biophysical properties, and phenomenological cellular imaging, a fundamental gap remains in understanding how molecular sequence grammar and dynamic cellular microenvironments integrate to predictably dictate the emergent material properties of these condensates. A critical, long-standing puzzle in cellular biology is how these finely tuned mesoscale phase transitions occasionally fail, leading to irreversible, aberrant aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Unraveling this multiscale complexity is beyond the computational and domain-specific capabilities of any single research laboratory. It requires synthesizing vast, disparate, and publicly available datasets—spanning transcriptomics, proteomics, structural biophysics (e.g., PDB, DisProt, PRIDE), metabolomics, and high-content cellular imaging (e.g., Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Currently, these multi-omic and multiscale datasets exist in isolated silos, severely limiting our ability to predict how biomolecular condensates assemble, function, and dissolve. To address this, we propose the establishment of the "Condensate Emergence Synthesis Working Group," requiring the unique collaborative infrastructure and support of NCEMS. This transdisciplinary initiative brings together researchers from six geographically diverse academic institutions, deliberately balancing early-career innovators with established pioneers across AI/machine learning, soft matter physics, structural biology, and cellular dynamics. The NCEMS infrastructure is essential not only for the logistical facilitation of intensive, hybrid synthesis meetings critical for cross-pollinating ideas among distinct disciplines, but also for standardizing community-scale data fusion. Using exclusively existing, publicly available data, our team will build an open-source data integration pipeline that harmonizes molecular features (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, valency, post-translational modifications) with spatial proteomics and quantitative live-cell imaging metrics. Building upon this integrated dataset, the Working Group will deploy advanced artificial intelligence methodologies, specifically geometric deep learning and multiscale graph neural networks, to bridge the spatial and temporal gaps between biomolecules and organelles. Our AI-driven models will predict how specific microenvironmental shifts (such as localized pH changes, molecular crowding, and ATP fluctuations) trigger mesoscale phase transitions, mapping the precise trajectory from monomeric proteins to functional mesoscale assemblies, and ultimately to higher-order cellular stress resilience. In strict adherence to community-created open science principles, all harmonized databases, predictive AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be publicly disseminated via open-access repositories (e.g., Zenodo, GitHub) ensuring complete FAIR compliance and reproducibility. Crucially, this working group will serve as an incubator for the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Trainees, including graduate students and postdoctoral fellows, will co-lead analytical sub-groups and participate in specialized cross-disciplinary hackathons focused on machine learning in the biosciences. By synthesizing siloed data to map the emergence of mesoscale properties, this project will answer novel questions about subcellular organization, pioneer innovative computational strategies, and provide an unparalleled collaborative training environment.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence in Biomolecular Condensates: A Multi-Omic Synthesis and AI-Driven Framework for Predicting Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation Dynamics
title_norm: decoding mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates a multiomic synthesis and aidriven framework for predicting liquidliquid phase separation dynamics
abstract_text: This research examines mesoscale emergence in cellular biology, specifically biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation, where individual molecular interactions generate emergent properties including viscoelasticity and multi phase architecture. However, understanding how isolated molecular components combine to produce these emergent biophysical characteristics at the mesoscale remains incomplete due to the disciplinary isolation of existing datasets. To identify the rules governing mesoscale emergence by linking microscale molecular inputs to mesoscale biophysical properties, this secondary data synthesis project will deploy MesoPhaser AI, an analytical framework utilizing multimodal graph neural networks and representation learning. Diverse databases including LLPSDB, AlphaFold DB, and BioGRID will be integrated into a knowledge graph where protein and RNA nodes are connected by edges representing experimentally validated interactions, affinities, and spatial proximities. This framework will elucidate the rules governing mesoscale emergence, providing critical insights into cellular organization mechanisms and abnormal phase transitions associated with neurodegenerative diseases and cancers.
full_text: This project investigates biomolecular condensates to determine how molecular properties combine and produce emergent biophysical characteristics at the mesoscale. The interactions causing phase separation are known but understanding of emergent properties remains incomplete across isolated disciplinary datasets. The proposed study identifies rules of mesoscale emergence to explain cellular organization and abnormal phase transitions in disease. This secondary data synthesis project uses data harmonization and the development of artificial intelligence architectures without generating experimental data. The MesoPhaser-AI framework applies multimodal graph neural networks and representation learning to process sequence and multi omics data. The team will validate results by predicting phase separation behavior of untested protein sequences using structural and network features. The project utilizes multiple datasets including AlphaFold DB and BioGRID and STRING and the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The team will integrate these sources by constructing a multi relational knowledge graph of proteins and their interactions. Disciplinary fragmentation of existing biological datasets will be mitigated by harmonizing all modalities into a single knowledge graph. The project milestones include data harmonization and construction of knowledge graphs followed by development of the artificial intelligence model. A cross disciplinary collaboration is required because linking physics to cellular phenotypes exceeds the expertise of any single laboratory. The team will deposit data in public repositories and share code on GitHub and publish open access findings. The diverse team of biologists and network theorists provides deep learning training for graduate students and postdoctoral scholars.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. Bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, these dynamic, membraneless compartments orchestrate vital processes ranging from gene regulation to stress response. While individual molecular interactions driving LLPS are increasingly understood, a fundamental, long-standing puzzle remains: how do diverse, dynamic molecular properties collectively give rise to the emergent biophysical characteristics of condensates—such as viscoelasticity, multi-phase architecture, and compositional specificity—at the mesoscale? Despite the explosion of publicly available data encompassing protein sequences, structural ensembles, multi-omic interaction networks, and high-resolution live-cell imaging, these datasets remain largely siloed. To address this, we propose the MesoCondensate Synthesis Working Group to map the principles of mesoscale emergence by integrating massive, publicly available, yet disparate biological datasets. In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, no new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will synthesize data from specialized phase separation databases (e.g., LLPSDB, CD-Code), global structural repositories (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-throughput interactomics (BioGRID, IntAct), transcriptomics, and open-source cellular imaging archives. Our transdisciplinary team—comprising structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, network theorists, and artificial intelligence experts across varied career stages and institutional contexts—will develop a novel analytical framework named MesoPhaser-AI. Using advanced multimodal deep learning, including graph neural networks, we will synthesize these multiscale datasets to decipher the hidden grammar of mesoscale emergence. Specifically, MesoPhaser-AI will predict how fundamental biomolecular features (intrinsically disordered regions, valency, electrostatic networks) integrate under varying thermodynamic and physiological conditions to yield emergent mesoscale properties. This community-scale synthesis requires the unique infrastructure and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS; synthesizing atomistic physics with cellular phenotypes is beyond the computational and intellectual scope of any single laboratory. The Working Group will stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration by bringing together domain experts who traditionally do not intersect, fostering novel perspectives on mesoscale biophysics. Crucially, this project champions Open Science and workforce development. All synthesized databases, knowledge graphs, and MesoPhaser-AI source code will be released publicly under FAIR and open-source licenses, establishing a gold-standard community resource. Furthermore, the Working Group will host Data-to-Emergence bootcamps and synthesis hackathons tailored for trainees (graduate students and postdoctoral scholars). These initiatives will equip the next generation of scientists with cutting-edge skills in AI, data integration, and reproducible team science. By unifying disjointed molecular data into a cohesive predictive model of mesoscale emergence, this project will transform our understanding of subcellular organization, unlocking new paradigms for how life organizes itself between the scale of molecules and whole cells.

title: Deciphering the Grammar of Mesoscale Emergence: An AI-Driven Synthesis of Multi-Omic and Biophysical Data to Predict Biomolecular Condensate Dynamics and Cellular Outcomes
title_norm: deciphering the grammar of mesoscale emergence an aidriven synthesis of multiomic and biophysical data to predict biomolecular condensate dynamics and cellular outcomes
abstract_text: The research domain investigates biomolecular condensates formed by liquid liquid phase separation and intrinsically disordered proteins, which drive critical mesoscale collective behaviors governing vital biological processes like cellular stress responses. Traditional reductionist models fail to explain collective molecular behaviors because unintegrated datasets obscure how specific sequence features determine condensate biophysical properties and downstream cellular stress adaptation. The project will achieve its primary objective by building a multiscale knowledge graph and applying sequence to function large language models, graph neural networks, and deep learning regressors to predict condensate properties and correlate them with multiomic stress profiles. Semantic web technologies and biological ontologies will integrate databases including PhaSepDB, DisProt, the Protein Data Bank, and the Gene Expression Omnibus into a unified knowledge graph connecting biomolecules, condensates, and phenotypes through relational edges. This predictive computational framework will transition the field beyond descriptive models by identifying the fundamental rules that connect molecular interactions directly to cellular stress response outcomes.
full_text: This project investigates how sequences of intrinsically disordered proteins determine properties of biomolecular condensates and control stress adaptation. Large datasets exist for protein interactions and stress responses but unintegrated data impede understanding of collective mesoscale behaviors. The primary objective builds a predictive multiscale knowledge graph to link molecular interactions with cellular outcomes using artificial intelligence. The analytical strategy constructs a knowledge graph from public databases to correlate predicted condensate behaviors with multi omic stress profiles. Key analytical methods apply biological ontologies and graph neural networks alongside large language models (ESM-2) and deep learning regressors. Molecular biologists on the team will independently validate the biological plausibility of predictions from the machine learning models. The study incorporates structural and genomic data from several public repositories including AlphaFold-DB and the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Semantic web technologies will integrate these distinct datasets into a unified knowledge graph through the application of biological ontologies. Graph nodes representing structural domains and condensates will connect via relational edges that indicate molecular interactions and cellular regulation. The massive scale of the proposed computational modeling and data synthesis exceeds the operational capacity of any single laboratory. This broad scope necessitates a cross disciplinary collaboration between data scientists for integration and biophysicists for mapping of ontologies. The team will share data on public repositories and publish source code in open access formats using software containers. Artificial intelligence experts and biologists will jointly train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers through data science bootcamps and hackathons.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergence at the mesoscale. Bridging the critical gap between individual interacting biomolecules and higher-order cellular organization, these membraneless organelles dynamically partition proteins and nucleic acids to regulate essential cellular outcomes, from stress adaptation to gene expression. Despite an explosion of publicly available data characterizing intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, and phenotypic stress responses, a fundamental, long-standing puzzle remains: How do atomic and molecular-level 'grammars' predictably encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates, and how do these mesoscale structures subsequently dictate macroscopic cellular phenotypes? Solving this requires a scale of data synthesis and computational modeling far beyond the capability of any individual laboratory.

This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the rules of mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates using artificial intelligence (AI) and multi-scale data integration. By uniting a diverse, transdisciplinary team of biophysicists, computational biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and cell biologists from multiple institutions across varying research levels, we will integrate heterogeneous public datasets. Specifically, we will synthesize biophysical condensate databases (e.g., PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, DisProt), multi-omic profiles from GEO and PRIDE (transcriptomics and proteomics under cellular stress), and structural interactome data (AlphaFold-DB, PDB). We will not generate new experimental data; instead, we will leverage these vast repositories to develop innovative AI architectures, including sequence-to-function Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs).

Our project has three distinct aims: (1) Synthesize molecular and biophysical datasets to construct a unified knowledge graph of condensate-forming proteins and their emergent physicochemical properties (e.g., viscosity, critical concentration thresholds). (2) Develop AI-driven analytical strategies to predict mesoscale condensate emergence based solely on input molecular features and environmental cellular conditions. (3) Map these emergent mesoscale properties to higher-order cellular outcomes by integrating stress-response transcriptomic and proteomic data, uncovering how condensate dynamics drive cellular survival and adaptation.

Crucially, this Working Group relies on the unique infrastructure and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS to foster cross-disciplinary synergy. The project will actively train the next generation of data-savvy scientists by embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a collaborative, team-science environment. Trainees will lead specific cross-disciplinary integration tasks and participate in data-science bootcamps, acquiring highly sought-after skills at the intersection of AI and biology. Furthermore, we are deeply committed to Open Science principles; all curated datasets, predictive models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available to the community via open-access repositories (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) using reproducible workflows. Ultimately, this synthesis will not only resolve critical mysteries regarding mesoscale biological organization but will also provide the broader scientific community with groundbreaking open-source tools to predict emergent cellular phenomena.

title: Unveiling the Rules of Mesoscale Emergence: A Multi-Omic Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Dynamics and Cellular Fate
title_norm: unveiling the rules of mesoscale emergence a multiomic synthesis of biomolecular condensate dynamics and cellular fate
abstract_text: Research on biomolecular condensates formed via liquid liquid phase separation is critical, as abundant yet isolated experimental data prevents a comprehensive understanding of mesoscale emergent properties across varying metabolic states. The field currently lacks a universal sequence grammar, defined biophysical parameters, and known thermodynamic thresholds necessary to understand and predict condensate formation and macro cellular behavior. This computational synthesis project will determine how intrinsically disordered regions dictate condensate rheology and identify phase transition thresholds by applying protein language models, percolation theory, and Graph Attention Networks to build MesoPredict. The project will integrate PDB, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, BioGRID, PRIDE, Human Protein Atlas, and Image Data Resource into a unified knowledge graph featuring molecular entities as nodes and dynamic interactions as edges. This predictive model will shift the domain toward systems level prediction of condensate behavior, providing a crucial framework for understanding cellular stress responses, cancer, and neurodegenerative disorders.
full_text: The research explores biomolecular condensates formed via liquid liquid phase separation to identify missing thermodynamic thresholds and sequence grammar. Abundant experimental data on individual condensates remain isolated and prevent comprehensive understanding of emergence across varied molecular compositions. This study questions how molecular domains dictate condensate rheology to enable systems level prediction for cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. This computational synthesis project harmonizes structural and biophysical data into a multi dimensional knowledge graph for machine learning models. The team applies dynamic network analysis and protein language models like ESM-2 to train Graph Attention Networks called MesoPredict. The predictive models will undergo retrospective analysis using held out spatial imaging data to infer cellular localization and phenotypes. The project incorporates data from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and the Human Protein Atlas alongside the Image Data Resource. The team will integrate these resources into a unified knowledge graph to link disparate biophysical attributes and cellular properties. This synthesized graph architecture represents molecular entities as nodes and defines their dynamic interactions as connecting network edges. The project advances through four methodological phases for data harmonization and model development supported by regular hackathons and meetings. Integrating multi omic data with artificial intelligence requires cross disciplinary expertise in structural biology and machine learning across multiple laboratories. The team will publish results in open access journals and share open source algorithms on GitHub using software containers. The fifteen member working group pairs senior computational scientists with early career biologists to provide extensive cross disciplinary training.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in biology. These dynamic, non-membrane-bound organelles assemble from individual macromolecules to exhibit entirely new collective properties—such as tunable viscosity, selective permeability, and spatially restricted biochemical reactions. They effectively bridge the gap between single biomolecules and higher-order cellular phenotypes. Despite an explosion of single-lab experimental studies, the universal sequence grammar, biophysical parameters, and thermodynamic thresholds governing this mesoscale emergence across space and time remain a long-standing puzzle. Furthermore, predicting how these mesoscale properties dictate macro-cellular behaviors, such as survival mechanisms during cellular stress, is currently beyond the computational and analytical capacity of any individual research group.

To address this critical gap, we propose the Working Group 'Condensome-AI', a transdisciplinary team comprising structural biologists, biophysicists, machine learning experts, and cell biologists. We will leverage artificial intelligence and advanced data science methodologies to synthesize massive, publicly available, yet currently siloed datasets. Specifically, we will integrate biophysical droplet databases (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold, PDB), global interactome datasets (BioGRID, PRIDE), and high-throughput cellular imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Image Data Resource). In strict adherence to NCEMS guidelines, this project will generate no new experimental data. Instead, it relies entirely on community-scale synthesis to construct a unified, predictive framework for mesoscale emergence.

Our project pursues three core scientific objectives: (1) Answer the novel question of how combinations of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and structured RNA-binding domains synergize to govern emergent rheological properties across different metabolic states; (2) Solve the long-standing mystery of how shifts in environmental energy and molecular composition trigger the sudden spatial and temporal appearance of these mesoscale structures; and (3) Develop 'MesoPredict,' an innovative, AI-driven analytical pipeline utilizing graph neural networks to predict condensate composition and subsequent cellular impacts directly from omics profiles.

Executing this synthesis requires the unique infrastructure and collaborative support of NCEMS. By bringing together diverse talent from distinct geographic locations and institutional tiers, we will foster a research environment impossible within traditional single-discipline grants. Our partnership emphasizes diversity and mentorship, deliberately pairing senior computational scientists with biology-focused graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through specialized computational bootcamps and collaborative working group sessions, we will actively train a data-savvy, next-generation workforce capable of navigating the intersection of AI and biological emergence.

Finally, our Working Group is deeply committed to rigorous open science practices. All synthesized datasets, AI/ML models, analytical workflows, and resultant code will be heavily documented, open-source, and distributed via community repositories like Zenodo and GitHub following FAIR data principles. By deciphering the complex language of mesoscale condensate emergence, this NCEMS-supported synthesis will fundamentally advance our understanding of cellular organization and provide a transformative, accessible resource for the entire molecular and cellular biosciences community.

title: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Structural Data to Decode the Emergent Rules of Biomolecular Condensate Formation at the Cellular Mesoscale
title_norm: synthesizing multiomic and structural data to decode the emergent rules of biomolecular condensate formation at the cellular mesoscale
abstract_text: Within mesoscale cellular biology, biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation represent critical structures that arise from multivalent interactions among hundreds of molecular species in fluctuating cellular environments. Because existing structural and omics data remain fragmented, the field lacks understanding regarding how dynamically changing protein and nucleic acid combinations predictably self assemble across varying cellular contexts. To predict in vivo threshold concentrations and model how sequence variations alter biophysical properties, this computational project will construct state dependent interactomes utilizing multi layer graph neural networks and biological large language models. The project will synthesize datasets from the Protein Data Bank, Gene Expression Omnibus, and STRING by weighting documented interaction edges dynamically using transcriptomic and proteomic co expression levels. Ultimately, this research will produce predictive models of condensate formation that account for global cellular states, providing crucial frameworks for understanding phase separation under true in vivo conditions.
full_text: This project explores mesoscale cellular biology to uncover how dynamic molecules predictably assemble into biomolecular condensates across varying contexts. Current knowledge details isolated structures but understanding remains incomplete because multi omics data are fragmented across sub disciplines. The primary question investigates environmental triggers of phase separation to build novel predictive models of global cellular states. The proposed study uses a purely computational design featuring a three phase pipeline for synthesis of multi modal data. Key methods involve a unified ontology alongside multi layer graph neural networks (GNNs) and large language models like ESM-2. The team will validate results through cross validation of artificial intelligence models using diverse experimental contexts from public data. Primary data sources include the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold Database alongside interaction repositories like BioGRID and STRING. The synthesis integrates distinct datasets by constructing graph neural networks with dynamic edge weights representing levels of co expression. Standard interaction networks lack state specific context but the team will mitigate this limitation using dynamic edge weights. The proposed milestones include complete harmonization of data and construction of interactomes prior to prediction of mesoscale emergence. This ambitious scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the required artificial intelligence pipelines exceed the expertise of single laboratories. The researchers will share synthesized datasets on public repositories and publish open source artificial intelligence models with documentation. The cross disciplinary team includes machine learning scientists and computational biophysicists to provide cross training for graduate students.

Because existing structural and omics data remain fragmented, the field lacks understanding regarding how dynamically changing protein and nucleic acid combinations predictably self assemble across varying cellular contexts. To predict in vivo threshold concentrations and model how sequence variations alter biophysical properties, this computational project will construct state dependent interactomes utilizing multi layer graph neural networks and biological large language models. The project will synthesize datasets from the Protein Data Bank, Gene Expression Omnibus, and STRING by weighting documented interaction edges dynamically using transcriptomic and proteomic co expression levels. Ultimately, this research will produce predictive models of condensate formation that account for global cellular states, providing crucial frameworks for understanding phase separation under true in vivo conditions.
abstract_original:
The emergence of mesoscale structures from nanoscale molecular interactions represents a fundamental frontier in the cellular biosciences. Among the most enigmatic of these phenomena are biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation. While condensates are critical for compartmentalizing cellular processes and mediating stress responses, a long-standing puzzle remains: how do specific, dynamically changing combinations of proteins and nucleic acids predictably self-assemble into mesoscale structures with distinct biophysical properties, and how do these emergent properties dictate higher-order cellular phenotypes? Understanding this mesoscale emergence requires shifting from reductionist studies of individual proteins to a holistic, systems-level integration of molecular data.

To address this, we propose the establishment of the Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group, a transdisciplinary initiative dedicated to decoding the rules governing emergent condensate formation. Crucially, this project will generate no new experimental data; instead, it will leverage the unprecedented wealth of publicly available multi-modal data. We will synthesize and integrate sequence and AI-predicted structural features (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-throughput transcriptomic and proteomic data mapping varied cellular states (GEO, PRIDE), molecular interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING), and curated phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE).

Integrating these disparate, vast datasets to predict mesoscale physical chemistry is well beyond the computational and biological capabilities of any single laboratory, making NCEMS support essential. Our Working Group unites diverse experts—machine learning scientists, computational biophysicists, structural biologists, and molecular geneticists—spanning R1 institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions (PUIs), and historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs). This inclusive collaboration guarantees a broad geographic and career-stage distribution, ensuring diverse scientific perspectives.

Methodologically, we will utilize advanced artificial intelligence and data science techniques, specifically multi-layer graph neural networks (GNNs) and large language models adapted for proteins, to map state-dependent molecular interactomes. By synthesizing these datasets, we aim to answer novel questions: Can we predict the threshold concentrations and environmental triggers required for phase separation in vivo across varying cellular stress states? How do subtle genetic variations propagate through interaction networks to alter the emergent biophysical properties of these mesoscale droplets?

In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, AI models, and analysis pipelines will be shared publicly via specialized open-science repositories, establishing gold-standard, reproducible workflows for the scientific community. Furthermore, this project strongly emphasizes training the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be fully integrated into the Working Group as co-leads on data synthesis efforts. Through dedicated cross-training in theoretical biophysics and machine learning, and by hosting annual open-science hackathons, we will equip the next generation of scientists with the transdisciplinary skills required to navigate the future of molecular and cellular biology. By mapping the transition from molecular components to mesoscale emergence, this synthesis project will provide unprecedented predictive insights into cellular organization, directly advancing the foundational mission of NCEMS.

abstract_original: The mesoscale organization of the cell, characterized by the emergence of membraneless biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), fundamentally governs spatial organization, biochemical reaction rates, and cellular adaptation. While biomolecules are well-characterized and cellular phenotypes broadly mapped, the mesoscale—the critical nexus where molecular rules translate into subcellular and cellular properties—remains poorly understood. Despite a recent explosion of publicly available data on intrinsically disordered proteins, phase separation, and high-content cellular imaging, the overarching principles governing how molecular interactions scale to emergent properties like condensate stoichiometry, viscoelasticity, and spatial dynamics remain a long-standing puzzle. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project leveraging artificial intelligence and advanced data science to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates across composition, space, and time. Conforming to the NCEMS mandate, this project will generate no new experimental data. Instead, it will synthesize massive, disparate, publicly available datasets, including structural predictions (AlphaFold, DisProt), proteomics and transcriptomics (PRIDE, GEO), specialized condensate repositories (LLPSDB, PhaSePro), and multi-channel cellular imaging datasets (Cell Painting from the Broad Bioimage Benchmark Collection). Integrating these distinct data types across scales requires a transdisciplinary approach that significantly exceeds the computational and biological expertise of any single laboratory. To address this challenge, our geographically and institutionally diverse team of biophysicists, computational biologists, structural biochemists, and AI experts will develop novel multimodal machine learning frameworks. Specifically, we will deploy spatially-aware graph neural networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning to harmonize molecular, mesoscale, and phenotypic data. Our key scientific objectives are to: (1) identify predictive sequence and structural motifs that drive condition-specific mesoscale condensate assembly; (2) map how variations in cellular energy and environmental stress alter the compositional flow of information within these mesoscale hubs; and (3) predict how these mesoscale changes cascade into observable cellular-level phenotypes, such as stress granule formation or transcriptional pausing. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative partnership will deliberately tap diverse new talent, integrating principal investigators from R1 universities with researchers from minority-serving institutions (MSIs) to ensure a wide array of scientific perspectives. Furthermore, we are deeply committed to training the future data-savvy workforce. Trainees, including graduate students and postdocs, will co-lead the data harmonization efforts through cross-institutional 'Synthesis Hackathons,' receiving rigorous training in reproducible team science, cloud computing, and advanced AI methodologies. Adhering strictly to Open Science principles, all synthesized databases, trained AI models, and analytical pipelines will be distributed via open-access platforms following FAIR data standards. Ultimately, this community-scale synthesis will answer fundamental questions regarding mesoscale emergence, transforming isolated public datasets into a predictive, holistic atlas of cellular organization while establishing innovative analytical strategies for the broader molecular biosciences community.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence: Synthesizing Structural, Proteomic, and Transcriptomic Data to Uncover Principles of Biomolecular Condensation
title_norm: decoding mesoscale emergence synthesizing structural proteomic and transcriptomic data to uncover principles of biomolecular condensation
abstract_text: In molecular and cellular biology, the formation of stress induced biomolecular condensates via liquid liquid phase separation plays a crucial role in mediating stress adaptation and driving neurodegenerative diseases. Because existing research isolates molecular studies from macroscopic observations, researchers currently lack a unified understanding of how atomistic properties scale up to govern condensate assembly and biophysical thresholds. To map stress granule interactions and predict mutation driven disruptions, this project will harmonize multiscale public data and apply graph neural networks, large language models, and coarse grained molecular dynamics to develop predictive thermodynamic models. Data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, PRIDE, and ClinVar will be integrated by standardizing structural, proteomic, and transcriptomic information into a mathematical graph defining biological components as nodes and energy potentials as edges. This project will establish a predictive computational framework linking molecular biophysics to cellular physiology, enabling researchers to screen disease associated mutations for structural disruptions without requiring new physical experiments.
full_text: This project examines cellular biology to understand how atomistic properties govern the assembly of stress induced biomolecular condensates. Biomolecular condensates mediate adaptation to stress and disease but current studies rely on isolated and unintegrated public datasets. The proposed study maps energetic interactions of stress granules to build a predictive framework for disease associated mutations. This project uses public data to harmonize multiscale databases and applies artificial intelligence to build predictive thermodynamic models. The team employs graph neural networks and coarse grained molecular dynamics alongside large language models such as ESM-2. The predictive framework undergoes computational validation against hold out datasets to test predictions of abnormal transitions in phase. The project utilizes public datasets from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and IntAct and ClinVar and the Human Cell Atlas. The team integrates structural and proteomic data into a mathematical graph architecture by defining biological components as nodes. Physical interactions and energy potentials act as edges to connect the distinct nodes within this unified mathematical graph. The successful execution of this complex project requires the integration of molecular biophysics with outcomes in cellular physiology. This integration necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration combining specialized expertise across polymer physics and structural biology and machine learning. The team deposits harmonized datasets into Zenodo and distributes code via GitHub to ensure open access to findings. The collaborative team includes postdocs and graduate students who receive cross disciplinary training in artificial intelligence through bootcamps.

abstract_original: Biological systems exhibit profound emergent properties at the mesoscale, where dynamic, transient interactions between individual biomolecules give rise to higher-order functional structures like biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles. Despite their critical roles in cellular regulation, stress response, and neurodegenerative diseases, the fundamental biophysical rules governing how these mesoscale properties emerge from atomistic and molecular features remain a long-standing puzzle. This project proposes a community-scale synthesis to elucidate the multiscale principles of stress-induced biomolecular condensation. By leveraging the vast, untapped wealth of publicly available structural, proteomic, and transcriptomic data, we aim to uncover the physical, spatial, and energetic drivers of mesoscale phase separation without generating any new experimental data. Our transdisciplinary Working Group will integrate distinct, heterogeneous public datasets—including AlphaFold-predicted and experimentally derived protein structures (PDB, EMDB), high-throughput interaction and stress-response proteomics (PRIDE, IntAct), and spatial and single-cell transcriptomics (GEO, Human Cell Atlas). We will utilize advanced artificial intelligence, specifically graph neural networks (GNNs) and large language models (LLMs) adapted for biological sequences, alongside multiscale physical modeling to bridge the gap between molecular-level properties (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, valency, RNA-binding motifs) and cellular-level outcomes (e.g., stress granule assembly and disassembly). This synthesis demands a transdisciplinary effort far beyond the capabilities of a single laboratory. Our Working Group unites polymer physicists, structural biologists, artificial intelligence experts, and cellular physiologists representing a wide array of geographic locations, career stages, and institutional classifications. NCEMS support is absolutely essential to provide the computational infrastructure, collaborative networking, and data-science scaffolding required to harmonize these massive, multi-scale databases into a unified, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. By synthesizing these disparate data layers, the Working Group will address three compelling objectives: (1) map the dynamic "mesoscale interactome" of stress granules across different temporal cellular states and energy landscapes; (2) deploy machine learning models to identify the emergent biophysical and informational thresholds that trigger mesoscale condensation; and (3) predict how genetic mutations or transcriptomic shifts perturb these emergent structures, linking molecular alterations to cellular pathogenesis. Furthermore, this project is deeply committed to Open Science and the cultivation of a data-savvy workforce. All harmonized datasets, AI model architectures, and analysis pipelines will be released publicly through open-access repositories following FAIR data principles and reproducible workflows. To train the next generation, the Working Group will host specialized, hands-on data bootcamps for involved graduate students and postdoctoral scholars, providing them with unparalleled cross-training at the intersection of machine learning, open science practices, and molecular biology. By mapping the critical mesoscale space between biomolecules and organelles, this project will solve a major puzzle in molecular emergence, create innovative analytical strategies, and establish a scalable, open-source paradigm for future biological synthesis.

abstract_original: The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties—emergence—is a defining feature of the molecular and cellular biosciences. At the mesoscale, one of the most profound unresolved emergent phenomena is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, membraneless compartments bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and functional subcellular organelles, playing critical roles in stress response, gene regulation, and disease pathogenesis. Despite a wealth of isolated molecular, structural, and phenotypic datasets, the overarching principles governing how atomic-level interactions scale to emergent mesoscale condensate properties remain largely elusive. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the spatiotemporal emergence of biomolecular condensates by integrating massive, disparate, publicly available datasets. We will synthesize structural data (AlphaFold, PDB), high-throughput interactomics (BioGRID, STRING), spatial transcriptomics and proteomics, and thousands of publicly deposited live-cell super-resolution microscopy datasets (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Because this undertaking vastly exceeds the computational and domain expertise of any single laboratory, it necessitates the transdisciplinary environment and resources uniquely provided by NCEMS. To solve this long-standing puzzle, our team of biophysicists, computational biologists, AI specialists, and cell biologists will employ advanced multimodal artificial intelligence and data science techniques. Specifically, we will develop novel Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to map multi-valent molecular interaction networks and integrate them with deep learning-based image analysis models capable of extracting biophysical mesoscale properties (e.g., viscoelasticity, droplet fusion rates) from archived imaging data. By synthesizing these scales, we will answer a critical, novel question: How do sequence-level variations and dynamic cellular conditions reliably encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates? Beyond scientific discovery, this Working Group is designed to foster a diverse, collaborative scientific community and train the future data-savvy workforce. Our team bridges varying career stages and geographical locations, integrating trainees (graduate students and postdoctoral fellows) directly into the core analytical pipeline. Trainees will benefit from dedicated mentorship, cross-disciplinary cross-training, and rigorous instruction in cloud computing, data synthesis, and machine learning. Furthermore, this project adheres strictly to Open Science principles. All aggregated datasets, curated metadata, trained AI models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available via public repositories, utilizing reproducible workflows (e.g., Jupyter Notebooks, Docker containers) to ensure maximum utility for the broader scientific community. Ultimately, this synthesis will yield a unified framework for mesoscale emergence, transforming isolated molecular observations into a holistic understanding of subcellular organization while establishing innovative analytical paradigms for future NCEMS initiatives.

Bridging the critical gap between individual macromolecules and complex cellular organelles, these membraneless compartments orchestrate vital processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress response. (2) Develop and train novel geometric deep learning models to predict emergent mesoscale physical properties—such as condensate liquidity, valency, and viscoelasticity—directly from these synthesized omics and structural data. The project will evaluate evolutionary conservation and identify stress induced molecular patterns by applying transformer based large language models and multimodal Graph Neural Networks to map single molecule features to mesoscale properties and cellular outcomes. abstract_original: The unexpected appearance of higher-order biological properties from fundamental molecular interactions is most strikingly exemplified at the mesoscale, the critical nexus between individual biomolecules and functional organelles. Biomolecular condensates, which form via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a paradigm-shifting emergent property at this scale, regulating essential cellular outcomes ranging from gene expression to stress adaptation. Despite an explosion of publicly available data characterizing intrinsically disordered proteins, biophysical phase boundaries, and cellular phenotypes, these datasets remain largely siloed. Consequently, a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences persists: How do the physicochemical properties and interaction networks of individual macromolecules predictably scale to dictate emergent mesoscale condensate dynamics and their subsequent cellular functions? To solve this, we propose the Predictive Rules of Emergent Condensates (PREC) Working Group. This transdisciplinary team will leverage AI and data science to synthesize existing, publicly available datasets spanning from the molecular to the phenotypic level. Our project strictly utilizes existing data, integrating biomolecular sequences and structural predictions from DisProt and the AlphaFold Database, specialized biophysical LLPS databases like PhaSePro and CD-CODE, and systems-level multi-omics and high-content imaging repositories such as the Human Protein Atlas and GEO. Integrating these disparate, multi-scale data sources to decode mesoscale emergence goes far beyond the capabilities of any single research lab, requiring the unique collaborative infrastructure and support provided by NCEMS. The PREC Working Group will bring together a diverse cohort of biophysicists, molecular biologists, AI researchers, and computational data scientists. By bridging these historically distinct fields, we will develop innovative analytical strategies, including multimodal Graph Neural Networks and transformer-based machine learning architectures. These models will be designed to map the multi-dimensional feature space of single molecules to the emergent properties of mesoscale condensates—such as rheology, stoichiometry, and spatiotemporal organization—and ultimately to their impact on subcellular and cellular health. Our synthesis project is driven by three core scientific objectives: First, to answer novel questions regarding the evolutionary conservation and divergence of condensate-driven emergent properties across different cellular lineages. Second, to solve the puzzle of how specific environmental stressors trigger widespread, synchronized mesoscale phase transitions by identifying hidden molecular grammars. Third, to develop and openly distribute a predictive algorithmic framework that maps molecular properties to mesoscale emergence. In strict adherence to open science principles, all curated datasets, AI models, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented and made publicly available via community-standard repositories like GitHub and Zenodo to ensure complete reproducibility. Furthermore, this project serves as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. We will actively recruit early-career researchers, graduate students, and postdocs from underrepresented backgrounds, providing them with unparalleled cross-training in molecular biophysics and advanced AI data science techniques. By synthesizing massive public datasets through a collaborative, community-scale effort, the PREC Working Group will illuminate the foundational rules of mesoscale emergence, transforming our understanding of cellular organization and establishing new computational paradigms for the biosciences.
